site.name: Grant C Anthony
site.about:
I have been taking photographs, on and off, for close to thirty years. It started with my father-in-law, whose influence got me going.

My wife is also a keen photographer, and an exceptionally good one. We travel together in our camper van, and on city breaks and photography holidays.

What I go out for is the experience: being in the moment, in the flow, where time gets lost. I keep my editing light. That side is my wife's passion more than mine.

In my bag: a Canon EOS R5 with 16-35, 24-70, 70-200 and 100-400 zooms, and a nifty fifty. Kase filters. A Three Legged Thing Winston and Corey, a Peak Design carbon-fibre tripod for cities, and a Leica D-Lux 8: truly pocket-sized, with a brilliant monochrome mode, which makes it great for street.
site.learnIntro: What I have learned in close to thirty years behind a camera, about light, composition and the craft.

glossary.def: A doubling or halving of the light. One stop brighter lets in twice as much light; one stop darker lets in half.
The adjustable opening in the lens. It controls how much light gets in and how much of the scene is sharp.
How aperture is written, such as f/2.8 or f/16. A smaller number means a bigger opening and more light.
How long the sensor is exposed to light, such as 1/250 s or 2 s. Fast speeds freeze motion; slow ones blur it.
How much the camera amplifies the signal from the sensor. Higher ISO brightens the image but adds grain.
How much of the scene, front to back, looks acceptably sharp. Smaller apertures and greater distance give more.
The lens setting in millimetres. Shorter (such as 16 mm) takes in a wide view; longer (such as 400 mm) magnifies a small part of it.
Neutral density filter. Dark glass that cuts the light evenly without changing its colour, so you can use slower shutter speeds.
A filter you rotate to cut reflected glare. It deepens blue skies and removes shine from water and wet leaves.
A filter that is dark at one end and clear at the other, used to hold back a bright sky.
A file holding everything the sensor recorded, without the camera's processing. It looks flat but gives the most room to edit.
The setting that makes white look white under different light, from warm tungsten to cool shade.
Taking several frames of the same scene at different exposures, to choose from or blend later.
Softening of the whole image at very small apertures, usually noticeable beyond about f/16.
Roughly the hour after sunrise and before sunset, when low sun gives warm, soft, directional light.
The time when the sun is just below the horizon, before sunrise or after sunset, and the sky turns deep blue.
Taking several frames focused at different distances and blending them so the whole subject is sharp.
The way distant objects look closer together in a telephoto photograph. It comes from standing far away, not from the lens itself.
The empty area around a subject. It gives the subject room and sets the mood.
The way parallel vertical lines appear to lean together when the camera is tilted up at a building.
A system in the lens or camera that reduces blur from hand shake. Turn it off on a tripod.
A lens that can shift the image up or down without tilting the camera, keeping verticals straight.

photos.title: Lofoten Boat
photos.description: Autumn in Lofoten. A small boat sits on still water below a mountain with cloud drifting across its shoulder. Orange trees line the far shore, and in the foreground golden seaweed and mossy rocks run down to the water, so the colour carries from front to back under a grey sky.

photos.title: Wall of Fame
photos.description: The Wall of Fame on Mathew Street, Liverpool, where each brick carries the name of an act that played the Cavern Club. In one stretch you get Chuck Berry, Howlin' Wolf, The Kinks, Eric Clapton, Elton John, The Stranglers and Oasis, with visitors' own names scratched in between. Shooting along the wall at an angle makes it run on and on, which is what it feels like reading it.

photos.title: Uttakleiv beach
photos.description: Uttakleiv beach, Lofoten, Norway. During a one-second exposure the outgoing waves smooth into soft trails around the rocks, while the sand stays sharp. Across the bay, low sun picks out the jagged ridge under a heavy sky.

photos.title: Rotten
photos.description: A painted portrait of Johnny Rotten on a pair of doors in Liverpool, Sex Pistols logo and all, with paint running down and names scratched into the stone either side.

photos.title: Lindisfarne
photos.description: Lindisfarne Castle stands on its rocky crag on Holy Island, Northumberland, a tidal island cut off from the mainland twice a day when the causeway floods. A two-second exposure blurs the cloud and the water at the shore, while the pebbles in the foreground stay sharp and lead the eye up to the castle.

photos.title: Fab4 and Liver Birds
photos.description: The Beatles stride along Liverpool's Pier Head, with a Liver Bird watching from the top of the Royal Liver Building.

photos.title: Reflections and Shadows
photos.description: Storsandnes beach, Lofoten, Norway. Low sun lights the mountains in warm gold, while the sky above stays grey and blue. As the waves pull back, the wet sand turns into a mirror, so the peaks appear twice: once in the light and once in the reflection.

photos.title: The Caledonian Railway Bridge
photos.description: The Caledonian Railway Bridge carries trains over the Clyde into Glasgow Central. From the water's edge you see what most people crossing it never do: rows of riveted arches, stone piers rising out of the river, and the whole structure running off into the distance. Most people only notice it as a sound overhead.

photos.title: Luskentyre ICM
photos.description: Luskentyre, on the Isle of Harris, is known for its pale sand and clear, turquoise water. Here the camera was swept sideways through a quarter-second exposure, so the detail gives way to the colours: sand, sea, the hills across the water and a clear blue sky, laid down in long horizontal strokes.

photos.title: Spikey
photos.description: Iron spikes set into a ledge in Liverpool, there to stop pigeons landing. Up close, in black and white, they look more like something from a dark fairy tale.

photos.title: South Uist
photos.description: South Uist, in the Outer Hebrides. A small stone building on the machair edge, its roof facing the hills and the sea loch beyond. Built from the same rock that's scattered across the grass around it, so it looks as if it grew there.

photos.title: Reflections of Bath
photos.description: The Great Bath at the Roman Baths, the heart of the bathing complex the Romans built around Bath's hot springs. With the water still, the colonnade and Bath Abbey's tower are mirrored almost perfectly, and black and white keeps the attention on the stone, the cloud and the reflection.

photos.title: Speicherstadt balconies
photos.description: The Speicherstadt, Hamburg's old warehouse district and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At night the red brick goes almost black, and one column of balconies lights up floor after floor. Straight on and dead centre, because a facade this ordered doesn't need anything else.

photos.title: Loch Maree
photos.description: Loch Maree, Wester Ross. A small island of Scots pines, shot straight into the sun. f/16 turns the sun into a star, and a 20-second exposure smooths the loch into a soft sheen around the rocks. Black and white, because the light and the shapes were the whole story.

photos.title: Green Staircase
photos.description: Hamburg. A stairwell from a time when even the stairs were built to impress: glazed green tiles, polished wooden rails, and two flights splitting perfectly left and right. Shot dead centre, at 16 mm, on a tripod for ten seconds, because symmetry only works if you stand exactly in the middle.

photos.title: One way
photos.description: Staple Street, Tribeca. One of the shortest streets in Manhattan, still cobbled, with the green skybridge built in 1907 overhead. A blue Vespa parked under the One Way sign, and the whole street to itself.

photos.title: Rings, rising
photos.description: Hamburg. Standing under a glass atrium at dusk and looking straight up: rings of light hung on steel poles, rising through a grid of glass into the blue. The building does the composing. All you have to do is find the spot where it lines up.

photos.title: Xiangqi
photos.description: Xiangqi, Chinese chess, played on a paper board laid across a stone ledge in Chinatown, New York. One hand reaching for a piece, the other man waiting, hands on his knees. The street carries on behind them and neither of them notices.

photos.title: Angel
photos.description: Antony Gormley's Angel of the North has stood on a hill above Gateshead since 1998: 20 metres tall, with wings 54 metres across. Everyone photographs the whole figure. Up close it becomes something else: rusted steel ribs and the clean diagonal of a wing against the sky.

photos.title: Scratch and sniff
photos.description: Scratchcard, mask pulled down, and a hydrant for company. New York.

photos.title: Cathedral in motion
photos.description: York Minster, one of the largest Gothic cathedrals in northern Europe, photographed with the camera moving. A vertical sweep during the exposure keeps the spires and tree trunks standing, because they run the same way as the movement, while the leaves and sky dissolve into brushstrokes. Warm light on the stone, green below.

photos.title: Walk
photos.description: A walk signal, and the one person standing still. Chinatown, New York.

lessons.title: The exposure triangle
lessons.summary: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO decide how bright a photograph is, and each one changes how it looks. Move the controls and see for yourself.
lessons.body:
Every exposure comes down to three settings. Each one lets in more or less light, and each one has a side effect you can see in the picture.

[[exposure]]

## Aperture

The aperture is the opening in the lens, written as an f-number. **A smaller number means a bigger opening**, so f/2.8 lets in far more light than f/16.

The full stops run f/1.4, f/2, f/2.8, f/4, f/5.6, f/8, f/11, f/16 and f/22. Each step along that list halves the light. The numbers look odd because each one is the one before multiplied by about 1.4, the square root of two.

It also controls depth of field. Wide open, only your subject is sharp and the background melts away. Stopped down to f/11 or f/16, everything from the foreground rocks to the far hills stays sharp, which is why most landscape work sits there.

Go much past f/16 and the whole picture starts to soften slightly. This is diffraction, and it is why f/22 is a last resort rather than a default.

## Shutter speed

How long the sensor is exposed. 1/1000 s freezes a wave mid-break. A full second turns moving water into mist.

The full stops run 1/1000, 1/500, 1/250, 1/125, 1/60, 1/30, 1/15, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 and 1 second. Some of the numbers are rounded, but each step is a doubling.

The catch is camera shake. A rough rule for handheld shooting: keep the shutter at least as fast as one over your focal length, so 1/50 s on a 50 mm lens and 1/200 s at 200 mm. Any slower and you need a tripod. On a camera with a smaller, crop sensor, multiply the focal length by the crop factor first.

Image stabilisation lets you hold the camera at slower speeds, but it only deals with your movement. A person walking through the frame still blurs.

## ISO

How strongly the camera amplifies the signal. Doubling the ISO brightens the image by one stop, but adds grain and loses detail in the shadows. Keep it as low as the light allows.

The full stops run ISO 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200 and 6400. Do not be so wary of ISO that you accept a blurred picture. Some noise can be cleaned up in editing. Camera shake cannot.

## Stops

The three are linked by **stops**. One stop is a doubling or halving of the light. Going from f/8 to f/5.6, from 1/125 s to 1/60 s, or from ISO 400 to 800 each adds one stop.

> Change one setting by a stop and you can balance it by moving another the opposite way.

That trade is the whole game. f/8 at 1/125 s and f/5.6 at 1/250 s give the same brightness. The difference is what you want sharp and what you want frozen.

Most cameras move in thirds of a stop. Between f/8 and f/11 you will find f/9 and f/10. Between 1/125 s and 1/250 s you will find 1/160 s and 1/200 s. Between ISO 100 and 200 you will find 125 and 160. Three clicks make one stop.

[[photo:One way]]

A scooter on a cobbled street at 24 mm, f/11, 1/200 s, ISO 500. Everything is sharp, from the front wheel to the fire escapes above.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Manual, so every change is yours and you see its effect straight away
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for general scenes; open to f/2.8 to f/4 for a soft background
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/250 s handheld, and never slower than one over the focal length
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100. Raise it only when the shutter would be too slow to hold
- **Metering:** Set the meter to zero, then add 1 to 2 stops for snow or take away 1 for dark scenes

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## What the meter gets wrong

The camera's meter suggests settings that will make the scene an average, mid-grey brightness. Most of the time that works. It fails when the scene is not average.

- **Snow, white sand or a pale sky** filling the frame get darkened to grey. Add 1 to 2 stops
- **A dark subject on a dark background** gets brightened to grey. Take away about 1 stop
- **Strong backlight** makes the meter darken the picture, and the subject in front goes too dark. Add exposure for the subject

In aperture priority or shutter priority, make these corrections with exposure compensation. In manual, set the exposure so the meter reads above or below zero by the amount you want.

## Worked examples

Each example starts from a meter reading and moves settings by whole stops. Count the stops on each side. They should match.

1. **A portrait with a soft background.** The meter reads f/8, 1/125 s, ISO 100. Opening up to f/2.8 is three stops (f/8 to f/5.6 to f/4 to f/2.8), so the shutter must be three stops faster: 1/125 to 1/250 to 1/500 to 1/1000 s
2. **Indoors, handheld at 50 mm.** The meter reads f/4, 1/15 s, ISO 100, which is too slow to hold. Speed the shutter up two stops to 1/60 s (1/15 to 1/30 to 1/60), then raise the ISO two stops (100 to 200 to 400) to keep the brightness
3. **Moving water at 1/2 s.** The meter reads f/8, 1/30 s, ISO 100. Getting to 1/2 s takes four stops: 1/30 to 1/15 to 1/8 to 1/4 to 1/2. Closing down to f/22 gives only three (f/8 to f/11 to f/16 to f/22), so you land at 1/4 s. The last stop has to come from a filter, such as a polariser or an ND
4. **Sunny 16, with no meter at all.** In bright sun, f/16 with a shutter speed of one over the ISO gives a correct exposure. At ISO 100 that is f/16 at 1/100 s. Trade from there: f/8 is two stops wider, so the shutter goes two stops faster, 1/100 to 1/200 to 1/400 s

## Learning it in the field

1. Set the camera to manual and the ISO to its lowest native setting, usually 100
2. Decide what matters most for this picture: depth of field, movement, or a clean file. Set that control first
3. Set the second control from the light. If you chose the aperture, turn the shutter speed until the meter reads zero
4. Check the shutter speed against the handheld rule. If it is too slow, raise the ISO until it is fast enough, or use a tripod
5. Take the picture and check the histogram
6. Correct in whole stops first, then fine tune in thirds
7. Move one setting a stop, balance it with another, and take the same frame again to see what changed

## Checking your result in camera

The screen on the back is a poor judge of brightness, especially in bright sun or in the dark. Use the histogram.

- A graph piled against the right edge means lost highlights. Bring the exposure down
- A graph piled against the left edge means lost shadows. Bring it up, unless you want a silhouette
- Turn on highlight warnings. Areas that blink have no detail left
- Zoom in on the subject to check focus and camera shake. A picture can look sharp on a small screen and soft on a large one

## Common mistakes

- **Leaving the ISO high.** After a dark interior, the camera is still at ISO 3200 the next morning in sun. Check it every time you start
- **Blaming the lens for blur.** If everything is soft, the shutter was too slow. If only some of it is soft, look at depth of field and focus
- **Stopping down for everything.** f/22 loses sharpness to diffraction. Use f/8 to f/11 unless you need the extra depth
- **Trusting the meter on snow and sand.** It turns white to grey. Add exposure
- **Changing two settings at once while learning.** Change one, see what it does, then balance it

## Going further

- **Auto ISO in manual.** Set the aperture and shutter speed yourself and let the camera choose the ISO. Useful when the light keeps changing but you want control of depth and movement
- **Exposing to the right.** Shooting RAW, expose as brightly as you can without losing highlights, then darken in editing. The shadows come out cleaner
- **Bracketing.** For high-contrast scenes, take three frames one or two stops apart and choose or blend afterwards
- **Long exposure.** Once you can count stops, ND filters make sense: a 10-stop filter is ten doublings of the shutter speed

## My one tip

I shoot in full manual nearly all the time. Don't be afraid of it. Out in the field, there is no better way to learn how the exposure triangle works. Every change you make, you see straight away.
lessons.challenge: Put the camera in manual at ISO 100. Photograph the same scene at f/4, f/8 and f/16, adjusting the shutter speed each time to keep the meter at zero. Write down each shutter speed and check it changed by two stops each time. Compare what is sharp in each.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The meter reads f/8 at 1/125 s. You open up to f/2.8. Which shutter speed keeps the same brightness?
* 1/1000 s
- 1/500 s
- 1/250 s

Q: You move from 1/125 s to 1/250 s. How do you keep the same brightness using the aperture?
* Open up one stop, for example from f/8 to f/5.6
- Close down one stop, for example from f/8 to f/11
- Leave the aperture alone and nothing changes

Q: Using the handheld rule on a full-frame camera, what is the slowest safe shutter speed at 200 mm?
* 1/200 s
- 1/50 s
- 1/20 s

Q: The meter turns a snowy field grey. What do you do?
* Add 1 to 2 stops of exposure
- Take away 1 to 2 stops of exposure
- Close the aperture to f/22

lessons.title: Reading the light
lessons.summary: The same hill looks completely different at seven in the morning and two in the afternoon. Learn to see the light before you look for a subject.
lessons.body:
Good landscape photographs are mostly about light. The subject matters less than you think: the same view can be flat at noon and extraordinary an hour after sunrise.

The light is also why I go out at all. Watching it build and change is when I lose track of time completely, and for me that is half the point of photography.

## Four things to read

Before you look for a subject, look at the light and work out four things.

- **Direction.** Where it comes from, relative to you and the subject
- **Quality.** Hard, with crisp shadows, or soft, with gentle ones
- **Colour.** Warm, cool or neutral
- **Contrast.** How far apart the brightest and darkest parts are

## Direction

- **Front light,** with the sun behind you, shows colour and detail but flattens shape, because the shadows fall behind the subject where you cannot see them
- **Side light** rakes across the surface. Every ridge, stone and ripple throws a shadow, so texture and depth appear
- **Back light,** with the sun in front of you, puts a rim of light round edges, makes leaves and grass glow, and turns solid shapes into silhouettes

Walk around the subject before you set up. A few steps can turn front light into side light, and change the picture with it.

## Hard and soft light

Hard light comes from a small source, such as the sun in a clear sky. It casts dark shadows with sharp edges. Soft light comes from a large source, such as a sky full of cloud, and wraps round the subject with gentle shadows.

Neither is better. Hard light suits strong shapes and graphic pictures. Soft light suits detail and colour. Midday sun is hard and comes from overhead, so shadows sit short and black under everything. That is why a view so often looks flat at noon.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority; manual at blue hour, when exposures run to several seconds
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11, for sharpness from front to back in a landscape
- **Shutter speed:** 1/100 s to 1/800 s in daylight and golden hour; several seconds at blue hour, on a tripod
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **White balance:** Daylight, so the warmth of golden hour stays; shoot RAW to adjust it later

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Golden hour

The hour after sunrise and the hour before sunset. The sun is low, so light comes in from the side, warm and soft, and every ridge and wall throws a long shadow. Texture appears that simply is not there at midday.

The further north you go, the more the timing swings with the seasons. In midsummer the golden light can last for hours. In midwinter the whole short day can feel like golden hour.

[[guide:planner]]

[[photo:First light]]

A dead tree lit against a dune that is still in shadow, at 400 mm, f/10, 1/100 s, ISO 100. The bright trunk against the dark background is the picture.

## Blue hour

The time just after sunset and just before sunrise, when the sun is below the horizon. The sky turns deep blue, street lights and windows come on, and towns look their best. Bring a tripod, because exposures run to several seconds.

[[photo:ericusspitze-blue-hour]]

Lit office windows reflected in still water under a deep blue sky. The windows and the sky are close in brightness, so both hold detail.

## Overcast

Cloud works like a huge softbox. Shadows vanish and colours deepen, which suits woodland, waterfalls and close detail. When the sky is a flat white lid, leave it out of the frame.

## Weather is the light

Some of the best light arrives either side of rain. A break in the cloud after a squall can spotlight one hillside while everything around it stays dark.

- Look for clearing showers in the forecast, not clear skies
- Arrive early and be prepared to wait
- Keep shooting as the weather moves through

[[photo:Storm over the dunes]]

Sunlit dunes and a twisted tree against a dark, purple storm sky, at 135 mm, f/11, 1/800 s, ISO 100. The bright ground against the dark cloud comes from the weather, not the landscape.

## Colour and white balance

Light has a colour. Golden hour is warm. Shade, blue hour and overcast days are cooler. Auto white balance tries to make everything neutral, so it can take the warmth out of a sunrise.

Set the white balance to Daylight and the colour you saw stays in the picture. Shoot RAW and you can change it afterwards in Lightroom without any loss of quality.

## Reading the light in the field

1. Arrive before the light you want, and look before you set up
2. Find the sun, or where it will be, and note its direction relative to the main view
3. Look at the shadows. Their length tells you how low the sun is; their edges tell you how hard the light is
4. Half close your eyes. Detail drops away and you see the big shapes of light and dark
5. Walk round the subject to try front, side and back light
6. Take a test frame and check the histogram
7. Keep shooting as the light changes. The best frame often comes a few minutes before or after the moment you planned for

## Checking your result in camera

- **Back light** often blows the sky. Turn on highlight warnings, expose for the bright areas and let the shadows go dark, or bracket
- **High contrast** shows as a histogram touching both edges at once. The scene holds more range than one frame can record. Bracket, or wait for softer light
- **Colour** on the screen depends on your white balance setting. If a warm scene looks grey, check the setting before you blame the light

## Common mistakes

- **Arriving as the light peaks.** By the time you are set up, it has gone. Be in place half an hour early
- **Leaving at sunset.** The colour in the clouds often comes after the sun has gone, and blue hour follows
- **Shooting into the sun without shade.** Flare washes out contrast. Use a lens hood, or shade the lens with your hand
- **Keeping a dull sky in the frame.** On a grey day, crop it out
- **Letting auto white balance cool a warm scene.** Use Daylight, or correct it in the edit

## Going further

- **The same place through the year.** The sun rises and sets in different places with the seasons, so one view can be side lit in winter and front lit in summer
- **Black and white.** When the colour is dull but the shapes and textures are strong, the light may suit monochrome
- **Back light for translucent subjects.** Leaves, petals, grass and spray all glow when the light comes through them

> Bad weather makes good photographs. Bad light does not.
lessons.challenge: Pick one view near home. Photograph it at sunrise, at midday and at sunset on the same day, from the same spot. Each time, note the direction of the light and the length of the shadows, then compare the three pictures.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does golden hour bring out texture?
* The low sun lights the scene from the side and casts long shadows
- The light is brighter than at midday
- The sky is completely clear

Q: The sun is directly behind you. How does the subject usually look?
* Colour and detail show, but shapes look flat
- Texture stands out strongly
- The subject becomes a silhouette

Q: Why can auto white balance spoil a sunrise?
* It tries to make the light neutral and removes the warmth
- It makes the picture darker
- It only works with RAW files

Q: What kind of forecast is most promising for dramatic light?
* Clearing showers
- Clear skies all day
- Steady rain all day

lessons.title: Night and blue hour in cities
lessons.summary: Cities come alive after sunset. For a short time the sky and the street lights balance perfectly, and that window is worth planning around.
lessons.body:
Cities change after the sun goes down. Lit windows, glowing signs and a deep blue sky make even ordinary buildings look special.

## Blue hour is the window

About twenty to forty minutes after sunset, depending on the season and how far north you are, the sky fades to deep blue while street and window lights come on. For a while the two are close in brightness, so one exposure holds detail in both. Later, the sky turns black and the lights burn out.

The same window opens before sunrise, in reverse. It is quieter, with fewer people and less traffic, but the lights may already be going off.

[[guide:planner]]

[[photo:Der Spiegel]]

Office buildings with lit windows, doubled in still water. The sky is still blue, so it separates the buildings from the night.

## What you need

- **A tripod.** In cities I use a Peak Design carbon-fibre tripod, because it is lighter and quicker to set up
- **A remote release,** or the 2-second self-timer, so pressing the button does not shake the camera
- **A head torch,** to see the controls and your footing
- **Spare batteries.** Long exposures and cold evenings drain them
- **A lens cloth,** for drizzle and condensation

## Settings

- **Mode:** Manual, switching to Bulb for exposures longer than 30 s
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; f/11 gives sharper, longer star points on lights
- **Shutter speed:** 1 s to 30 s, lengthening every few minutes as the light drops
- **ISO:** Lowest native, usually 100; up to 400 if people or flags are smearing
- **Focus:** Manual, set while there is still light so the lens cannot hunt
- **White balance:** Shoot RAW; Daylight keeps lights warm, Tungsten around 3200 K deepens the blue

- Tripod, lowest ISO, f/8 to f/11, and let the shutter run for as long as it needs
- Shoot in RAW and set the white balance afterwards. Mixed street lighting confuses the camera
- Bracket your exposures. City scenes at night often have more range than one frame can hold
- At small apertures, bright lights turn into star shapes
- Turn off image stabilisation on a tripod, unless your lens is designed to detect one
- Focus while there is still light, then switch the lens to manual focus so it cannot hunt in the dark

## Working out the time

The light falls quickly, so the exposure keeps getting longer. Here is a worked example.

1. Early in blue hour, the meter reads **2 seconds at f/8, ISO 100**
2. A few minutes later the light has dropped by one stop. The same settings now need 4 seconds
3. After another stop, 8 seconds
4. If people or flags are smearing and you want a shorter time, raise the ISO. ISO 100 to 400 is two stops, so 8 seconds becomes 2 seconds
5. To bracket two stops either side of a 4-second exposure, shoot 1 second, 4 seconds and 16 seconds

Most cameras only time exposures up to 30 seconds. Beyond that, use Bulb mode with a remote or the camera's own bulb timer.

## The method in the field

1. Arrive before sunset, find your spot and compose while you can still see
2. Set up the tripod on solid ground, with the centre column down
3. Focus, then switch to manual focus
4. Set the lowest ISO, f/8 to f/11 and RAW, and turn off stabilisation
5. Start shooting as the first lights come on, and take a frame every few minutes
6. Check the histogram every few frames and lengthen the exposure as the light drops
7. Bracket when the lights get bright against the sky
8. Keep going until the sky is black, then compare the frames at home

Then switch the 2-second timer off when the camera comes off the tripod. Forgetting to is my longest-running mistake.

## White balance under street lights

Cities mix old orange street lamps, cool white LEDs and greenish fluorescent tubes. No single setting makes them all neutral.

- **Daylight** keeps the lights warm and the sky blue
- **Tungsten,** around 3200 K, deepens the blue of the sky and makes warm lights look more neutral
- **RAW** lets you choose later in Lightroom, and try both

## Stars and points of light

Small, bright lights turn into stars at f/8 and smaller. The number of points depends on the aperture blades. A lens with an even number of blades gives the same number of points; an odd number gives twice as many. The smaller the aperture, the sharper and longer the points.

## Movement

Anything moving during a long exposure turns into a streak. Traffic becomes ribbons of red and white light, and people walking past disappear or leave ghosts.

Someone standing still for most of the exposure records as a solid figure. Someone walking through records faintly or not at all.

## Checking your result in camera

- In the dark, the screen looks brighter than the file really is. Trust the histogram
- Turn on highlight warnings. Small blinking lamps are normal. Large blinking windows or signs mean the exposure is too long, so bracket
- Zoom in on a lit edge to check for vibration and focus
- Compare the sky colour across frames. The best balance often lasts only a few minutes

## Common mistakes

- **Arriving late.** By the time you have found a spot, the blue has gone
- **Waiting too long.** Once the sky goes black, the lights are far brighter than the sky and detail is lost in both
- **Shooting from a bridge with traffic.** Vehicles and footsteps make bridges move. Wait for a lull, or set up on solid ground
- **Flare and ghost images.** Bright lights reflect inside the lens. Remove any protective filter, which adds extra glass for the light to bounce off
- **Condensation.** As the air cools, the lens can mist over. Check the front element between frames

## Practical points

- Get there before sunset to find your spot and compose while you can still see
- Reflections in water and wet streets double the light, so rain is not always bad news
- Check whether tripods are allowed. Many bridges, viewing platforms and private squares do not permit them
- Keep your kit close and stay aware of your surroundings

## Going further

- **Blending.** Take a frame early for the sky and a later one for the lights, then combine them in Photoshop
- **Light trails.** Ten to thirty seconds turns traffic into streams of light. The Long exposure lesson covers it in detail
- **After rain.** Wet streets reflect every sign and window, and add light to the lower half of the frame

> Arrive in daylight. Leave in the dark.

* The sky and the artificial lights are close in brightness

- The sky is completely black

* 8 seconds
- 4 seconds
- 16 seconds

* It makes the blue deeper
- It turns the sky orange
- It has no effect on the sky

Q: Your long exposure from a busy bridge is soft. What is the likely cause?
* Traffic and footsteps made the bridge vibrate
- The water reflected too much light
- The aperture was too small

lessons.title: Shooting into the sun
lessons.summary: Turn round and face the light. Silhouettes, sunstars and glowing edges, and how to expose them without flare, blown skies or harm to your eyes.
lessons.body:
Point the camera at the sun and shapes turn to silhouettes, edges glow, and the sun itself can become a star. It is also the hardest light to expose, and the only kind of photography that can hurt your eyes.

## Eye safety first

- **Never look at the sun through an optical viewfinder.** The lens focuses sunlight straight into your eye, and a long lens makes it worse. Retinal damage can be permanent, and it does not hurt while it happens
- **Compose on the screen.** Use live view or an electronic viewfinder, so you are looking at a display, not at the sun
- **Keep the time short.** The same focused light falls on the shutter and sensor. Compose, shoot and point the camera away. Do not leave it aimed at the sun on a tripod while you wait
- **Take most care with telephoto lenses** and a high, bright sun. A low sun through haze is gentler, but still not safe to stare at

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, metering the sky beside the sun, with minus 1 to minus 2 stops for silhouettes
- **Aperture:** f/11 to f/16 for a sunstar; never past f/16, where diffraction softens the whole picture
- **Shutter speed:** Whatever the meter gives, often near 1/250 s at f/11; 1/500 s or faster for a walking figure
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **Drive:** Three-frame bracket, two stops apart, on a tripod when both sky and land need detail

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Backlight and silhouettes

Backlight comes from behind the subject. It outlines edges and makes grass and leaves glow.

A silhouette takes it to the end: the subject goes black against a bright sky. It works when the outline alone says what something is. A tree or a figure on a ridge reads instantly. Two people standing close merge into one shape and stop making sense.

1. Put a subject with a simple outline against open sky, not against land
2. Move until there is a gap of sky between separate shapes
3. Meter from the bright sky beside the sun, not from the sun or the subject
4. Outside manual, dial in one to two stops of negative exposure compensation
5. Check the sky keeps its colour and the subject has gone properly dark

## Sunstars

Shoot a bright point of light at a small aperture and it turns into a star. The points come from diffraction at the edges of the aperture blades.

- **Use f/11 to f/16.** Smaller apertures give sharper, longer points
- **Do not go past f/16.** Diffraction softens the whole picture beyond that, so the star improves while everything else gets worse
- **Partly hide the sun** just behind a tree trunk, a building or a ridge. A sliver of sun is a smaller point of light than the full disc, and gives a crisper star
- **Count your blades.** An even number of blades gives that many points: 8 blades, 8 points. An odd number gives double: 9 blades, 18 points. The count is in the lens specifications

Move a few centimetres and the star changes. Take several frames and choose at home.

[[photo:Loch Maree]]

Straight into the sun at f/16, with the sun turned to a star at the top of the frame and the pines silhouetted against the sky. A 20-second exposure smooths the loch around the rocks.

## Flare and ghosting

Light from the sun bounces between the glass surfaces inside the lens and shows up in two ways.

- **Veiling flare:** a haze across the frame that lifts the blacks and drains contrast
- **Ghosts:** coloured blobs or rings, usually on a line from the sun through the centre of the frame

To keep it down:

- **Clean the front of the lens and any filter.** Dust and smears scatter light into haze
- **Remove any protective filter.** Every extra piece of glass adds surfaces for light to bounce between
- **When the sun is just outside the frame, shade the lens** with a hood, your hand or a hat, keeping it out of the picture
- **When the sun is in the frame, you cannot shade it.** Accept some flare, or on a tripod take two frames: one normal, one with a fingertip or small card held so it just covers the sun. The ghosts vanish from the second. Blend the clean area into the first in editing

## Exposing for the highlights

No camera holds detail in the sky round the sun and in the shadows facing you at once. Choose what gives.

The sun itself will always be pure white, and that is fine. Expose so the bright sky beside it keeps its colour, and let the shadows fall where they fall. Shadows can usually be lifted a little in editing. Highlights that have gone pure white cannot be brought back.

Turn on the highlight warning and use the histogram. A small spike against the right edge for the sun is acceptable. A large block of flashing sky is not.

## Bracketing and blending

For detail in both sky and land, take several exposures and combine them. Set the camera on a tripod to bracket three frames, two stops apart.

A worked example. The camera meters the scene at **f/11, 1/250 s, ISO 100**.

1. Two stops under: 1/250 ÷ 4 = 1/1000 s. This frame holds the sky around the sun
2. The metered frame: 1/250 s
3. Two stops over: 1/250 × 4 = 1/62.5, which the camera rounds to 1/60 s. This frame holds the foreground

Keep the aperture fixed and change only the shutter speed, so depth of field and the sunstar match in every frame. Lightroom can merge them with Photo Merge, HDR.

I tend to blend exposures, because graduated filters give artefacts. A grad darkens everything above a straight line, including trees, rocks or buildings that rise through it.

[[photo:Botallack]]

The sun sits low over the sea and lays a path of light across the water, while the pink flowers and grass on the cliff in front keep their colour and detail.

## When the sun is low

Shooting into the sun works best when it is near the horizon: dimmer, warmer, easier to expose, and throwing long shadows towards you. That means the hour or so after sunrise and before sunset.

[[guide:planner]]

Check where it will set as well as when. In Scotland the summer sun rises in the north-east and sets in the north-west, while in winter it stays low in the south. Choose a spot where the sun lands behind your subject, not off to one side.

## Worked scenarios

- **Trees on a skyline.** Walk until the sun sits just behind the edge of a trunk. Set f/16 and ISO 100, compose on the screen, bracket three frames two stops apart, then point away
- **A walker on a ridge at sunset.** Meter the sky beside the sun and take two stops off. Use 1/500 s or faster, and shoot when their legs are apart, so the outline reads as walking
- **Backlit grass, sun just out of frame.** Hold your hand above the lens to kill the flare. Expose for the grass, often a stop brighter than the camera suggests, so the glow comes through

## Common mistakes

- **A grey, washed-out picture.** Veiling flare. Clean the glass, remove the protective filter, or shade the lens if the sun is outside the frame
- **A white blob instead of a star.** The aperture is too wide, or the full sun is in open sky. Close to f/11 to f/16 and tuck the sun behind an edge
- **A soft picture at f/22.** Diffraction. Open up to f/16
- **A silhouette that does not read.** Shapes overlap or sit against land. Move until each has sky around it

## Checking in camera

1. Read the histogram and highlight warning, not the brightness of the screen
2. Zoom in on the sun to check the star is crisp
3. Scroll across the frame for ghosts. They are faint on a small screen and obvious later
4. Point the camera away from the sun while you review

## Going further

- **Long exposure into the sun,** smoothing water under a sunstar. See the Long exposure lesson
- **Black and white,** where backlight leaves only shape and tone. See the Black and white lesson
- **Blending by hand,** with layers and masks in Photoshop, once automatic merges stop giving you what you want

> Put the light behind the subject and let the outline do the work.

* On the rear screen or an electronic viewfinder, pointing away again as soon as you have shot
- Through the optical viewfinder, as long as you use a wide lens
- Through the optical viewfinder at f/16, because the small aperture protects your eye

- 1/60 s

Q: The sun is in the frame and there are ghosts across the picture. What fixes them?

- Fitting a lens hood
- Closing the aperture to f/22

lessons.title: Planning a photography trip
lessons.summary: Good light is mostly luck, but you can tip the odds. Time, weather and a bit of homework put you in the right place when it happens.
lessons.body:
We travel in our camper van and go on city breaks and photography holidays. Wherever you go, good photographs come from being in the right place at the right time, and that is something you can plan for.

## Know when the light happens

Golden hour and blue hour times change every day and with every place. Check them before you go.

[[guide:planner]]

For each day, note four times: the start of morning blue hour, sunrise, sunset and the end of evening blue hour. Everything else in the plan hangs off those.

Golden hour is not a fixed hour. Far north in summer, the sun stays low for much of the evening. Nearer the equator it rises and sets steeply, and the warm light is brief. The further from home you travel, the more it is worth checking rather than assuming.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority handheld; manual on a tripod for blue hour, so exposure stays fixed
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/16 for landscapes; f/16 suits deep scenes with a long lens
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s or faster handheld; 1 s to 30 s on a tripod in blue hour
- **ISO:** 100 on a tripod; 400 to 1600 handheld on city breaks as the light fades
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 35 mm full frame for wide views; 100 mm to 400 mm for details
- **White balance:** Daylight, fixed, so the camera does not cancel the warm golden hour colour

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Choose the season

- **The sun moves along the horizon.** In the northern hemisphere it rises north of east and sets north of west in summer, and rises south of east and sets south of west in winter. A view that lines up with the sunset in June may not in December
- **Day length changes the effort.** In a northern summer, sunrise can be very early and sunset very late. In winter both fall at easier hours
- **Some subjects only exist for a few weeks,** such as autumn colour, snow or flowers on the cliffs

## Scout first

- Look at the place on a map and in other people's photographs, to see what is there and where the light falls
- Note which way the main view faces. East-facing scenes suit sunrise; west-facing scenes suit sunset
- Visit in the middle of the day if you can, when the light is poor, to find your spot without pressure
- Find a second spot facing a different way, in case the light or the weather goes the wrong way

## Watch the weather, not just the forecast icon

- Clearing showers and broken cloud give better light than a clear blue sky
- Still, cold mornings bring mist and reflections
- Wind matters as much as rain: it ruins reflections and shakes tripods
- Tide times matter on the coast

Around the British coast there are usually two high tides a day, roughly 12 hours 25 minutes apart, so high tide comes about 50 minutes later each day. Spring tides, with the biggest range, fall around new and full moon. Always check you cannot be cut off.

## A worked example

Here is a sunrise plan worked backwards from the light.

1. Sunrise is at 06:40, and the planner shows blue hour starting at 06:05
2. You want 15 minutes to find your spot and set up, so you need to arrive by 05:50
3. The walk in takes 40 minutes, so leave the car park at 05:10
4. The drive takes 25 minutes, so leave at 04:45
5. Allow 30 minutes to get up and out: the alarm goes at 04:15

Write the times down the night before. At 04:15 nobody does sums well.

## On the day

1. Check the forecast the night before and again when you wake
2. Charge the batteries and empty the cards the night before, and pack the bag then
3. Arrive early, walk the spot, and set up before the light starts
4. Take a test frame and check the composition and the histogram
5. Shoot through the whole window, not just the peak
6. Stay after the light ends, then keep the camera out on the walk back

## Pack for the conditions

- Spare batteries, especially in the cold
- A head torch for early starts and late finishes
- Something to sit on and something warm. Good light often means waiting
- A light travel tripod for city breaks, where you will carry it all day
- A long lens as well as a wide one. It lets you pick out details and work from further back

## Busy places

Famous places draw other photographers, so plan for them as well as the light. On a photography holiday in Namibia with James Kerwin, I used the 100-400 mm at Deadvlei so I could stand back, rather than walk into the scene and end up in someone else's photograph. The best light there came before the sun cleared the dunes.

[[photo:Deadvlei]]

A dead tree in front of sunlit dunes, with smaller trees spread across the pan behind. Taken with the 100-400 at 100 mm, f/16, 1/125 s, ISO 100.

## Checking as you go

- Review a few frames on site at full magnification, not just on the small screen. A soft frame is easy to fix while you are still there
- Check the histogram at the start of each session; the light at dawn changes fast
- Back up the cards each evening on a trip

## Common mistakes

- **Planning one spot only.** If the light goes the other way, you have nowhere to go
- **Forgetting the walk in the dark.** It always takes longer than in daylight
- **Trusting a clear forecast.** Clear skies are easy but rarely dramatic
- **Leaving as soon as the sun is up or down.** Some of the best light comes just after
- **Ignoring the tide.** Check it for the picture, and for the way back

## Leave room for luck

A plan gets you there. What you find when you arrive is often better. Keep the camera out on the walk back.

[[photo:Botallack]]

The low sun over the sea, with old stone buildings on the cliffs and pink flowers along the path in the foreground.

## Going further

- **Go back.** The same place in a different season, tide or weather is a new picture
- **Moon phases.** A full moon rises around sunset, so it can sit in a blue hour sky
- **Guided photography holidays.** A guide who knows the location knows where the light falls and when

> Plan for the light. Stay open to everything else.

* Broken cloud and clearing showers
- A clear blue sky all day
- Thick, flat cloud

Q: Blue hour starts at 06:05. You want 15 minutes to set up and the walk in takes 40 minutes. When must you leave the car park?
* 05:10
- 05:25
- 05:50

Q: Around the British coast, roughly how much later is high tide each day?
* About 50 minutes
- About 12 hours
- About 5 minutes

Q: In the northern hemisphere in winter, where does the sun rise?
* South of east
- North of east
- Due east all year

lessons.title: The rule of thirds
lessons.summary: Split the frame into nine and put what matters where the lines cross. The simplest way to stop every picture looking like a snapshot.
lessons.body:
Most beginners put the subject in the middle of the frame. It is the obvious place, and it is usually the dullest. The rule of thirds is the quickest fix.

[[guide:thirds]]

## How it works

Imagine two lines across the frame and two lines down it, splitting it into nine equal parts. Place your subject on one of the four points where the lines cross, and run strong edges such as the horizon along one of the lines.

An off-centre subject creates tension. The eye has somewhere to go, and the empty part of the frame starts to matter.

The grid is a guide, not a target to hit to the pixel. A subject close to a crossing point does the same job as one exactly on it.

## What counts as the subject

The part you place is the part the eye goes to first. That is not always the whole object.

- **People and animals:** the eyes, or the whole face if the person is small in the frame
- **A tree or a building:** the trunk or the main mass, not the tips of the branches or the chimney
- **A small figure, boat or car in a big landscape:** the whole thing, because it is small enough to act as a point
- **Lines and edges:** the horizon, a shoreline or the edge of a shadow go along a line, not through a point

When there are two subjects, try them on opposite crossing points, such as top left and bottom right. The eye then travels between them across the whole frame.

[[photo:Red dress]]

The figure in red stands low on the left, well apart from the tree, and the line where the pale ground meets the dark dune runs across the lower part of the frame.

## Use the grid in your camera

Almost every camera and phone can show a thirds grid on screen. Turn it on and leave it on. After a few weeks you will place things on the thirds without thinking.

The setting is usually in the display or shooting menu, under a name such as grid display or grid lines. Some cameras offer finer grids as well. The three by three grid is the one you want for this.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, so attention stays on placement rather than exposure
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for landscapes; f/2.8 to f/5.6 for portraits and street
- **Shutter speed:** 1/250 s to 1/500 s for people walking; at least one over the focal length otherwise
- **ISO:** ISO 100 to 400 in daylight; raise it in poor light rather than accept a blurred frame
- **Focus:** Single-point autofocus, with the point moved onto the subject instead of focusing and recomposing
- **Display:** Three by three grid turned on and left on

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## The method in the field

1. Decide what the photograph is about before you lift the camera. If you cannot say it in a few words, keep looking
2. Turn on the grid and frame loosely, with the main subject roughly on a crossing point
3. Choose which crossing point. Put the subject on the side that leaves space where it is looking or moving
4. Run the horizon or the strongest line along the upper or lower third, not through the middle
5. Move your feet, not just the camera. One step to the side changes what sits behind the subject
6. Put the focus point on the subject itself. Focusing in the centre and then recomposing can shift the focus off the subject, especially at wide apertures
7. Check the edges for anything bright, distracting or cut in half, then take the picture
8. Take a second frame with the subject on the opposite third and a third frame with it centred. Compare them later on a bigger screen

## Give it room

If your subject is looking or moving, put the space in front of it, not behind. A walker heading left belongs on the right third, with the empty frame ahead of them.

Put the same walker on the left third, facing the left edge, and the picture feels cramped, as if they are about to walk out of it. Occasionally that tension is the point, for example a figure leaving a scene. Most of the time it just looks like a mistake.

The same applies to a face in profile, a car, a bird in flight or a boat under way. Give the direction of travel about two thirds of the frame.

## Worked scenarios

- **A lone tree on a hillside.** Put the trunk on the left or right vertical line and the skyline along the upper third. If the sky is plain grey, push the skyline higher still and let the slope fill the frame
- **A head-and-shoulders portrait.** Put the nearer eye on an upper crossing point. In an upright frame the eyes often land on the upper third line naturally if you leave a little space above the head
- **A boat on a loch.** The boat is small in the frame, so it is the point. Put it on a lower crossing point, run the far shore along the upper third, and let the water fill the rest
- **A busy street.** Choose the third first, then wait for someone to walk into it, instead of chasing people with the camera

[[photo:Chinatown]]

The woman in sunglasses sits on the left third, with her face close to the upper left crossing point. The yellow posts in the lower right corner balance her across the frame.

## Cropping afterwards

The grid works in editing too. Lightroom's crop tool can lay a thirds grid over the picture while you crop.

It helps to know where the lines fall. In a frame 6000 pixels wide and 4000 tall, the vertical thirds sit at 2000 and 4000 pixels across (6000 ÷ 3 = 2000). The horizontal thirds sit at about 1333 and 2667 pixels down (4000 ÷ 3 ≈ 1333).

Change the shape and the grid moves with it. Crop the same frame to a 4000 by 4000 square and the vertical thirds now fall at about 1333 and 2667 pixels across the new frame. A subject that was on a third before may not be on one after, so check the grid again after every change of shape.

Cropping also costs detail. A crop that keeps two thirds of the width and two thirds of the height keeps 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9 of the pixels, which is less than half. Get the placement close in camera and use the crop for fine adjustment.

## Checking your result

- Look at the picture small, as a thumbnail on the camera's playback screen. Placement and balance show up better small than full size
- Notice where your eye lands first. If it is a bright patch at the edge and not the subject, recompose or fix the edge
- Check the space in front of anything that is looking or moving
- Compare the off-centre frame with the centred one you took as a test. If the centred one is stronger, the scene probably wanted symmetry

## Common mistakes

- **Everything on a third.** Several things, each on its own crossing point, compete with each other. Choose one main subject and let the rest support it
- **The horizon on a third but the subject in the middle.** Place the main subject first, then the lines
- **Focusing and recomposing at a wide aperture.** The focus can slip off the eyes. Move the focus point instead of the camera
- **Room behind the subject instead of in front.** Swap sides
- **Trusting the grid over the picture.** If the frame feels wrong with the subject exactly on the point, nudge it until it feels right

## When to break it

- Symmetry and reflections usually want the centre
- A single small subject in a big empty space can sit almost anywhere
- Square frames often suit a central subject
- A face looking straight into the lens often has more force in the centre

## Going further

- **Leading lines.** Once the subject is placed, use a line to walk the eye to it
- **Horizon placement.** Decide whether the photograph is about the land or the sky, then give that part two thirds of the frame
- **The golden ratio.** A similar grid with its lines about 38% and 62% of the way across, instead of 33% and 67%. It sits the subject a little closer to the centre
- **Negative space.** Make the subject small and let the empty part of the frame carry the mood

> The rule of thirds is a starting point, not a law. Learn it well enough that breaking it is a choice.

For three of those scenes, also take one frame with the subject on the opposite third and one with it centred, then compare all three at home.

- In a corner of the frame

Q: You crop to keep two thirds of the width and two thirds of the height. How much of the original picture is left?
