- One third

lessons.title: Where to put the horizon
lessons.summary: High, low or dead centre. Where the horizon sits decides whether a photograph is about the land or the sky.
lessons.body:
The horizon is usually the strongest line in a landscape. Where you put it tells the viewer what the photograph is about before they have looked at anything else.

[[guide:horizon]]

## Read the scene first

Before you place the horizon, decide which half has more to say. Look at the sky: texture, colour, movement, light breaking through. Then look at the land: rocks, flowers, a path, patterns in sand or water.

Whichever half carries the picture gets the room. If you cannot choose, that is often a sign the scene is a reflection, or that the horizon should not be in the frame at all.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11, so the foreground and the horizon are both sharp
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; slower is fine on a tripod in dawn light
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100; raise it only if the handheld shutter speed drops too low
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 100 mm full frame, depending on how much of the scene you want
- **Display:** Grid and electronic level switched on

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Low horizon: sky-led

Put the horizon on the lower third when the sky is doing something worth showing: storm cloud, a sunset, a big clearing after rain. The land becomes a thin base for the drama above it.

[[photo:Storm over the dunes]]

The heavy cloud takes up more than half the frame, while the dunes and the twisted tree give it a base along the bottom.

A low horizon still needs something on the land. A small, clear shape against the sky, such as a tree, a building or a figure, stops the base being just a dark strip.

## High horizon: land-led

Put it on the upper third when the interest is in front of you: rocks on the shore, patterns in the sand, a path leading in. On a flat grey day this is often the only way to make a landscape work, because it leaves the dull sky out.

[[photo:Botallack]]

The sea horizon sits high in the frame, leaving most of the picture for the flowers, the path and the cliffs leading round to the buildings on the headland.

## Centred: for reflections

A horizon through the middle splits the frame in two equal halves. That usually feels static, which is exactly why it suits a mirror-calm loch. The reflection and the scene balance each other.

If you centre it, centre it exactly. A horizon slightly off the middle looks like a mistake, not a choice.

Calm water is most likely early in the morning, before the wind gets up. If you use a polariser, turn it while watching the reflection: at one angle it can remove the reflection you came for.

## Where the camera puts the horizon

With the camera held level, a distant horizon falls across the middle of the frame. To move it to the lower third you tilt the camera up. To move it to the upper third you tilt it down.

How far you tilt depends on the lens. A full-frame sensor is 24 mm tall in landscape format. Moving the horizon from the centre to a third line moves it one sixth of the frame height, which is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 mm on the sensor.

- **At 16 mm:** the tilt is about 14 degrees, because 4 ÷ 16 = 0.25, and the angle whose tangent is 0.25 is about 14 degrees
- **At 100 mm:** the tilt is only about 2.3 degrees, because 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04

That is why tilting causes problems with a wide lens and hardly any with a long one. Tilting up makes trees and buildings near the edges lean inwards. Tilting down makes them lean outwards. If that matters, keep the camera level and crop, step back and use a longer focal length, or straighten the lean afterwards.

## Keep it level

A sloping horizon is the most common mistake in landscape photography, and the easiest to fix. Turn on the level in your camera, or straighten it afterwards. On the coast, a tilted sea looks as if it is draining out of the picture.

- **The electronic level** in the viewfinder or on the screen is the quickest check. Many cameras show tilt forward and back as well as side to side
- **A level tripod is not a level camera.** The head sits on top of the legs, so check the camera itself
- **The sea is the only horizon you can trust.** Hills and fields slope naturally. On land, check a vertical such as a building or a fence post instead
- **In Lightroom,** the crop tool has a straighten option. Drag it along the horizon and the picture rotates to match. Rotating trims the corners, so leave a little room at the edges when you frame

## Wide lenses and curved horizons

Many wide lenses bend straight lines that do not pass through the centre of the frame. A horizon near the top or bottom edge can bow into a slight curve. A horizon through the centre stays straight. Lens profile corrections in Lightroom remove most of this, so turn them on before you judge whether the horizon is level.

## The method in the field

1. Decide whether the photograph is about the land, the sky or a reflection
2. Turn on the grid and the electronic level
3. Place the horizon on the lower third, the upper third or dead centre to match
4. Check the edges for trees or buildings leaning because of tilt, and step back with a longer lens if they distract
5. Check that the horizon does not cut through a head, the top of a tree or the peak of a hill
6. Check the exposure. The sky is usually much brighter than the land, so look at the histogram and the highlight warning
7. Take the frame, then take the other two placements for comparison

## Exposure and the horizon

The half you give the most room to is the half you expose for. With a low horizon, protect the sky and let the land go darker. With a high horizon, expose for the land and accept a brighter sky, or leave the sky out.

If you need detail in both, a graduated ND filter darkens the sky without touching the land. The alternative is two frames, one for each, blended in editing.

## Worked scenarios

- **A storm moving over a beach.** Horizon on the lower third, exposure set for the cloud, a figure or a rock on the sand for scale
- **A flat grey day on a rocky shore.** Horizon on the upper third, or point the camera down and leave it out altogether
- **A calm loch at dawn.** Horizon dead centre, polariser turned to keep the reflection
- **A sunset behind a dark ridge.** The ridge line is your horizon. Put it on the lower third and let it fall to silhouette

## Common mistakes

- **A sloping horizon.** Use the level, or straighten in editing
- **Centring by habit.** Without a reflection, a centred horizon usually feels undecided. Move it to a third
- **A horizon through a subject.** A line cutting through someone's neck or across the top of a tree draws the eye to the wrong place. Raise or lower the camera
- **Leaning edges from a tilted wide lens.** Level the camera and crop, or use a longer lens
- **Levelling by a hillside.** Land slopes. Use a vertical or the camera's level

## Going further

- **Leave it out.** Some of the strongest landscapes have no horizon at all, just texture, water or pattern
- **Rule of thirds.** Combine the horizon on one third with the main subject on a crossing point
- **Leading lines.** Use a path or shoreline to carry the eye from the foreground up to the horizon

> Decide what the photograph is about, then give it the most room.
lessons.challenge: Find one open view and take three photographs from the same spot: horizon on the lower third, on the upper third and through the middle. Use the electronic level for all three. At home, decide which tells the story best, and check whether any trees or buildings at the edges started to lean when you tilted.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The sky is full of storm cloud. Where do you put the horizon?
* On the lower third
- On the upper third
- Out of the frame entirely

Q: When does a centred horizon work well?
* With a mirror-calm reflection
- With a dull grey sky
- With an interesting foreground and a plain sky

Q: With the camera level, where does a distant horizon fall in the frame?
* Across the middle
- Along the upper third
- Along the lower third

Q: Why does tilting to move the horizon cause more leaning with a 16 mm lens than with a 100 mm lens?
* The wide lens needs a much bigger tilt, about 14 degrees against about 2 degrees
- Wide lenses have no electronic level
- Long lenses correct the lean automatically

lessons.title: Leading lines
lessons.summary: Roads, walls, rivers and shorelines can walk the eye straight to your subject. Find the line first, then the point it leads to.
lessons.body:
The eye follows lines. Put a line in the frame that runs towards your subject and you have done half the work of telling people where to look.

[[guide:lines]]

## Where to find them

- Roads and paths running away from you
- Dry stone walls and fences crossing a hillside
- Rivers, burns and the curve of a shoreline
- Piers, railings and rows of windows in town
- Tide lines, ripples in sand and the edge of the surf
- Shadows, especially late in the day when they are long
- Staircases, handrails and the joins in a pavement
- Light trails from traffic at night

Lines do not have to be drawn. A row of lamp posts, a line of boats or a person's gaze all act as lines, because the eye joins the dots.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 with a wide lens, so the line stays sharp from front to back
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; the faster end with a long lens
- **ISO:** 100 to 400 in daylight; raise it in poor light rather than slowing the shutter
- **Focal length:** 16 to 24 mm full frame to sweep lines in; 100 to 200 mm to stack them
- **Focus:** About a third of the way into the scene; check the line is sharp where it starts

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## What different lines do

- **Diagonals** feel active. They create movement and depth, and they are the strongest leading lines
- **Converging lines** run away from you and meet in the distance. They pull the eye into the frame and make it feel deep
- **Horizontal lines** feel calm and stable. They lead across the frame, not into it
- **Vertical lines** feel strong and upright. They lead the eye up, which suits trees and buildings

## Make them lead somewhere

A line that runs out of the side of the frame takes the eye with it. The strongest lines start near a corner or the bottom edge and end at something worth looking at: a building, a peak, a figure.

The end of the line is the point of the picture. If the line leads to nothing, the viewer arrives and finds an empty space. Look for a clear subject where the line ends or where several lines meet.

[[photo:Sprinkenhof]]

The wet road leads in from the bottom edge, and the walls on either side close in towards the lit tower in the centre, where the road and the walls meet.

## Get low and go wide

A wide-angle lens close to the ground stretches lines out and makes them converge faster. A wall that looks ordinary at head height can sweep right through the frame from knee height.

Strictly, it is your position that changes the line, not the lens. Getting close to the start of the line makes the near part look large and the far part look small. The wide lens is what lets you stand that close and still fit the whole line in.

## Long lenses and stacked lines

A long lens does the opposite. From far away the line is seen almost side on, so it looks flatter and the parts of it stack up. Dune ridges, rows of hills and layers of streets work this way. The lines stop pulling you in and start to form layers and pattern instead.

[[photo:Mulberry Street]]

The street, the railings on the left and the lights strung overhead all run back towards the tall tower in the distance, which sits where the lines meet.

## Curves

Straight lines are direct and strong. Curves, like an S-bend in a river or a road winding through a glen, slow the eye down and make it wander. Both work. Choose the one that matches the mood.

An S-curve works best when it starts near a bottom corner and winds up through the frame. Higher ground helps: from above you see more of the bend, and from ground level it can flatten into a straight strip.

## Lines in buildings

Looking up at a building makes its vertical lines lean in towards the top of the frame. That can be a strong leading line in its own right, pulling the eye up to the roof or the sky.

If you plan to straighten, leave room around the building when you frame. The correction stretches the top of the picture and crops the edges.

## The method in the field

1. Find the subject, or a place where a subject will appear
2. Look for a line that runs towards it: a path, a wall, a shoreline, a shadow
3. Walk until the line starts near a corner or the bottom edge of the frame and ends at the subject
4. Try lower. Crouch or put the camera near the ground and see whether the line becomes stronger
5. Choose the lens. Wide and close to make the line sweep in, long and further back to stack lines into layers
6. Set an aperture that keeps the line sharp from front to back if it is the main structure, often f/8 to f/11 with a wide lens
7. Check that the line does not run out of the side of the frame, then take the picture
8. Take one frame from head height as well, to compare

## Worked scenarios

- **A path through a field to a tree.** Stand on the path, camera low, so the path enters from the bottom edge and ends at the trunk. Put the tree on a third
- **A pier at sunset.** Stand at one side so the pier runs in diagonally from a bottom corner, not straight up the middle
- **A wall on a hillside.** Find where the wall starts close to you and climbs towards a peak or a cottage
- **A city street.** Stand in the middle of a pavement or crossing (safely) and let the kerbs and building fronts converge on a figure or a landmark

## Common mistakes

- **A line that leads nowhere.** Find a subject at the end, or wait for one to arrive
- **A line that leaves the frame.** Move until it ends inside the picture
- **A line straight up the middle.** Often static. Step sideways and let it enter from a corner
- **Too many lines.** Several lines pulling in different directions confuse the eye. Simplify the frame
- **A soft foreground.** If the line starts close to the lens, make sure it is sharp where it starts

## Checking your result

- Follow the line on the screen with your eye. Where you end up is where the viewer ends up
- Check the bottom corners. Leading lines usually start there, and clutter there blocks the way in
- Compare the low frame with the head-height frame and keep the one that pulls harder

## Going further

- **Rule of thirds.** End the line on a crossing point
- **Framing.** Combine a line with a frame, such as a path seen through an archway
- **Light trails.** At night, traffic draws its own lines through a long exposure
- **Pattern and repetition.** Use stacked lines from a long lens as the subject itself

> Find the line first. Then walk until it points where you want.
lessons.challenge: Find a path, wall or shoreline. Photograph it from head height, then from knee height with your widest lens, then from further back with your longest lens. Compare how strongly each version pulls you in, and where the eye ends up.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Where does a leading line usually work best?
* Starting near a corner or the bottom edge and ending at the subject
- Running out of the side of the frame
- Running straight across the middle

Q: What really makes a line sweep in when you use a wide lens close to the ground?
* Your position close to the start of the line, which the wide lens lets you fit in
- The wide lens bends the line
- The low angle raises the horizon

Q: What does a long lens from far away do to lines?
* Flattens them so they stack into layers
- Makes them converge faster
- Turns straight lines into curves

Q: How do curves differ from straight lines?
* They slow the eye down and make it wander
- They always look stronger
- They only work in black and white

lessons.title: Framing within the frame
lessons.summary: An archway, a window or a gap in the trees puts a border inside your photograph and holds the eye on what matters.
lessons.body:
A natural frame is anything in the scene that surrounds your subject: a doorway, branches, a window, the gap between two buildings. It adds depth, gives context and keeps the eye from drifting off the edges.

[[guide:frame]]

## Why it works

The frame creates layers. Something close, the subject further away, and the space between them make a flat image feel three-dimensional. It also shows where you were standing, which tells a story of its own.

It also does the job of the picture's edges. The eye tends to wander outwards. A frame inside the frame stops it and turns it back towards the subject.

## Where to look

- Doorways and arches in old towns and castles
- Overhanging branches at the edge of a wood
- Rock arches and caves on the coast
- Bridges, seen from underneath
- Windows, from inside looking out or from outside looking in
- Gaps between buildings, and the walls of a courtyard seen from below
- Fences, railings and gates
- Shadows, which can frame a lit patch of street

[[photo:Courtyard skylight]]

Looking straight up, the brick walls of the courtyard surround the glass skylight on all four sides, and the round tower in the lower left corner breaks into the frame.

## Keep the frame quiet

The frame should support the subject, not compete with it. It works best when it is darker than the view, or simpler. A shadowy archway around a bright street is the classic example.

A busy frame, with bright patches, signs or texture as strong as the subject, pulls the eye back to the edges. If the frame is busy, make it darker, softer or smaller in the picture.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, with spot or centre-weighted metering on the view so the dark frame does not fool it
- **Aperture:** f/11 to f/16 to keep frame and view sharp; around f/2.8 to melt the frame into a soft border
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld in daylight; slower on a tripod when stopped down in shade
- **ISO:** 100 to 400 in daylight; raise it only if the shutter speed gets too slow to hold
- **Focal length:** 24 mm to 35 mm full frame for arches and doorways; step back to fit the frame in
- **Focus:** About 1.8 m at 24 mm and f/11 for both sharp; otherwise on the subject

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Exposure

When the frame is in shade and the view is in light, the camera cannot always hold detail in both. Decide which matters.

- **Expose for the view** and let the frame fall dark, even to silhouette. This is usually the stronger picture, and it keeps the frame quiet
- **Use spot or centre-weighted metering** on the view, so the dark frame does not fool the meter into brightening everything
- **Check the histogram.** The dark frame will sit on the left. What matters is that the view is not pushed against the right edge
- **If you need detail in both,** take two frames, one for each, and blend them in editing

## Focus and depth

Decide what should be sharp. At f/11 or f/16 both the frame and the view stay crisp. At f/2.8 the frame melts into a soft border and the subject stands out. Both are valid choices.

Here is a worked example. You stand with an archway 1 metre away and a view in the distance, using a 24 mm lens on a full-frame camera.

1. At f/11 the hyperfocal distance is about 1.8 metres. The sum is 24 × 24 = 576, divided by 11 × 0.03 = 0.33, which gives about 1745 mm, plus the 24 mm focal length, so roughly 1.77 metres
2. Focus at about 1.8 metres and everything from about half that distance, 0.9 metres, to the far distance is acceptably sharp. The arch at 1 metre is just inside
3. At f/2.8 the hyperfocal distance is about 6.9 metres (576 ÷ 0.084 ≈ 6857 mm, plus 24 mm). Focus on the view 20 metres away and sharpness only starts at about 5 metres, so the arch at 1 metre becomes a soft border

The 0.03 mm in the sum is the usual allowance for full frame. Phone apps will do the sum for you, but knowing it tells you why stepping back from the frame makes it easier to keep sharp.

## The method in the field

1. Find the subject first, then look for something near you that could surround it
2. Move until the frame sits around the subject, not across it. Small steps sideways or up and down change the shape a great deal
3. Decide whether the frame should be sharp or soft, and set the aperture to match
4. Focus on the subject, or at the hyperfocal distance if you want both sharp
5. Meter for the view and let the frame go darker
6. Check that the frame does not touch or cut into the subject. Leave a gap between them
7. Check the edges of the whole picture for anything bright creeping in around the frame
8. Take a version without the frame as well, to see what it adds

## Partial frames and edges

A frame does not need four sides. A single branch across the top, or a wall down one side, is enough to close off that edge and hold the eye in.

## Worked scenarios

- **A castle through an archway.** Stand back far enough that the arch fits inside the frame with some wall around it. Meter for the castle and let the arch go dark
- **A loch through branches.** Use f/2.8 and get close to the leaves, so they become a soft border across the top
- **A street seen through a window.** Press the lens against the glass to cut out reflections, and keep the window edges straight
- **A figure in a doorway.** The doorway is the frame and the figure is the subject. Wait until they step into the lit part

## Common mistakes

- **A frame brighter than the view.** The eye goes to the edges. Change position, or expose so the frame darkens
- **The frame touching the subject.** A branch that meets the top of a tower merges with it. Move until there is clear space between them
- **A frame cut off awkwardly.** If half an arch sits at the edge, either include more of it or leave it out
- **Too much frame.** If the frame fills most of the picture, the subject becomes small and lost. Step forward
- **The wrong thing in focus.** Decide before you shoot whether the frame or the view should be sharp

## Going further

- **Leading lines.** Combine a path or a wall with a frame, so the eye is led in and then held
- **Rule of thirds.** The frame does not have to be central. Place the opening on a third
- **Silhouettes.** Push the frame fully to black for a graphic picture
- **Foreground interest.** Use shallow depth of field and something very close to the lens as a soft, colourful frame

> A frame does not have to be complete. Two branches can be enough.
lessons.challenge: Find an archway, window or gap in the trees. Photograph the view through it once at f/2.8 and once at f/11, metering for the view each time. Then take one frame without the frame in it, and compare what the frame adds.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What makes a natural frame work best?
* Being darker or simpler than the view through it
- Being brighter than the subject
- Being as detailed as possible

Q: At 24 mm and f/11 on full frame, the hyperfocal distance is about 1.8 m. Focused there, roughly where does acceptable sharpness begin?
* About 0.9 m
- About 1.8 m
- About 5 m

Q: The archway is in shade and the view is in sun. What do you expose for?
* The view, letting the frame fall darker
- The archway, letting the view blow out
- An average of both, every time

Q: Does a frame need to go all the way round the subject?
* No, two branches can be enough
- Yes, or it does not count as a frame
- Only in portrait format

lessons.title: Symmetry and patterns
lessons.summary: Reflections, repeating shapes and perfect balance. When to centre everything, and why breaking a pattern is often the photograph.
lessons.body:
Most composition advice tells you to move the subject off-centre. Symmetry is the exception. When a scene is balanced, centring it is the strongest choice.

[[guide:symmetry]]

## Kinds of symmetry

- **Mirror symmetry:** one half reflects the other across a line. A reflection in still water mirrors top to bottom. A doorway or a church nave mirrors left to right
- **Radial symmetry:** shapes repeat around a centre point, like a stairwell seen from below, a rose window or a dome
- **Repetition:** the same shape again and again across the frame, such as windows, posts or creels

In each case, find the line or point the scene is balanced on and place it exactly.

## What you need

- **A tripod,** for precise placement. Moving a few millimetres is far easier on a tripod than by hand
- **The grid display and the electronic level** in your camera. Turn both on
- **Lens corrections.** Wide lenses can bow straight lines near the edges, which shows at once in a symmetrical frame. Lightroom's lens corrections remove most of it
- **A polariser,** used with care. It cuts glare, but at full strength it will also remove the reflection you came for

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, on a tripod for precise placement
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11, for sharpness from edge to edge
- **Shutter speed:** Any speed on a tripod with the 2-second timer; 1/125 s or faster handheld
- **ISO:** 100 to 400 on a tripod; raise it only when handheld in dim interiors
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 35 mm full frame for interiors and reflections; 70 mm to 200 mm for patterns
- **Exposure:** Expose for the brighter half of a reflection, keeping its highlights off the right edge

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Reflections

Still water is the easiest symmetry to find. Get to a loch early, before the wind gets up, put the horizon through the middle and let the reflection mirror the scene. A low angle, close to the water, makes the reflection larger.

A few things decide how good the reflection is:

- **Wind.** Even a light breeze breaks the surface. Calm water is more likely early in the morning and around sunset
- **Puddles.** After rain, a puddle a few centimetres across can reflect a whole building if you put the lens right down beside it
- **Brightness.** The reflection is usually a little darker than the scene above it. Expose for the brighter half, check the histogram, and lift the reflection slightly in editing if it needs it
- **The polariser.** Turn it while watching the screen. At one point the reflection fades and you see into the water. Turn it back until the reflection is at its strongest

## Built symmetry

Architecture is full of it: bridges, doorways, church interiors, corridors. Stand exactly in the middle, keep the camera level and square to the subject, and check the edges match. Being a few centimetres off-centre is very obvious in a symmetrical frame.

Symmetry in a building is usually designed in on purpose, so the centre line is there to be found: the middle of a door, the peak of a gable, a line of floor tiles.

[[photo:Speicherstadt balconies]]

A column of lit, curved balconies runs up the centre of a brick facade, with matching round and arched windows on either side.

## Keeping lines straight

When you tilt the camera up at a building, its vertical lines lean towards each other. In a symmetrical frame the lean looks like a mistake unless it is clearly the point.

- Keep the back of the camera vertical, using the level, and step back or use a wider focal length to fit the building in
- Crop away the extra foreground afterwards
- Or correct it in editing with a perspective tool, such as Transform in Lightroom

Looking straight up, at a stairwell or a dome, the opposite applies. There are no verticals to keep straight, so aim the lens directly at the centre and let everything converge on it.

[[photo:Spiral]]

Concentric rings and radiating beams converge on a perforated disc of light in the exact centre of the frame.

## The field method

1. Find the line or point of symmetry: the centre of the arch, the axis of the corridor, the middle of the dome
2. Stand on that line. Use floor tiles, paving joints or a centre mark to place your feet
3. Set up the tripod and level the camera with the electronic level, both side to side and front to back
4. Turn on the grid and line the centre of the scene up with the centre of the frame
5. Compare matching features near the left and right edges. If one side shows more, move the whole tripod sideways. Panning the head instead turns the camera off square
6. Take the frame, then check it in playback before you move

## Patterns

Repetition is pleasing to the eye: rows of windows, ripples in sand, stacked lobster creels on a harbour wall. Fill the frame so the pattern seems to carry on beyond the edges.

- **Use a longer lens from further back.** At a distance, repeated objects near and far look more similar in size, instead of shrinking quickly into the distance. A 70-200 mm zoom suits this well
- **Choose square on or angled.** Square on gives a flat, graphic pattern. An angle gives a pattern that recedes. Both work. Something in between usually looks undecided
- **Look for low light.** Side light raises the texture in sand, stone and wood, and turns a flat surface into a pattern of light and shadow

## Break the pattern

The strongest pattern photographs often contain one thing that does not fit. A single red door in a terrace. One gull on a row of posts. The pattern sets up an expectation and the break becomes the subject.

The break works best when it is clearly different: a different colour, a different shape, or the only thing that moves. If the pattern is static, set up and wait for a person, a bird or a patch of light to supply it. Then place the break with care, either dead centre in a strict grid, or clearly off-centre so the regular pattern has room around it.

## Worked scenarios

- **A still loch at dawn.** Put the shoreline across the exact middle of the frame. Lower the tripod until the lens is close to the water, so the reflection is as large as possible. If a breeze ruffles the surface, wait for it to settle
- **A church nave.** Stand on the centre line of the aisle, level the camera, and use a wide focal length such as 16 mm to take in both rows of columns. Check that the end window sits in the middle and the first columns are the same distance from each edge
- **A harbour wall of creels.** Stand back with a telephoto and fill the frame edge to edge with the stack. Then look for the one creel in a different colour, or wait for a gull to land

## Common mistakes

- **Nearly symmetrical.** A frame that is almost centred looks like an error. Centre it exactly, or move clearly off-centre
- **A tilted horizon.** In a reflection the tilt shows twice. Use the level, and straighten in editing if needed
- **Bowed lines.** Wide-angle distortion curves straight edges near the sides of the frame. Apply lens corrections or zoom in slightly
- **Clutter on one side.** A bin, a sign or half a person on one edge breaks the balance. Move, wait or crop
- **A pattern that stops.** If the end of the pattern shows inside the frame, the eye goes straight to it. Zoom in or move closer until the pattern fills the frame

## Checking it in camera

Zoom into the playback image and compare matching points at the left and right edges, such as the bottom corners of a doorway. They should sit the same distance from the edge and at the same height. Then check the centre line and horizon against the grid. Do it before you leave. A small error is hard to fix later without cropping away part of the scene.

## Going further

- **Framing a person.** Put one figure in the centre of a symmetrical doorway or arch, so the architecture frames them
- **Abstracts.** Move close to a pattern until it loses its context and becomes shape and tone
- **Black and white.** Removing colour makes line and repetition stronger

> Symmetry is calm. A broken pattern is a story.
lessons.challenge: Find a symmetrical subject, such as a doorway, a bridge or a reflection. Centre it exactly using the grid and the level, then check both edges in playback. Next, find a repeating pattern such as windows, posts or boats, fill the frame with it, and wait for or find one thing that breaks it.
lessons.quiz:
Q: How do you make a reflection look larger?
* Lower the camera, closer to the water
- Raise the camera as high as possible
- Use a longer shutter speed

Q: You fit a polariser to photograph a reflection in a loch. How should you set it?
* Turn it until the reflection is at its strongest
- Turn it to full strength to remove all glare
- It makes no difference to water, so leave it anywhere

Q: In a symmetrical frame, the left edge shows more of the building than the right. What is the best fix?
* Move the whole tripod sideways until both edges match
- Pan the tripod head towards the right
- Zoom out until both edges are in

Q: Why photograph a row of repeated objects with a longer lens from further back?
* Near and far objects look more similar in size
- It makes the pattern brighter
- It lets you use a faster shutter speed

lessons.title: The golden ratio
lessons.summary: The spiral and the phi grid, where they come from, and how much weight to give them.
lessons.body:
The golden ratio is about 1.618 to 1. Painters and architects have used it for centuries, and photographers borrow it as two composition guides: the golden spiral and the phi grid.

[[guide:golden]]

## Where the number comes from

Split a line into two parts so that the whole line divided by the longer part equals the longer part divided by the shorter. Only one ratio works, and it is about 1.618. It is written with the Greek letter phi (φ). Euclid described it around 300 BC.

It also appears in the Fibonacci sequence, where each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. Divide each number by the one before and the answers close in on phi: 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6, 13 ÷ 8 = 1.625 and 21 ÷ 13 = about 1.615.

One more property gives you the phi grid. 1 ÷ 1.618 is about 0.618, and 1 minus 0.618 is 0.382.

## The golden spiral

Divide a golden rectangle into a square and a smaller golden rectangle, then keep going. A curve drawn through the squares makes a spiral that tightens towards one point. Line up that point with your subject, and let a curve in the scene, such as a shoreline or a sweep of cloud, follow the spiral round.

Each square is about 0.618 times the size of the one before, so the spiral grows by a factor of about 1.618 with every quarter turn.

The spiral can face any of four ways. Flip it to suit the photograph, not the other way round.

The nautilus shell is often given as an example of the golden spiral in nature. Its spiral does not in fact match the golden ratio, which is a fair reminder that the idea has been oversold.

## The phi grid

The phi grid places its lines at about 38% and 62% of the frame, instead of the thirds at 33% and 67%. The difference is small. It pulls the subject slightly closer to the centre, which can feel calmer than a strict thirds placement.

## A worked example

My camera, a Canon EOS R5, makes files 8192 pixels wide and 5464 pixels tall. Here is where the lines fall across the width, measured from the left edge.

- **Thirds:** 8192 ÷ 3 = about 2731 pixels, and 8192 × 2 ÷ 3 = about 5461 pixels
- **Phi grid:** 8192 × 0.382 = about 3129 pixels, and 8192 × 0.618 = about 5063 pixels
- **The gap:** 3129 minus 2731 is 398 pixels, about 5% of the width

Down the height, the thirds fall at about 1821 and 3643 pixels (5464 ÷ 3 and 5464 × 2 ÷ 3), and the phi lines at about 2087 and 3377 (5464 × 0.382 and 5464 × 0.618).

So moving a subject from a thirds line to a phi line shifts it about 400 pixels towards the centre. It is visible, but subtle.

The frame itself is not a golden rectangle: 8192 ÷ 5464 is about 1.5. To crop to a true golden rectangle and keep the full width, divide the width by 1.618. 8192 ÷ 1.618 = about 5063 pixels tall, so you lose 5464 minus 5063 = 401 rows.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, so attention stays on the point of interest and the curve
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for landscapes and architecture, so the curve and the subject both stay sharp
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/250 s handheld, and never slower than one over the focal length
- **ISO:** ISO 100 to 400 outdoors; 800 to 3200 under a dim interior roof
- **Focus:** Single-point autofocus on the point of interest, not on the curve
- **Framing:** Shoot RAW and leave a small margin at the edges for refining the crop

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## How to see it in the field

The spiral is not something to measure at the scene. It is a way of looking for two things together:

- A point of interest: a figure, a tree, a bright window
- A curve that leads towards it: a path, a river, the edge of a dune, a curved wall or stair

When you find both, place the point off-centre and let the curve sweep in from the opposite side of the frame. A method that works with any camera:

1. Compose with the thirds grid on, if your camera has no phi grid option
2. Place the subject just inside a thirds intersection, a little towards the centre
3. Leave a small margin around the edges, so you have room to refine the placement in the crop
4. In editing, turn on the spiral overlay and flip it until the tight end sits on the subject
5. Adjust the crop slightly. If the subject and the curve only fit with a heavy crop, go back to thirds

[[photo:Rings]]

A lit ring sweeps round a dark column under a glass roof, with smaller rings hanging above it. Strong curves like these are where the spiral overlay is most useful when cropping.

## Cropping with the overlays

- Most editing software can show a spiral and phi grid when cropping
- Try it when cropping, not just in camera
- If it does not fit naturally, do not force it

In Lightroom's crop tool, the O key cycles through the overlays, including the golden spiral and the golden ratio grid, which is the phi grid. Shift+O changes the orientation of the spiral.

## How much it matters

Be a little sceptical. There is not much evidence that the golden ratio looks better than other off-centre placements, and plenty of great photographs ignore it entirely. Treat it as one more way of checking a composition, and a useful one for curved subjects.

## Common mistakes

- **Forcing it.** Bending the crop to fit the spiral, at the cost of a cramped edge or a cut-off subject
- **The wrong orientation.** The spiral should wind in towards the subject. Flip it until the curve in the scene and the curve in the overlay agree
- **Treating it as precise.** The phi lines are close to the thirds. A few pixels either way makes no visible difference
- **Seeing it everywhere.** With enough curves in a scene and freedom to flip the overlay, almost any picture can be made to fit. That is a reason to use it lightly, not proof that it works

## Going further

- **Other overlays.** Lightroom also offers diagonal and triangle overlays. They suit pictures built on strong diagonal lines
- **Dynamic symmetry.** A related system of grids built from diagonals, worth reading about if the spiral interests you
- **Compare blind.** Make two crops of the same picture, one on thirds and one on phi, and ask someone which they prefer without saying which is which

> Guides help you see. They do not take the photograph for you.
lessons.challenge: Take five photographs you already like. Crop each with a thirds overlay and then a golden spiral or phi grid, and note which ones each guide improves. Note also how far the subject moved between the two crops.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Roughly what is the golden ratio?
* 1.618 to 1
- 1.5 to 1
- 3 to 1

Q: A frame is 8192 pixels wide. Roughly where does the left phi grid line fall?
* About 3129 pixels from the left edge
- About 2731 pixels from the left edge
- About 4096 pixels from the left edge

Q: Where are the phi grid lines compared with the thirds?
* Slightly closer to the centre
- Further out towards the edges
- In exactly the same place

Q: How much weight should you give the golden ratio?
* Treat it as one useful way of checking a composition
- Always follow it exactly
- Ignore it completely

lessons.title: Composing a landscape
lessons.summary: A wide view rarely works on its own. Give the eye a way in, a place to rest and a reason to stay.
lessons.body:
Stand in front of a great view, take a picture, and it often looks smaller and emptier than it felt. The scene needs structure.

## What you need

- **A wide zoom** for big foregrounds, such as a 16-35 mm, and **a telephoto zoom** for picking out part of a view
- **A tripod,** so you can refine the composition slowly and use a small aperture in low light
- **A polariser,** to cut glare on wet rock and leaves and deepen a blue sky. It works most strongly when the sun is at right angles to the direction the lens points
- **The grid display and electronic level** turned on in the camera

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, with the camera on a tripod
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; avoid f/16 and f/22, where diffraction softens fine detail
- **Shutter speed:** 1/250 s down to several seconds on the tripod; slow speeds are fine in low light
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 35 mm full frame for foregrounds; around 135 mm to stack distant layers
- **Focus:** Hyperfocal at f/11: about 0.8 m at 16 mm, about 1.77 m at 24 mm
- **Filter:** Polariser for glare on wet rock and leaves, strongest with the sun at right angles

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Find a foreground

Get low and put something close to the lens: rocks, heather, a fence post, ripples on the shore. It gives depth and a starting point for the eye. Use a smaller aperture such as f/11 so it stays sharp along with the distance.

A foreground works best when it points into the scene or echoes something in it: rocks that lead towards a headland, a stream that runs towards the mountain.

## Keeping it all sharp

f/11 on its own does not make everything sharp. Where you focus matters as much.

The hyperfocal distance is the closest point you can focus on and still keep the far distance acceptably sharp. Focus there, and everything from about half that distance to the horizon looks sharp. The formula is the focal length squared, divided by the aperture number times the circle of confusion, plus the focal length. For a full-frame camera the circle of confusion is usually taken as 0.03 mm.

Here is a worked example at 16 mm and f/11.

1. 16 × 16 = 256
2. 11 × 0.03 = 0.33
3. 256 ÷ 0.33 = about 776 mm. Add the 16 mm and you get about 792 mm, so about 0.8 metres
4. Focus at 0.8 metres and everything from about 0.4 metres to the horizon is acceptably sharp

At 24 mm and f/11 the same sum gives 576 ÷ 0.33 = about 1745 mm, plus 24 mm is about 1.77 metres. The nearest sharp point is then about 0.9 metres away, so a foreground closer than that will be soft.

"Acceptably sharp" is judged at normal viewing sizes. For large prints, treat these distances as a minimum and check the foreground in playback.

Stopping down further is not a free fix. On a high-resolution sensor, diffraction starts to soften fine detail beyond about f/11, so f/16 and f/22 trade overall crispness for extra depth.

## Use lines

Roads, rivers, walls and shorelines lead the eye through the frame. Diagonals feel more dynamic than lines running straight across.

Lines work best when they start near the bottom edge or a bottom corner and lead towards the main subject. A line that runs out of the side of the frame takes the eye out with it.

[[photo:Botallack]]

Pink and white flowers fill the foreground, a path drops towards the rocky cove, and the cliff line leads out to stone buildings on the headland and the low sun over the sea.

## Foreground, middle and background

Strong landscapes usually have something at each depth: a foreground to step into, a middle ground to cross and a background to finish on. If one layer is empty, the picture can feel flat or unfinished.

A telephoto does the opposite job to a wide lens. Standing further back, it compresses distance, so the layers stack up and distant hills, dunes or ridges look closer together than they are. That suits views where the shapes, rather than the space between them, are the subject.

[[photo:Storm over the dunes]]

At 135 mm, a twisted, leafless tree fills the right of the frame, with orange dunes behind it and purple storm cloud above.

## Place the horizon on purpose

The rule of thirds is a useful starting point, not a law. If the sky is the story, give it two thirds of the frame. If it is a dull grey, give it a sliver or leave it out. Either way, keep the horizon level.

Avoid the exact middle unless you want symmetry, such as a reflection. In most landscapes a central horizon splits the picture into two halves competing for attention.

A sea horizon near the top or bottom of a wide-angle frame can bow from lens distortion. Lens corrections in Lightroom fix most of it.

## Light and timing

Composition and light work together. Low side light, early and late in the day, picks out the shape of the land and gives texture to rock, grass and sand. Light from high overhead flattens it.

[[guide:planner]]

Use the planner to find when the sun will be low, then arrive early enough to settle on a composition before the light arrives. That is when the same view gives a different picture every few minutes, so keep looking rather than taking one frame and leaving.

## The method in the field

1. Walk the location before setting up. Look at the view from several heights and positions, not only the first spot you reach
2. Decide what drew you in. That is your subject
3. Find a foreground that leads towards it, and a line that connects the two
4. Set the tripod low, compose and level the camera
5. Place the horizon deliberately: high for a strong foreground, low for a strong sky
6. Set f/11 and focus at the hyperfocal distance for your focal length. If the foreground is closer than half that distance, plan to focus stack
7. Walk your eye round the edges of the frame, then take the shot
8. Check it in playback before you move on

## Simplify

Most weak compositions have too much in them. Before you press the shutter, walk your eye round the edges of the frame and ask what each thing is doing there.

- Move a few steps to separate overlapping shapes
- Zoom in on the part of the view that drew you in
- Try a portrait frame as well as a landscape one

## Common mistakes

- **No foreground,** so the picture has no depth. Get lower and closer to something
- **A foreground with no link** to the background. Look for one that points into the scene
- **A soft foreground.** Focusing on the horizon with a wide lens often leaves close rocks soft. Focus nearer, as in the worked example
- **A sloping horizon.** Use the electronic level, and straighten in editing if needed
- **Mergers.** A tree growing out of a hilltop, or a post touching the horizon. Move until the shapes separate
- **A blown sky.** If the histogram is pressed against the right edge, reduce the exposure slightly, or take a second, darker frame for the sky and blend the two

## Checking it in camera

Magnify the playback image twice: once on the nearest part of the foreground and once on the horizon. Both should look crisp. Then look at the whole frame small, which shows the balance of light and dark more clearly than looking at it full size. Finally, check the histogram is not pressed hard against either edge.

## Going further

- **Focus stacking.** Take several frames focused at different distances and blend them in Photoshop (Edit, Auto-Align Layers, then Edit, Auto-Blend Layers, Stack Images) for more depth than any single aperture gives
- **Exposure blending.** Combine a frame exposed for the sky with one exposed for the land
- **The intimate landscape.** Use a telephoto to pick out one small part of the view: a single tree, a patch of light on a hillside

> If it does not add to the picture, it takes away from it.
lessons.challenge: At your next view, take one photograph as you first see it. Then get low with something close to the lens, focus at the hyperfocal distance for your focal length, and take a second. Magnify both foregrounds in playback and compare the two.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why put something in the foreground?
* It adds depth and gives the eye a starting point
- It hides the sky
- It makes the exposure easier

Q: Using a circle of confusion of 0.03 mm, roughly what is the hyperfocal distance at 16 mm and f/11?
* About 0.8 metres
- About 8 metres
- About 8 centimetres

Q: You focus at a hyperfocal distance of 1.8 metres. Roughly what range is acceptably sharp?
* From about 0.9 metres to the horizon
- From 1.8 metres to the horizon only
- From the lens to 1.8 metres

Q: The sky is flat and grey. What do you do?
* Give it a sliver of the frame or leave it out
- Give it two thirds of the frame
- Put the horizon in the middle

lessons.title: Minimalism
lessons.summary: One subject, a lot of empty space and nothing else. Minimalism is the art of taking things out until the picture breaks, then putting one back.
lessons.body:
Minimalist photographs strip a scene down to as little as possible: usually one subject and a large area of empty space. Done well they are calm, strong and memorable. Done badly they are just empty.

[[guide:space]]

## What you need

Very little, which is part of the appeal.

- **A telephoto zoom,** to isolate a subject from busy surroundings. A 70-200 or 100-400 mm lets you crop the scene in camera from a distance
- **A wide lens,** for the opposite approach: a small subject in a big sky or a wide sea
- **Exposure compensation** you can set quickly. Bright, plain scenes fool the meter
- **A clean sensor and lens.** Plain skies show every speck of dust

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, with exposure compensation ready to dial in
- **Aperture:** f/5.6 to f/8; smaller apertures show sensor dust in plain skies
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; 1/500 s or faster at 400 mm
- **ISO:** 100 to 400, kept low so plain sky, fog and water stay smooth
- **Focal length:** 70 to 400 mm full frame to isolate; 16 to 24 mm for a small subject in big space
- **Exposure compensation:** +1 to +2 stops for snow, fog or sand; minus for dark scenes

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Negative space

The empty area around the subject is called negative space. It is not wasted. It gives the subject room, sets the mood and makes something small feel significant. A lone boat on a flat calm sea is more powerful than the same boat in a busy harbour.

Negative space does not have to be white or empty sky. A plain wall, deep shadow, a smooth slope of sand or flat water all count, as long as nothing in it competes with the subject.

[[photo:Bleached]]

A single pale, bare tree stands on bright white ground against a soft, hazy wash of light. At 400 mm almost everything else is left out of the frame.

## Where to find it

- Fog and mist, which erase the background
- Flat calm water and plain skies
- Snow, sand and beaches at low tide
- Long exposures, which smooth water and cloud into plain tone
- Plain walls in towns, with one person, door or window

## Isolating with a long lens

A telephoto is one of the easiest ways to simplify. Its narrow angle of view takes in only a small slice of background, so it is easier to find a plain one behind your subject. Move a few steps sideways and the background behind the subject changes completely.

## Keep it simple, but not empty

The subject still needs to be placed with care. Thirds work well, and so does putting a small subject low or to one side so the space reads as deliberate. Check every edge of the frame for a stray branch, post or bird that pulls the eye away.

Give the space a direction. A subject facing or moving into the space feels settled. The same subject facing out of the frame, with all the space behind it, feels uneasy. Either can work, but choose it.

There is no rule for how small the subject can be, but the sums help. In a 3:2 frame, a subject one tenth of the width and one third of the height covers 1/10 × 1/3 = 1/30 of the picture. That can still hold the frame, if it is the only thing with real contrast.

## Colour and tone

Limit the palette. Two or three tones, or one colour against neutral grey, works better than a full range. Many minimalist images are slightly overexposed to keep the space clean and light.

A single strong colour against muted surroundings becomes a subject on its own, even when it is small.

[[photo:Red dress]]

A figure in a red dress and a bare tree stand on pale ground in front of a dark, plain slope of sand. The red is the only strong colour in the frame.

Black and white is another way to reduce a picture to tone. The Black and white lesson covers how to judge it.

## Exposing bright, plain scenes

The camera's meter assumes the scene averages out to mid grey. Point it at snow, fog, white sand or a bright sky and it darkens everything towards grey. Add exposure compensation to bring the brightness back.

Here is a worked example. The camera meters a misty beach at **f/8, 1/500 s, ISO 100**, and the result looks dull and grey.

1. Dial in +2 stops of exposure compensation
2. Each stop doubles the time, so 1/500 s becomes 1/250 s, then 1/125 s
3. Check the histogram. The graph should sit well to the right without pressing against the right edge
4. If the highlight warning flashes across the space, come back by a third or two thirds of a stop

Dark minimal scenes work the other way. A subject against deep shadow may need minus compensation to keep the shadow black rather than a muddy grey.

## The method in the field

1. Find the space first: fog, water, sky, sand, a plain wall
2. Look for one subject with clear contrast against it, in tone, colour or shape
3. Choose the lens: telephoto to cut out clutter, wide to make the space feel vast
4. Place the subject low, to one side or on a thirds point, with space in the direction it faces
5. Walk your eye round every edge and remove anything that does not belong, by moving, zooming or waiting
6. Set exposure compensation and check the histogram
7. Take one version with the subject smaller and one with it larger. The right size is rarely obvious at the scene

## Common mistakes

- **Empty, not minimal.** Space with no subject, or a subject too weak to hold it. Make sure one thing clearly stands out
- **Grey snow and grey fog.** The meter at work. Add exposure compensation
- **Clutter at the edges.** A half-visible post, a distant person, a strand of grass. Check all four edges and the corners
- **Dust spots.** Small apertures and plain skies show sensor dust clearly. Check at 100% in editing and remove the spots, or clean the sensor
- **A tilted horizon.** With nothing else in the frame, even a slight slope is obvious. Use the level
- **Banding.** Smooth gradients in sky or fog can break into visible steps when pushed hard in editing. Shoot RAW and edit gently

## Checking it in camera

Look at the playback image small, the size of a thumbnail. A strong minimalist picture still reads at that size: one clear shape and a clean space. Then zoom into each corner for stray detail, and check the histogram and the highlight warning.

## Going further

- **High key.** Push the exposure further so the space goes almost white, while the subject keeps its detail
- **Long exposures** with ND filters, to turn busy water and cloud into plain tone
- **Minimal street.** Wait by a plain wall or a band of light for one person to walk into the frame

> Keep taking things out until it stops working. Then put the last one back.
lessons.challenge: Make a photograph with one subject taking up less than a tenth of the frame. Check every edge before you press the shutter. If the space is bright, add exposure compensation and check the histogram, then take a second version with the subject a different size.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is negative space?
* The empty area around the subject
- The dark parts of the image
- The space behind the camera

Q: The meter reads 1/500 s for a bright, misty beach. You add +2 stops by shutter speed alone. What is the new shutter speed?
* 1/125 s
- 1/250 s
- 1/1000 s

Q: Why does snow often come out grey straight from the camera?
* The meter assumes the scene averages out to mid grey
- Snow reflects less light than it appears to
- The white balance is set wrongly

Q: Why does a telephoto help with minimalist pictures?
* Its narrow angle of view takes in a small slice of background that is easier to keep plain
- It always makes the subject brighter
- It removes the need to check the edges

lessons.title: Reflections
lessons.summary: Still water, puddles, wet sand and glass give you the same subject twice. Get low, wait for calm, and focus on the reflection, not the surface.
lessons.body:
A reflection gives you the same subject twice, once upside down and slightly changed. The second version is darker, softer and often more interesting than the first.

## Where reflections hide

- **Still water.** Lakes, canals and harbours. Sheltered water, such as a dock or an enclosed pool, stays calm when open water does not
- **Puddles.** A puddle a metre across can hold a whole building if you get low enough
- **Wet sand.** A wave drawing back leaves a thin film of water that mirrors the sky for a few seconds
- **Glass.** Office blocks and shop windows reflect the street. A shop window also shows what is inside, so you get two layers
- **Metal.** Car bodywork and polished steel bend the reflection with their curves

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, exposing for the brighter half, usually the sky; the reflection sits about a stop darker
- **Aperture:** f/11 to f/13, to hold a near puddle edge and a distant reflection both sharp
- **Shutter speed:** 1/100 s or faster handheld and on wet sand; several seconds on a tripod to smooth ripples
- **ISO:** 100 to 800; raise it only to keep 1/100 s in dull light
- **Focal length:** 24 mm to 35 mm full frame, the wider end for puddles so they fill the foreground
- **Focus:** On the reflected subject, not the surface; about 1.75 m at 24 mm and f/11
- **Filter:** Polariser off, or rotated to the position that keeps the reflection at full strength

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Where to put the line

The line where the scene meets its reflection works like a horizon. See the Where to put the horizon lesson for the general rule.

- **Halfway** gives you symmetry. Use it when the reflection is close to perfect and the subject can carry a formal, balanced picture. See the Symmetry and patterns lesson
- **Low in the frame** gives the scene the weight. Use it when the water is rippled or the sky is the best part
- **High in the frame** gives the reflection the weight. Use it when the reflection is cleaner than the real thing, or the scene above is cluttered

Whichever you choose, keep the line level. A tilted waterline is easy to spot, because the reflection tilts with it.

[[photo:Reflections of Bath]]

The edge of the pool sits close to the middle of the frame, and the columns and abbey tower are mirrored almost perfectly below. 24 mm, f/13, 1/100 s, ISO 200.

## Why the reflection is darker

Water reflects only part of the light that falls on it. The rest passes into the water or is absorbed. Looking steeply down, you see little reflection and a lot of what is under the surface. Looking across at a shallow angle, the reflection gets much stronger.

So a reflection is almost always darker than the scene, often by around a stop. That is useful: it tells the viewer which half is real.

- Expose for the brighter half, usually the sky
- If the gap is too wide, a soft graduated ND filter over the top half evens it out
- In editing, lift the reflection a little, but not to match. A reflection as bright as the scene looks fake

## Get low

The lower the camera, the shallower the angle to the surface, and the bigger the reflection becomes. From standing height, a small puddle shows a patch of sky. Put the camera a few centimetres above it and the same puddle can hold a whole building.

1. Find a puddle with something tall beyond it, and stand so the subject is directly behind it
2. Lower the camera until the lens is just above the water. A tilting screen saves lying in it
3. Shuffle sideways and forwards until the reflected subject sits inside the puddle, not across its edge
4. Use a wide lens so the puddle fills the foreground

## Wind and timing

The smallest breeze breaks a reflection into ripples. Wind is often lightest around dawn, so a calm early morning is the most reliable time for a mirror finish. A sheltered spot helps at any hour.

Wind comes in gusts, and the water can settle for a few seconds between them. Compose, then wait with your finger on the button. On wet sand, shoot just after a wave draws back.

If the water will not settle, a long exposure of several seconds averages the ripples into a smooth surface, and the reflection returns as a soft glow. See the Long exposure lesson.

## Polarisers

A polariser removes reflections, so it can ruin a reflection picture.

- Light reflected off water and glass is partly polarised, so a polariser cuts it. The effect is strongest when you look at the surface at roughly 35 to 40 degrees
- Rotate the filter while you watch the screen. One position kills the reflection; a quarter turn from it keeps it at full strength. Or take the filter off
- Reflections in bare metal are barely polarised, so a polariser does little to them

See the Filters lesson for how a polariser works.

## Focusing on the reflection

The reflection is not on the surface of the water. A mirror image sits as far behind the surface as the subject is in front of it, so to the lens a reflected building is roughly as far away as the real one.

- Focus on the reflection, or on the real subject, which is at much the same distance
- Focus on a leaf, a ripple or the edge of the puddle and the reflection will be soft
- Autofocus often grabs the surface. Use a single small focus point on a high-contrast edge in the reflection, or focus manually with the screen magnified

## Depth of field

Often you want the puddle edge and the reflected building both sharp. They are at very different distances, so you need depth of field.

A worked example, on full frame. At 24 mm and f/11, the hyperfocal distance is about 24 × 24 ÷ (11 × 0.03) = 576 ÷ 0.33, which is about 1.75 m. Focus there and everything from about 0.9 m to infinity is acceptably sharp. A puddle edge 1 m away and a building 50 m away will both hold.

If the puddle edge is nearer than that, you will have to choose. A soft puddle edge with a sharp reflection usually looks better than the other way round.

[[photo:Reflections and Shadows]]

Wet sand reflects the sunlit peaks and the grey sky above them, and the reflection is darker and softer than the mountains themselves. 35 mm, f/11, 1/100 s, ISO 800.

## Worked scenarios

- **A city puddle after rain.** Camera almost on the ground, wide lens, f/11, focus on the building beyond. Wait for the last raindrop ripples to die away
- **A lake at dawn.** Arrive before sunrise, polariser off. Put the line halfway if the reflection is perfect. If a breeze starts, move the line lower and let the scene take the weight
- **Wet sand.** Stand where the waves just reach and shoot a burst each time one draws back. 1/100 s or faster keeps the edge of the retreating water crisp
- **A glass tower.** Step sideways until the reflected building sits in a clean run of glass, not across a joint

[[photo:Der Spiegel]]

The lit windows and the deep blue sky are repeated in the water in front of the buildings. The reflections are softer and darker than the buildings above them.

## Turn it upside down

A reflection on its own, with ripples breaking straight lines into wobbling shapes, makes a strong abstract. Flip it upside down afterwards (Lightroom's Flip Vertical does it) and it reads the right way up but strangely painted. See the Abstract lesson.

## Common mistakes

- **Polariser left on.** The reflection fades. Take it off or rotate it
- **Focused on the surface.** Focus on the reflected subject instead
- **A tilted waterline.** Use the camera's electronic level. Straightening later loses the edges of the frame
- **Camera too high.** Get lower
- **Line placed by habit.** Give the stronger half more room, or commit to the middle
- **Your own reflection** in glass. Change your angle

## Checking in camera

1. Magnify the screen on the reflection and check it is sharp
2. Check the waterline against the level or the grid
3. Check the histogram: the sky should not press against the right edge, and the reflection should hold shadow detail
4. Scan the surface for ripples, leaves and litter

## Going further

- **Shop windows,** where the street and the display merge into one layered picture
- **Night reflections** on wet tarmac and dark water. See the Night and blue hour in cities lesson

> Look down. The best picture of a building is sometimes in the puddle at your feet.
lessons.challenge: After rain, find one puddle with something tall behind it. Take the same subject three ways: from standing height, with the camera a few centimetres above the water, and with the reflection alone cropped tight and flipped upside down afterwards. Focus on the reflected subject each time.
lessons.quiz:
Q: You are photographing a building reflected in a puddle 1 m away. The building is 40 m away. Where should you focus for the sharpest reflection?
* On the building or its reflection, at around 40 m
- On the surface of the puddle, at 1 m
- Halfway, at about 20 m

Q: Why is a reflection usually darker than the scene it reflects?
* Water reflects only part of the light; the rest passes into it or is absorbed
- The camera meters the reflection separately
- Reflections are always in shadow

Q: Your reflection has almost disappeared and you can see stones under the water. What is the likely cause?
* A polariser is turned to the position that cuts the reflection
- The shutter speed is too fast
- The aperture is too small

Q: On full frame at 24 mm and f/11, the hyperfocal distance is about 1.75 m. Roughly what is sharp if you focus there?
* From about 0.9 m to infinity
- From 1.75 m to infinity only
- From about 0.2 m to 3.5 m

lessons.title: Telephoto landscapes
lessons.summary: Landscapes are not only for wide-angle lenses. A long lens picks one shape out of a big view and stacks distant layers on top of each other.
lessons.body:
The usual advice for landscapes is to go wide. Plenty of strong landscape photographs come from the other end: a 100-400 mm zoom. Every Deadvlei photograph on this site was taken with it.

[[guide:focal]]

## What compression really is

People say long lenses compress a scene, making distant things look closer together. Strictly, the lens is not doing it. Perspective depends only on where you stand. A long lens lets you stand far back and still fill the frame, and from far back the near and far objects look closer in size. That is the effect you see when you move the slider.

Here is a worked example. A tree stands 100 metres from you, with a dune 400 metres away behind it.

1. From here the dune is four times further away than the tree, so it is drawn at a quarter of the tree's scale: 100 ÷ 400 = 0.25
2. Walk back 300 metres. The tree is now 400 metres away and the dune 700 metres: 400 ÷ 700 = about 0.57
3. Next to the tree, the dune now looks more than twice as large as it did before: 0.57 ÷ 0.25 = about 2.3
4. To keep the tree the same size in the frame from four times further away, you need four times the focal length: 100 mm becomes 400 mm

Zooming changes only the crop. Walking changes the relationship between the layers. Use your feet first, then the zoom ring.

## Why it works for landscapes

- It isolates one shape, such as a single tree, a ridge or a patch of light, from a cluttered view
- It stacks layers: hills, mist and dunes pile up into bands of tone
- It makes distant mountains and dunes loom over the foreground
- It cuts out a dull sky or an untidy edge

[[photo:Shadow line]]

Shot at 400 mm. The dune edge and the shadow become a simple graphic line because the lens cuts away everything around them.

## What you need

- **A long lens.** A 70-200 mm is a good start. A 100-400 mm reaches further
- **A solid tripod.** Mine is a Three Legged Thing Winston. If the lens has a tripod collar, mount the collar rather than the camera, so the weight sits over the tripod head
- **A remote release,** or the 2-second self-timer, so pressing the button does not shake the camera

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, or manual for matching frames
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; stopping down further gains little and costs sharpness through diffraction
- **Shutter speed:** Any speed on a tripod in still air; handheld, at least 1/400 s at 400 mm full frame
- **ISO:** 100 to 400; raise it if wind moves the subject and a faster speed is needed
- **Focal length:** 70 mm to 400 mm full frame; 200 mm to 400 mm to isolate one shape
- **Focus:** Magnified live view on the main layer, then switch to manual so the lens cannot hunt
- **Stabilisation:** Off on a tripod, unless the lens is designed to detect one

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Seeing with a long lens

A wide view shows you everything at once. A long lens makes you look for one thing. Before you set up, zoom to the longest end and sweep slowly across the view, as you would with binoculars. Look for:

- One clear shape against a plain background
- Ridges, dunes or trees that overlap, each a slightly different tone
- A patch of light falling on one part of the scene while the rest is in shadow
- Repeated shapes, such as rows of trees, field edges or ripples in sand

A valley at dawn is a good example. Wide, it is a pleasant view with a lot of empty sky. At 300 mm, aimed where three ridges overlap, it becomes a stack of bands, each paler than the one in front, because there is more haze between you and each further ridge.

The long lens also helps when you are not alone. In Deadvlei, on a photography holiday in Namibia with James Kerwin, I used the 100-400 so I could stand back, rather than walk into the scene and end up in someone else's photograph.

[[photo:First light]]

Shot at 400 mm. The tree stands against a plain, dark background with no horizon or sky, so its shape is all there is to look at.

## Light and timing

A long lens shows only a small piece of the scene, so the light on that piece matters more. Side light, a gap in the cloud or the first sun catching a ridge will carry a telephoto picture. In Deadvlei the best light came before the sun cleared the dunes.

[[guide:planner]]

## Sharpness: shake, wind and haze

- Long lenses magnify shake. Use a tripod, or keep the shutter at least as fast as one over the focal length. At 400 mm that is 1/400 s. On a camera with a 1.6 crop factor it is 1/640 s, because 400 × 1.6 = 640
- Image stabilisation buys you a few stops handheld, but it cannot freeze a tree moving in the wind
- Heat haze softens distant detail on hot days and over warm ground. Early morning is clearer
- Wind matters more. Shelter the tripod and hang your bag from it

## Depth of field at a distance

You do not always need a small aperture. With everything far away, f/8 to f/11 is usually enough for front-to-back sharpness. Stopping down further gains little and costs a little sharpness through diffraction.

The numbers show why. The hyperfocal distance is the focal length squared, divided by the aperture times 0.03 mm (a common figure for full frame).

- At 400 mm and f/11: 400 × 400 = 160,000, and 11 × 0.03 = 0.33. 160,000 ÷ 0.33 is about 485,000 mm, or about 485 metres. Focus there and everything from about 240 metres to the horizon is acceptably sharp
- At 100 mm and f/11: 100 × 100 = 10,000, and 10,000 ÷ 0.33 is about 30,000 mm, or 30 metres

So at 400 mm, a tree 100 metres away is sharp from only about 83 to 126 metres. A distant dune behind it will be soft, whatever aperture you use. Decide which layer matters and focus on that.

## The method in the field

1. Walk the view with the lens at its longest end before you set up, and find the one shape or layer you want
2. Choose your position. Move back or forward to change how the layers sit against each other, then zoom to frame
3. Set up the tripod on firm ground and mount the lens by its collar if it has one
4. Turn off image stabilisation, unless your lens is designed to detect a tripod
5. Set f/8 to f/11 and a low ISO, and check the shutter speed. If the wind is moving the subject, raise the ISO to get a faster speed
6. Focus on the main subject using magnified live view, then switch to manual focus so the lens cannot hunt
7. Fire with the remote or the 2-second timer, and take several frames. Haze shimmers, and one frame is often sharper than the rest
8. Check the result, as below, before moving on

## Common mistakes

- **Soft distant detail.** Usually heat haze rather than focus. Go out earlier, before the ground warms up
- **Blur from shake.** A slow shutter speed on a light tripod in wind. Lower the centre column, hang your bag from the hook, and use a faster speed if you can
- **Focus on the wrong layer.** Autofocus picks the most contrasty thing. Magnify live view and place the focus yourself
- **Autofocus hunting in mist or low contrast.** Focus on an edge with contrast at the same distance, or focus manually
- **Flat, grey pictures.** Haze lowers contrast over long distances. A little added contrast or dehaze in editing brings it back
- **Too much in the frame.** If you can name three subjects, zoom in or move until there is one

## Checking your result

Zoom in to 100 percent on the playback screen and look at the subject and the furthest detail. Compare two or three frames from the same burst; haze and wind often make one sharper than the others. Then check the histogram, because distant scenes in bright light can look fine on the screen and still clip in the highlights.

## Going further

- **Telephoto panoramas.** Take several overlapping frames at 200 mm and merge them in Lightroom. You keep the compressed look with far more detail and a wider shape
- **Abstracts.** Ripples in sand, patterns of fields and lines of trees become graphic designs at long focal lengths
- **Small in the landscape.** A person, animal or building placed small in a big, plain scene gives a sense of scale

> Go wide to show where you were. Go long to show what you saw.

For one of them, take the same framing from two positions, one near and one far back, zooming to keep the subject the same size, and compare the background.
