- High ISO

lessons.title: Long exposure
lessons.summary: Leave the shutter open for seconds or minutes and the moving world disappears. Water turns to mist, clouds to streaks, traffic to ribbons of light.
lessons.body:
A long exposure records everything that happens while the shutter is open. Anything still stays sharp. Anything moving smears, fades or vanishes. That contrast is the whole effect.

[[guide:longexp]]

## What you need

- **A solid tripod.** Even a breath of wind on a light tripod will blur a 30-second exposure. Mine is a Three Legged Thing Winston
- **ND filters,** to cut the light in daylight. I use Kase
- **A remote release,** or the 2-second self-timer, so pressing the button does not shake the camera
- **Spare batteries.** Long exposures, cold weather and live view all drain them fast
- **A lens cloth.** Sea spray and drizzle on the filter show up as soft blotches

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Manual, switching to Bulb with a remote for anything beyond 30 s
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; close to f/16 only when one more stop of time is needed
- **Shutter speed:** 1/4 s to 4 s for water on rocks, 10 s to 30 s for mist, minutes for cloud
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **Focus:** Autofocus before fitting the filter, then switch the lens to manual focus
- **Filter:** 6 stops for half a second to two seconds in daylight, 10 stops for longer; none at night

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## ND filters

A neutral density filter is dark glass that cuts the light without changing its colour. Strength is measured in stops, and every stop doubles the exposure time.

- **3 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 1/15 s. Softens waterfalls and waves
- **6 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 1/2 s. Smooths moving water
- **10 stops:** 1/125 s becomes 8 s. Flattens the sea and streaks the clouds
- **15 stops:** 1/125 s becomes about 4 minutes. Turns the sea to glass and drags clouds into long smears

The 10-stop is the one most people start with. A 6-stop is more useful than it sounds, because many of the best water pictures sit between half a second and two seconds, not thirty.

## Working out the time

Phone apps will do the sums, but it helps to understand them, so you can check the app or manage without it.

Here is a worked example. Without a filter, the camera meters a seascape at **f/11, 1/60 s, ISO 100**.

1. Fit a 10-stop filter. Ten doublings of 1/60 s is 1/60 × 1024, which is about 17 seconds
2. You want more blur. Close the aperture one stop to f/16 and the time doubles to about 34 seconds
3. You want the sea completely flat. Swap to a 15-stop filter at f/11 and the time becomes about 9 minutes

Most cameras will only time exposures up to 30 seconds. Beyond that, use Bulb mode with a remote or the camera's own bulb timer.

## The method in the field

1. Set up the tripod on firm ground and push the legs well in on sand or soft earth
2. Compose and focus without the filter, while you can still see clearly. Then switch the lens to manual focus so it cannot hunt
3. Turn off image stabilisation, unless your lens is designed to detect a tripod
4. Take a meter reading without the filter and note the settings
5. Fit the filter without knocking the focus ring or the zoom
6. Work out the new time, set it, and fire with the remote or the 2-second timer
7. With a DSLR, cover the viewfinder during the exposure so light cannot leak in
8. Check the histogram and the edges of the frame, then adjust and go again

Then remember to switch the timer off when the camera comes off the tripod. Forgetting to is my longest-running mistake.

I never rely on a single frame. I take a lot of shots at a few different exposure times and choose afterwards. A few seconds either way changes how the water looks, and it is far easier to pick the right one at home than to guess on the spot.

## Choosing a shutter speed for water

There is no correct time. Each range gives a different look.

- **1/4 s to 1 s:** waves keep their shape but gain soft, flowing texture. Water running back off rocks leaves fine white trails
- **1 to 4 seconds:** waves become streaks and swirls. Often the most interesting range on a rocky shore
- **10 to 30 seconds:** the sea turns to mist around the rocks
- **1 minute and beyond:** the water goes completely flat and glassy, and the clouds drag into long streaks

Time your exposure with the waves. Starting just as a wave pulls back from the rocks gives a different picture from starting as one breaks over them.

Keep something solid in the frame, such as rocks, a pier or a post, so the smoothness has something to contrast with.

[[photo:Lofoten shore]]

Rock and sand anchor the foreground and stay sharp, while the sea beyond is softened by the moving water.

[[photo:Lindisfarne]]

Two seconds. The water at the edge of the shore softens into a white haze, while the pebbles in front stay sharp.

## Clouds

Moving cloud needs much longer than water: usually 30 seconds to several minutes, depending on the wind. It works best when the clouds are moving towards or away from you, because the streaks then radiate out from the horizon. Clouds moving across the frame just smear sideways.

On a clear day there is nothing to streak, so save the 15-stop filter for days with broken, fast-moving cloud.

## Light trails

At night you do not need a filter. Ten to thirty seconds at f/8 to f/11 turns traffic into streams of red and white light, while the buildings stay sharp.

- Start the exposure just as traffic enters the frame, so the trails run all the way through
- Busy roads give dense ribbons. Quieter roads give single, cleaner lines
- Bridges and junctions where roads curve make the trails more interesting than a straight road
- Buses are tall, so their lights draw a higher line than cars

[[photo:Chilehaus]]

A single car passing during the exposure leaves a thin red line at the base of the building, while the lit facade stays perfectly still.

## Blue hour

After sunset the light falls fast enough that exposures of several seconds happen without any filter. Still water becomes a mirror and lit windows glow. The light can halve in a few minutes, so check the exposure again every few frames.

## Common mistakes

- **Soft pictures from a moving tripod.** Lower the centre column, hang your bag from the hook and shield the camera from the wind with your body
- **A colour cast.** Strong ND filters often add a warm or cool tint. Shoot RAW and correct the white balance afterwards, or take one test frame and set a custom white balance
- **Dark corners.** Stacking filters on a wide lens can vignette. Use one stronger filter instead of two weaker ones, or zoom in slightly
- **Light leaks.** Gaps around a square filter holder, or an uncovered DSLR viewfinder, let in stray light that shows as hazy patches or streaks
- **Noise and hot pixels.** Very long exposures heat the sensor. Long-exposure noise reduction fixes much of it, but it doubles the wait, because the camera takes a second, dark frame of the same length
- **Water on the filter.** Check the front of the filter between every frame on the coast

## Reading the histogram

The screen on the back of the camera is a poor judge of brightness at night or in bright sun. The histogram is honest. Make sure the graph is not pushed hard against either edge. A long exposure of a bright sea often wants the graph sitting slightly to the right, so the shadows in the rocks hold detail.

## Going further

- **Stacking instead of filtering.** No ND filter? Take twenty or thirty short exposures in a row and average them in Photoshop (Layer, Smart Objects, Stack Mode, Mean). The moving water smooths out just as it would in one long frame
- **Blending exposures.** Take one long exposure for the water and a shorter one for a bright sky, then combine them in editing
- **Night skies.** Point the camera at the Pole Star and leave it for 30 minutes or more, and the stars draw circles around it. The method is the same, only longer

> Find something that will not move, then let everything else go.

lessons.title: Filters
lessons.summary: Most effects can be added later in editing. Two cannot: a polariser removing glare, and an ND filter slowing the shutter. Those are the filters worth carrying.
lessons.body:
I carry Kase filters, and in practice I reach for two kinds: neutral density filters for long exposures and a polariser. Almost everything else can be done afterwards in editing. These two cannot.

## What you need

- **A polariser.** Buy one for your largest filter thread and use step-up rings for smaller lenses. A 77 to 82 mm step-up ring lets an 82 mm filter fit a 77 mm lens
- **One or two ND filters.** A 6-stop and a 10-stop cover most needs
- **A square filter holder,** if you want graduated filters or to stack more than one filter
- **A blower and a lens cloth**
- **A padded pouch.** Loose filters in a bag pick up scratches quickly

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority with a polariser; manual with a strong ND, where metering can struggle
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/16 for landscapes; as wide as f/2 with an ND in bright sun
- **Shutter speed:** Expect one to two stops slower with a polariser, so 1/250 s becomes 1/125 s or 1/60 s
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **Focus:** Focus and compose before fitting a dark ND, then switch to manual focus
- **ND exposure:** Multiply the metered time by 8 for 3 stops, 64 for 6 stops, 1024 for 10 stops

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## The polariser

A polariser cuts reflected glare. Turn the ring and you can watch the sky deepen, clouds stand out, the shine disappear from wet leaves and the surface of water turn clear enough to see the stones below.

[[guide:polariser]]

- It works best with the sun at right angles to the direction you are pointing
- On a wide lens it can darken one part of the sky more than another, so watch the edges
- It costs one to two stops of light
- Take it off at night and when there is nothing to remove

## Why it works

Light reflected from water, glass, wet rock, leaves and paint is partly polarised: it vibrates mostly in one direction. Light from a clear blue sky is polarised too, most strongly in a band at right angles to the sun. A polariser only lets through light vibrating in one direction, so turning it blocks more or less of the glare.

To find the strongest band, point your index finger at the sun with your thumb sticking up at a right angle. Rotate your hand, keeping your finger on the sun. Wherever your thumb points, the sky will darken most.

## Using a polariser, step by step

1. Fit the polariser and compose the picture
2. Watch the screen or viewfinder and turn the ring slowly. The effect repeats every half turn, so you never need to turn it further than that
3. Stop where the picture looks best, which is not always the strongest setting. On a lake you may want to keep some reflection of the hills
4. If you turn the camera from landscape to portrait, or recompose, turn the ring again. The effect moves with the camera
5. Check the shutter speed. You have lost one to two stops, so 1/250 s becomes 1/125 s or 1/60 s

Rainbows are polarised light. Turned one way, a polariser makes a rainbow stronger. Turned the other way, it removes it completely.

## Where a polariser does little

- With the sun directly behind you or straight ahead
- On reflections from bare metal, which are not polarised in the same way
- On the sky in flat, overcast light, though it will still cut the shine from wet leaves and rocks
- At night, when you need every bit of light

## ND filters

An ND filter is plain dark glass that lets you use a slow shutter speed in daylight. The Long exposure lesson covers them in detail.

- **3 stops:** softens moving water a little
- **6 stops:** turns waves into texture
- **10 stops:** flattens the sea and streaks the clouds

Every stop doubles the exposure time, so a 6-stop filter multiplies it by 64 and a 10-stop by 1024. Makers label strength in different ways: a 3-stop filter may be called ND8 or 0.9, a 6-stop ND64 or 1.8, and a 10-stop ND1000 or 3.0. For the sums, the field method and the right shutter speeds for water and cloud, go to the Long exposure lesson.

ND filters also let you open the aperture in bright sun. At ISO 100 a sunny scene meters around f/16 at 1/100 s. Opening to f/2 is six stops (f/16, f/11, f/8, f/5.6, f/4, f/2.8, f/2), so the time becomes 1/100 ÷ 64, about 1/6400 s. That is beyond many shutters. A 3-stop ND brings it back to 1/800 s, because 6400 ÷ 8 = 800.

## Graduated filters

A grad is dark at the top and clear at the bottom, to hold back a bright sky. They are less essential than they used to be, because you can take two exposures and blend them, but they still save time in the field.

I tend to blend exposures instead, because graduated filters can give artefacts. The commonest is anything that rises above the horizon, such as a tree, a building or a hill, being darkened along with the sky.

- **Hard grads** have a sharp line. They suit flat horizons such as the sea
- **Soft grads** fade gradually. They suit broken horizons such as hills
- **Reverse grads** are darkest in the middle, for a sunset sitting on the horizon

To choose the strength, meter the sky and the foreground separately at the same aperture. If the sky reads 1/500 s and the foreground 1/60 s, the difference is three stops (1/500 to 1/250 to 1/125 to 1/60), so a 3-stop grad, often labelled 0.9, will even them out.

[[photo:Botallack]]

The sun is in the frame, so the sky is far brighter than the flowers in the foreground. Scenes like this are where a grad, or two exposures blended later, holds detail at both ends. Pointing almost straight at the sun, a polariser would do little here.

## Filters you can leave at home

- **UV and clear filters.** On a digital camera they do little except protect the front of the lens, and an extra layer of glass can add flare
- **Coloured filters for black and white.** The conversion sliders do the same job afterwards. See the Black and white lesson
- **Warming and cooling filters.** White balance does this in editing

## Common mistakes

- **A dark band across a blue sky.** A polariser on a wide lens covers a wide range of angles to the sun. Zoom in, or turn the polariser to a weaker setting
- **Slow shutter speeds by accident.** A polariser left on as the light fades costs you up to two stops. Take it off when it is not doing anything
- **Dark corners.** Stacking filters on a wide lens can vignette. Use one stronger filter, a slim polariser, or zoom in slightly
- **Darkened trees and buildings.** Anything that rises above the horizon under a grad turns dark too. Use a soft grad, or blend exposures instead
- **Flare.** Every filter adds two more surfaces to catch the light. With the sun near the frame, shade the filter with your hand or take it off

## Checking your result

Take one frame with the filter and one without, and compare them on the screen. Look at the sky near the edges for an uneven band, and at the corners for darkening at the widest focal length. Check the histogram, since a grad that is too strong can make the sky darker than the land.

## Looking after them

- Keep them clean. A smudge shows up badly in a long exposure
- Blow off grit before you wipe, or you will drag it across the glass
- Use a lens hood or shade the filter if the sun is near the frame
- Check for colour casts on very dark ND filters and correct them afterwards

## Going further

- **Polariser and ND together.** On a wet, rocky shore a polariser cuts the glare on the rocks and adds one to two stops to a long exposure
- **Blending exposures.** Bracket a scene with a bright sky and blend the frames in Lightroom or Photoshop instead of using a grad
- **Long exposure.** The next step for ND filters, with worked examples and the field method

> If software can do it later, leave the filter in the bag.
