Q: Your shutter speed is 1/250 s. You fit a polariser that costs two stops. What is the new speed?
* About 1/60 s
- 1/500 s
- 1/125 s

Q: Why do you need to turn the polariser again after switching from landscape to portrait?
* The filter turns with the camera, so the angle of polarisation changes
- The polariser stops working in portrait orientation
- The focal length has changed

lessons.title: Black and white
lessons.summary: Take the colour away and a photograph is only light, shadow, shape and texture. Some pictures get stronger. Some fall apart.
lessons.body:
Black and white is not colour with something missing. It is a different way of seeing, built entirely on tone: how light or dark each part of the picture is.

## What you need

- **Any camera.** No special kit is needed
- **RAW files,** so the colour information is still there when you convert
- **A monochrome picture style** set in the camera, so the screen or viewfinder shows you the scene in tone

My Leica D-Lux 8 is truly pocket-sized and has a brilliant monochrome mode, which makes it a good camera for black and white on the street.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, with 0 to minus 2/3 stop compensation to protect bright skies
- **Aperture:** f/5.6 to f/11; the smaller end for texture and architecture in depth
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; the faster end for people on the street
- **ISO:** 100 to 800; keep it low where you plan to darken the sky in the edit
- **Picture style:** Monochrome, with RAW files, so the screen shows tone and the colour is kept

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## When it works

- Strong light and deep shadow
- Texture: stone, bark, weathered skin, sand
- Shape and line, especially in architecture
- Street scenes where colour is cluttered or distracting
- Dull, grey days, where the colour has nothing to offer anyway

[[photo:Walk]]

On a busy street, colour pulls the eye everywhere: signs, clothes, vans. In mono only the shapes and the light are left, and the woman at the crossing becomes the subject.

[[photo:Reflections of Bath]]

Stone, still water and a heavy sky, with no colour to compete. The colonnade and the Abbey tower appear twice, once in the light and once in the reflection.

## When it does not

If the picture is about colour, such as a sunset, autumn leaves or a red dress against sand, converting it throws away its reason to exist. Converting a weak photograph to black and white rarely rescues it.

## When I decide

For me it varies. Some days I go out having decided I am only shooting black and white. Sometimes I take the shot as colour and decide in the edit. And sometimes I decide on the spot, when the textures are there in front of me.

## Seeing in tone

Without colour, the eye goes to the brightest part of the picture and to the edges where light meets dark. So look for those first.

- **Light direction.** Side light rakes across stone, bark and sand and shows the texture. Flat, front light hides it
- **Separation.** Your subject needs to be lighter or darker than what is behind it. A dark figure against a pale wall works. A dark figure against a dark doorway disappears
- **Shape.** Silhouettes, strong lines and repeated forms all survive the loss of colour

Squinting helps. It blurs the detail and leaves only the big areas of light and dark. If the picture still has a clear shape when you squint, it will probably work in mono.

Two worked scenarios:

- **A red door in a grey stone wall.** In colour the door leaps out. In black and white the red and the grey may be the same brightness, and the door vanishes into the wall. Either plan to darken the red when you convert, or find an angle where light falls on the door and not the wall
- **A green field under a blue sky.** Both can come out as the same mid-grey. Darken the sky in the conversion and the field stands clear of it

## Colour still matters

Two colours of the same brightness turn into the same grey, and the picture goes flat. Film photographers used coloured filters to control this. Digital conversions do the same thing with sliders.

[[guide:mono]]

A straight conversion of this photograph turns the sky and the dune into almost the same grey. A red filter darkens the sky and leaves the dune bright, which is why it was the classic landscape filter.

A coloured filter lightens its own colour and darkens the colours opposite it:

- **Red:** darkens blue sky and green foliage strongly, lightens reds and warm skin
- **Orange:** a milder version of red. Darkens the sky and keeps skin looking natural
- **Yellow:** the gentlest. Slightly darkens blue sky
- **Green:** lightens foliage and darkens reds

In Lightroom the black and white mix sliders do the same job. Pull the blue slider down and the sky darkens, as it would with a red or orange filter. Push the orange slider up and sand and skin brighten.

## How to work

- Shoot in colour, ideally RAW, and convert later. You keep every option
- Set the camera's picture style to monochrome if you want to see in black and white while shooting. RAW files still keep the colour
- Push the contrast more than feels comfortable, then back off a touch
- Make sure something in the frame is close to pure black and something close to pure white

## Converting, step by step

1. Straighten and crop, and set the white balance in colour first. In Lightroom the white balance still changes how each colour converts to grey
2. Convert with a black and white profile
3. Set the black and white points. Hold Alt (Option on a Mac) while dragging the Blacks and Whites sliders, and the picture shows you exactly where the tones start to clip
4. Use the black and white mix sliders to separate areas that have gone the same grey
5. Add contrast, either with the contrast slider or a gentle S-shaped tone curve
6. Darken the edges or the sky, and lighten the subject, with masks. This is the digital version of dodging and burning
7. Look at the result small, as a thumbnail, and large. The thumbnail shows whether the shape works; the large view shows halos and noise

My own editing is light: Lightroom, with an occasional small tweak in Photoshop. A conversion and a few contrast adjustments are usually all a black and white photograph needs from me.

[[photo:Sprinkenhof]]

At night the lit windows become the brightest tones and the brickwork falls to near black. The wet ground carries the light down to the bottom of the frame.

## Common mistakes

- **Muddy greys.** No true black and no true white. Set the black and white points
- **A flat picture.** Colours of the same brightness have merged. Separate them with the mix sliders
- **Halos and noise in the sky.** The blue slider pulled down too far. Ease it back and darken the sky with a graduated mask instead
- **Blown highlights.** A white sky with no detail looks harsh in mono. Expose for the highlights when you shoot
- **Rescue conversions.** A weak colour photograph is usually a weak black and white photograph. Start with one that has strong light or shape

## Checking in camera

With a monochrome picture style set, the screen shows the scene in tone, so you can judge the shape and separation on the spot. The histogram is drawn from the processed preview, not the RAW file, so treat it as a guide and leave a little room at the bright end.

## Going further

- **High key and low key.** Pictures built almost entirely from light tones, or almost entirely from dark ones
- **Toning.** A slight warm or cool tint, added with colour grading in Lightroom
- **Long exposures in mono.** Smooth water and streaked cloud suit black and white. See the Long exposure lesson
- **Grain.** A little added grain can suit a gritty street photograph. Use it sparingly

> Look for light and shape. Colour can lie about a photograph; tone cannot.
lessons.challenge: Spend one walk shooting only black and white. Set the camera to monochrome so you see in tone, and keep the RAW files. At home, convert your best frame twice: once straight, and once using the mix sliders to separate two areas that went the same grey. Compare them.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why can two different colours look flat in black and white?
* Colours of the same brightness turn into the same grey
- Black and white removes all contrast
- The camera cannot record them

Q: In Lightroom's black and white mix, which slider do you pull down to darken a blue sky?
* Blue
- Orange
- Green

Q: What does a green filter, or the green slider pushed up, do?
* Lightens foliage
- Darkens foliage
- Darkens a blue sky strongly

Q: When converting, why hold Alt (Option) while dragging the Blacks and Whites sliders?
* It shows where the tones start to clip
- It converts the photograph to black and white
- It resets the sliders

lessons.title: Editing lightly
lessons.summary: Editing is not cheating, and it does not have to take hours. A few small adjustments bring a photograph back to what you saw.
lessons.body:
I keep my editing light. I use Lightroom, with an occasional small tweak in Photoshop. The aim is to bring the photograph back to what I saw, not to turn it into something it was not.

My wife, who is also a keen and exceptionally good photographer, loves editing. I am not keen on it myself. Either way, the same few steps do most of the work.

[[guide:beforeafter]]

## What you need

- **Editing software.** Lightroom does everything in this lesson
- **RAW files,** for the most room to adjust
- **A screen that is not too bright.** A screen at full brightness makes every photograph look brighter than it is, and you will edit them too dark
- **Somewhere without glare** on the screen

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, exposing so the brightest sky keeps detail; shadows lift cleanly from RAW later
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for scenes like a coast at sunset; wider only when you want shallow focus
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; slower on a tripod once the light fades
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100, for the cleanest shadows to lift in editing
- **Focal length:** Frame slightly wider than the final picture, leaving room to straighten and crop
- **File format:** RAW, 14-bit if offered, for 16,384 levels per channel instead of a JPEG's 256

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Why RAW files look flat

A RAW file holds everything the sensor recorded, without the camera's own processing. That gives you room to adjust, but it means the file looks dull until you do. A little contrast and colour is not exaggeration; it is finishing the job.

The room is real. A 14-bit RAW file records 16,384 levels of brightness in each colour channel, because 2 multiplied by itself 14 times is 16,384. An 8-bit JPEG has 256. That is why you can lift shadows in a RAW file without the tones breaking into bands.

## A simple order of work

- **Straighten and crop.** Level the horizon first
- **White balance.** Make whites look white, or warm or cool the photograph on purpose
- **Exposure.** Set the overall brightness
- **Highlights and shadows.** Recover detail at both ends
- **Contrast and texture.** Add a little, then back off
- **Colour.** Small changes to saturation or individual colours
- **Spot removal.** Dust spots and small distractions

## The order in practice

Here is the same list worked through on one photograph: a coast at sunset that looks dull and slightly dark straight from the camera.

1. **Straighten.** The horizon tilts down to the right. Use the straighten tool and drag along the horizon. Then crop to remove any distraction at the edges
2. **White balance.** The camera chose a neutral setting and the sunset looks grey. Warm it a few hundred kelvin, for example from 5200 K to 5800 K. For reference, daylight is around 5500 K, shade around 7000 K, and household tungsten bulbs around 3000 K
3. **Exposure.** Raise it until the mid-tones look right. Each whole step on the exposure slider is one stop: +1 doubles the brightness. Here +0.7 is enough
4. **Highlights and shadows.** Pull highlights down until the sky near the sun shows detail again, and lift shadows until the rocks are no longer black holes
5. **Contrast and texture.** Add a little contrast to counter the lifted shadows
6. **Colour.** Use vibrance rather than saturation. Vibrance boosts muted colours more than strong ones and protects skin tones
7. **Spot removal.** Turn on the dust spot view and clean the sky, where dust shows most

Do the steps in this order. Each one changes the next, and going back and forth wastes time.

[[photo:Storm over the dunes]]

Warm sand and a cool, purple-grey storm sky in the same frame. Push the white balance too far either way and you lose one of them.

## Cropping without losing too much

Cropping throws pixels away, so it helps to know how many. A 45-megapixel file from my Canon EOS R5 is 8192 by 5464 pixels.

- **4:5 crop at full height:** 5464 × 4 ÷ 5 = about 4371 pixels wide. 4371 × 5464 is about 23.9 million pixels, roughly half the file
- **Square crop:** 5464 × 5464 is about 29.9 million pixels

Either is still plenty for screens and for most prints. A tight crop from a small part of the frame is where quality starts to suffer.

## Converging verticals

For buildings, the Transform tool in Lightroom straightens converging verticals. I use it only when the photograph calls for it. When the lean is the point of the picture, I leave it.

## Signs you have gone too far

- Halos along the edges where sky meets land
- Skies darker than the ground in daylight
- Colours that look like no real place
- Shadows lifted until the picture looks grey

A useful habit: leave an edit overnight and look at it again before you share it.

## Common mistakes

- **Editing on a bright screen.** Photographs look fine on your screen and dark everywhere else. Turn the brightness down to around the middle
- **Starting every photograph from scratch.** Photographs taken in the same light need the same edit. Edit one, then copy or sync its settings to the rest and adjust from there
- **Over-sharpening.** Fine white lines along edges and a gritty sky. Look at 100 percent and reduce the amount
- **Too much noise reduction.** Skin and stone go smooth and waxy. Accept a little grain
- **Saturation instead of vibrance.** Saturation pushes strong colours over the edge first. Vibrance is gentler

## Checking your edit

- Press the backslash key in Lightroom's Develop module to flip between before and after. If the after looks nothing like the place, step back
- Press J to show clipping warnings. Red areas have lost highlight detail and blue areas have lost shadow detail
- View at 100 percent to check for halos, noise and over-sharpening
- View small, as a thumbnail, to check the overall balance of light and dark

[[photo:Bleached]]

Most of this frame is pale, so the histogram sits well to the right. That is not a fault to fix. Pulling the highlights down here would only turn the white ground grey.

## Going further

- **Masks.** Darken a sky or lighten a face without touching the rest of the photograph
- **Presets of your own.** Save the settings you use most as a starting point
- **Merging.** Lightroom can merge brackets into one high dynamic range file and overlapping frames into a panorama
- **Black and white.** The conversion and its sliders have their own lesson

> Edit until it looks like the moment. Then stop.
lessons.challenge: Edit one photograph using only the first five steps on the list, in order. Then compare it with a version you have edited before and see which you prefer. Use the backslash key to check before and after, and press J to check for clipping.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does a RAW file look flat straight from the camera?
* It has none of the camera's own processing applied
- The camera recorded it badly
- RAW files are always underexposed

Q: You raise the exposure slider by +1. What happens to the brightness?
* It doubles
- It rises by 10 percent
- It halves

Q: You crop an 8192 by 5464 pixel file to 4:5 at full height. Roughly how many pixels remain?
* About 24 million
- About 45 million
- About 12 million

Q: Which of these is a sign of overediting?
* Halos where the sky meets the land
- A level horizon
- Accurate white balance

lessons.title: Cropping and aspect ratios
lessons.summary: The shape of the frame changes what a photograph is about. Choose it in camera where you can, crop with care, and know what each crop costs in pixels.
lessons.body:
Aspect ratio is the shape of a photograph: its width compared with its height. The camera gives you one shape, but it is not always the right one. A crop can turn a cluttered frame into a strong picture, or throw away pixels you will need later.

## What aspect ratio means

An aspect ratio is written as width to height. A 3:2 frame is one and a half times as wide as it is tall. Turn the camera on its side and the same frame becomes 2:3.

The sensor sets the starting shape. Full-frame and APS-C sensors record 3:2. Four Thirds sensors and most phones record 4:3. Everything else is a crop.

## The common shapes

- **3:2.** The native shape of most cameras, and of a 6x4 inch print
- **4:3.** Slightly squarer
- **1:1.** The square. Every edge is the same length, so nothing pulls the eye one way
- **4:5.** A tall, compact portrait shape, the same as a 10x8 inch print
- **16:9.** The widescreen shape of televisions and most computer screens
- **2:1, 3:1 and 4:1.** Panoramic shapes, from a gentle letterbox to a long strip

## How the shape changes the picture

The same scene reads differently in each shape, because the frame's edges push the eye along its longest side.

- **Square** settles the eye in the middle. It suits centred subjects, symmetry and balance. See the Symmetry and patterns lesson
- **Tall** shapes lead the eye from bottom to top. They suit height, trees, buildings and lines running away from you. See the Leading lines lesson
- **Wide** shapes lead the eye from side to side. They suit horizons, coastlines and anything that stretches. See the Where to put the horizon lesson

Ask what the picture is about, then choose the shape that gives that thing the most room.

[[photo:Uttakleiv beach]]

A tall 2:3 frame leaves room for the sand and a large rock at the bottom, smaller rocks in the middle, and the jagged ridge and heavy sky above.

## Composing for the crop in camera

If you know the final shape, frame for it when you take the picture.

- **Use the camera's aspect ratio setting or overlay.** Many cameras can show 1:1, 4:3 or 16:9 frame lines in the viewfinder or on the screen. With RAW files, many cameras still record the whole sensor and only mark the shape, so you can change your mind later. JPEGs are cut to the shape. Check your manual
- **Leave room at the edges.** Frame a little looser than you think you need. You can always crop in. You cannot crop out
- **Keep the subject away from the edges you plan to cut.** A 3:2 frame cropped to 4:5 loses its sides

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority for single frames; manual for panorama frames, so every frame matches
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for landscapes, so fine detail holds up after a heavy crop
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; any speed on a levelled tripod
- **ISO:** 100 to 400, keeping noise low so a crop can be enlarged cleanly
- **Focal length:** A little wider than needed, leaving room at the edges to crop in later
- **File format:** RAW, as many cameras then keep the full 3:2 sensor behind an aspect overlay; check the manual

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Cropping in Lightroom

I edit mainly in Lightroom. The crop tool there works in the same order every time.

1. Straighten first. Use the angle slider, or the straighten tool, and drag it along a horizon or a vertical edge. Straightening rotates the frame, so it trims the corners and changes what is left to crop
2. Choose the aspect ratio from the menu, or type a custom one
3. Lock it, with the padlock, so dragging a corner keeps the shape
4. Press X to swap between landscape and portrait orientation of the same ratio
5. Press O to cycle through the overlays: thirds, grid, diagonal, golden ratio and others. Pick the one that helps you place the subject
6. Drag the crop box and slide the picture inside it until the edges are clean

## What a crop costs

Every crop throws pixels away. A worked example with a 45-megapixel full-frame file, 8192 by 5464 pixels. That is the size my Canon EOS R5 records. 8192 × 5464 = 44,761,088, about 44.8 megapixels.

1. **Crop to 4:5 at full height.** The height stays at 5464. The width becomes 5464 × 0.8 = 4371 pixels (rounded). 4371 × 5464 = 23,883,144, about 23.9 megapixels. You keep a little over half the file
2. **Crop to 1:1 at full height.** 5464 × 5464 = 29,855,296, about 29.9 megapixels. You keep two thirds of the file
3. **Crop to 3:1 at full width.** The height becomes 8192 ÷ 3 = 2731 (rounded). 8192 × 2731 = 22,372,352, about 22.4 megapixels

On a large file that still leaves plenty. On a smaller file it adds up fast.

## Print sizes

To find how big a file will print, divide the pixels by the print resolution. 300 pixels per inch is the usual standard for prints viewed up close.

- **Full 3:2 file:** 8192 ÷ 300 = 27.3 inches, and 5464 ÷ 300 = 18.2 inches. About 27 by 18 inches
- **4:5 crop:** 4371 ÷ 300 = 14.6 inches, and 5464 ÷ 300 = 18.2 inches. About 14.6 by 18.2 inches, or roughly 37 by 46 cm

Large prints seen from across a room are often fine at around 200.

## Panoramas: one frame or several

A panorama can come from a single frame cropped to a strip, or from several frames stitched together.

A single frame is quick and copes with movement, but loses height. Stitching keeps the full height and adds width.

1. Level the tripod, so the horizon stays straight as you turn
2. Set exposure, white balance and focus manually, so every frame matches
3. Overlap each frame with the last by about a third
4. Shoot from one end to the other, then merge in Lightroom with Photo Merge, Panorama

Three landscape frames with a third overlapped come to roughly 8192 + 2 × 5461 = 19,114 pixels wide before trimming, at the full 5464 height. That is about 3.5 to 1, at over 100 megapixels.

[[photo:Luskentyre ICM]]

At 1600 by 422 pixels, about 3.8 to 1, the shape follows the long horizontal strokes of sand, sea, hills and sky left by sweeping the camera sideways. See the Intentional camera movement lesson.

## Sharing online

Instagram accepts photos from 4:5 portrait to 1.91:1 landscape; anything outside that range is cropped or has to be padded.

- **A 3:2 landscape** is 1.5 to 1, inside the range, so it posts as it is
- **A tall 2:3 portrait** is taller than 4:5. Crop it to 4:5, or pad the sides with a border
- **A wide panorama** is wider than 1.91:1. Crop it, or pad the top and bottom

Padding with a plain border keeps the whole picture. This site posts to Instagram that way: a picture outside the allowed range gets a plain border.

Two worked scenarios, using the photographs on this page.

1. **Uttakleiv beach, 1706 by 2560 pixels (2:3).** To pad it to 4:5 at full height, the width becomes 2560 × 0.8 = 2048. The border adds 2048 minus 1706 = 342 pixels, or 171 each side. To crop it instead, the height becomes 1706 ÷ 0.8 = 2133 (rounded), losing 427 pixels, about a sixth of the height
2. **Luskentyre ICM, 1600 by 422 pixels.** To pad it to 1.91:1 at full width, the height becomes 1600 ÷ 1.91 = 838 (rounded), so the border adds 416 pixels, 208 top and bottom. Cropping it to 1.91:1 at full height leaves 422 × 1.91 = 806 pixels of width. Half the picture goes

[[photo:Scratch and sniff]]

A square frame. The hydrant on the left and the seated man on the right balance each other across the middle, and a 1:1 picture sits inside Instagram's range, so it posts as it is.

## Common mistakes

- **Cropping too tight.** The subject jams against the edge and has nowhere to sit. Leave space in the direction it faces or moves
- **Crooked horizons.** Straighten before you crop, not after. See the Where to put the horizon lesson
- **Cropping out the breathing room.** Empty sky or sea is often what makes the subject stand out. See the Minimalism lesson
- **Upscaling to make up for a crop.** Enlarging a small crop adds pixels but not detail. Frame closer in camera, or print smaller

## Checking your crop

- Look at each edge in turn for anything half in and half out
- Turn the overlay off and look at the picture on its own
- Check the pixel dimensions against the size you need
- Look again the next day, before you commit

## Going further

- **Shoot for the crop,** using one in-camera aspect ratio for a whole outing, so you learn to see in that shape
- **Stitch a panorama** and compare it with a single frame cropped to the same shape

> Choose the shape for the picture, not the picture for the shape.
lessons.challenge: Take one scene and frame it three times: square, tall and wide, leaving room at the edges. Crop each in Lightroom with the aspect ratio locked, and work out how many megapixels each one keeps.
lessons.quiz:
Q: A 45-megapixel 3:2 file is 8192 by 5464 pixels. Cropped to 4:5 at full height, roughly how many megapixels are left?
* About 23.9 megapixels
- About 36 megapixels
- About 44.8 megapixels

Q: Roughly how wide will an 8192-pixel-wide file print at 300 pixels per inch?
* About 27 inches
- About 82 inches
- About 8 inches

Q: In Lightroom, why straighten before you set the crop?
* Straightening rotates the frame and trims the corners, which changes what is left to crop
- Lightroom cannot straighten a picture once it has been cropped
- Straightening changes the aspect ratio

Q: You want to post a tall 2:3 portrait to Instagram without losing any of it. What do you do?
* Pad the sides with a plain border to make it 4:5
- Upload it as it is, because Instagram accepts any shape
- Upscale it until it fits

lessons.title: Intentional camera movement
lessons.summary: Move the camera during a long exposure on purpose and a wood becomes a painting. Easy to try, hard to master, and impossible to repeat exactly.
lessons.body:
Intentional camera movement, or ICM, breaks the first rule of photography: keep the camera still. Instead you move it deliberately while the shutter is open, turning a scene into streaks and washes of colour.

[[guide:icm]]

## What you need

- **Any camera with shutter priority or manual mode**
- **An ND filter,** 3 or 6 stops, to get slow speeds in daylight
- **A zoom lens,** if you want to try zoom bursts
- **No tripod.** Most ICM is handheld. A tripod helps only for zoom bursts and controlled pans
- **Plenty of card space.** You will take a lot of frames

## The settings

- **Mode:** Shutter priority, so the speed is fixed and the camera sets the aperture
- **Aperture:** f/11 to f/16 in daylight; around f/8 for city lights at night
- **Shutter speed:** 1/4 s to 1/2 s; city lights at night often need 1/2 s to 1 s
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100
- **Focus:** Autofocus on the subject, then switch to manual focus so it cannot hunt
- **Filter:** 3-stop ND under overcast light, 6-stop ND in bright sun, none at night

Start around 1/4 s to 1/2 s. In daylight that is a long exposure, so you will need a small aperture such as f/16, the lowest ISO, and often a neutral density filter to cut the light further. Shutter priority mode makes it easy to set the speed and let the camera handle the rest.

Two worked examples:

- **An overcast wood.** At f/16 and ISO 100 the camera meters 1/30 s. To reach 1/4 s you need three stops less light: 1/30 to 1/15 to 1/8 to 1/4. A 3-stop ND filter does it exactly
- **Bright sun on the coast.** At f/16 and ISO 100 the camera meters 1/100 s. A 6-stop filter multiplies the time by 64: 1/100 × 64 = 0.64 s, about two thirds of a second. Open up one stop to f/11 and it halves to about 1/3 s

Turn off image stabilisation. It tries to cancel the very movement you are making.

## The movement

- **Vertical sweeps** along tree trunks are the classic. Start moving before you press the shutter and keep moving after it closes
- **Horizontal sweeps** along a horizon turn the coast into bands of sea, land and sky
- **Zoom bursts:** turn the zoom ring during the exposure for lines radiating from the centre
- **Small shakes or twists** give a softer, painterly texture

## The method, step by step

1. Find the subject and decide which way its main lines run
2. Set shutter priority, a starting speed of 1/4 s and the lowest ISO, and fit an ND filter if the aperture cannot close far enough
3. Focus on the subject, then switch to manual focus. Autofocus will hunt once you start moving
4. Turn off image stabilisation
5. Hold the camera firmly, with your elbows in, and start the movement before you press the shutter
6. Keep the movement smooth and keep going until after the shutter closes. A jerky start or stop shows as a hard edge
7. Check the frame, then change one thing at a time: the speed of the movement, its length, or the shutter speed

## Choose the subject carefully

ICM works best with strong, simple shapes and good colour. Lines that run in the direction of the movement stay as clean streaks; anything at an angle smears. Birch trees, autumn colour, bluebells, a sunset over the sea and city lights at night are all good starting points. Contrast helps too. Pale trunks against dark ground, or bright lights against a dark sky, keep their shape far better than a scene where everything is a similar tone.

## Worked scenarios

- **A birch wood.** Pale trunks against darker ground. Sweep upwards at 1/4 s, along the trunks. Keep bright sky out of the top of the frame, or it will smear white down over the trees
- **The coast.** Hold the horizon level and sweep sideways at 1/2 s. Place the horizon off centre so the sea and sky form bands of different widths
- **City lights at night.** No filter is needed. A lit street often meters around 1/2 s to 1 s at f/8 and ISO 100. Small twists and shakes turn each light into a loop or squiggle
- **A zoom burst.** Pick a subject in the centre of the frame, such as a single tree or a lit window. Start the exposure and turn the zoom ring steadily through its range. A tripod keeps the centre crisp

## Done for real

[[photo:cathedral-in-motion]]

A vertical sweep. The spires and tree trunks run the same way as the movement, so they hold their shape while the leaves and sky dissolve into texture.

[[photo:Luskentyre ICM]]

A horizontal sweep at 1/4 s. The movement runs along the shoreline, so the sand, the turquoise water, the hills and the sky stay as separate bands of colour.

## Common mistakes

- **It just looks like camera shake.** The shutter was too fast or the movement too small. Slow down to 1/4 s or longer and make the sweep bigger
- **Grey mush.** The shutter was too slow or the movement too long. Speed up, or shorten the sweep
- **Movement across the lines.** Sideways sweeps on vertical trees smear everything. Move in the direction of the main lines
- **A white smear from the sky.** Bright areas spread across the frame. Leave the sky out, or reduce the exposure
- **Hard edges at the start or end.** The movement started or stopped while the shutter was open. Start before you press and keep going after

## Checking your result

Sharpness does not matter here, so do not zoom in. Look at the whole frame on the screen and ask whether the main shapes are still recognisable. Check the histogram: bright areas smeared over the frame can clip. If every frame looks the same, change the movement, not just the settings.

## Expect a low hit rate

No two frames are the same. Shoot dozens, vary the speed and the length of the sweep, and expect to keep a handful. That unpredictability is part of the appeal.

## Going further

- **Multiple exposures.** If your camera has a multiple exposure mode, combine several short sweeps in one frame for a layered, painted look
- **ICM in black and white.** With colour gone, the picture rests on the streaks of light and dark. See the Black and white lesson
- **Long exposure.** The opposite approach: keep the camera completely still and let the world move. See the Long exposure lesson

> You are not recording the scene. You are painting with it.
lessons.challenge: Find a stand of trees with straight trunks. Shoot twenty frames at 1/4 s with vertical sweeps, varying the speed and length of the movement. Then shoot ten more sweeping sideways across the same trunks, and compare the two sets.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is a good starting shutter speed for ICM?
* Around 1/4 s to 1/2 s
- 1/1000 s
- 30 seconds

Q: An overcast wood meters 1/30 s at f/16 and ISO 100. How strong an ND filter gets you to 1/4 s?
* 3 stops
- 1 stop
- 10 stops

Q: Why start moving before you press the shutter?
* So the movement is smooth for the whole exposure, with no hard edge at the start
- So the autofocus has time to lock
- So the camera can measure the movement

Q: Why do vertical sweeps suit tree trunks?
* Lines running with the movement stay as clean streaks
- Trees move in the wind
- Vertical movement freezes the leaves

lessons.title: Architecture
lessons.summary: Buildings do not move and the light on them is predictable, which makes architecture the most patient subject there is. The hard part is the lines.
lessons.body:
A building is a composition someone has already designed. Your job is to find the angle and the light that show what the architect intended, or something they never saw.

One of my brothers is an architect, which probably explains why I notice the design of a building as much as the building itself.

## What you need

- **A wide zoom,** roughly 16 to 35 mm on full frame, for narrow streets, courtyards and interiors
- **A longer lens,** around 70 to 200 mm, for details, and for standing far enough back to keep the camera level
- **A tripod** for blue hour and interiors, where one is allowed. In cities I carry a light carbon-fibre Peak Design tripod. It is easier to carry all day and quicker to set up
- **A level.** The camera's electronic level is enough, as long as you switch it on
- **A polariser,** to control reflections in glass and deepen a blue sky

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, with exposure bracketing at blue hour
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11, for depth of field across the facade
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s by day; 1/4 s to 4 s on a tripod at blue hour
- **ISO:** 100 on a tripod; 800 to 3200 handheld where tripods are not allowed
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 35 mm full frame for streets and interiors; 70 mm to 200 mm for details
- **Focus:** On the facade
- **Stabilisation:** Off on a tripod, unless the lens detects one; on when handheld

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Commit to an angle

There are two strong ways to photograph a building, and one weak one.

- **Straight on:** stand square to the facade with the camera level, so every vertical stays vertical. Calm, graphic, exact.
- **Looking up:** point the camera steeply upwards and let the lines rush together. Dramatic and dizzying.
- **Half-way:** a slight upward tilt, where the walls lean just enough to look like a mistake. Avoid it.

Decide which of the first two you are making before you lift the camera. If you cannot choose, keep walking until the building tells you.

[[photo:Speicherstadt balconies]]

Straight on and dead centre. Every line is parallel to the frame, so the repetition does all the work.

## Converging verticals

Tilt the camera up and parallel walls appear to lean in towards the top. Sometimes that is the point. When it is not, you can correct it.

[[guide:verticals]]

There are three ways to deal with it:

- Step back and use a longer lens, so you can keep the camera level
- Correct it in the edit with a perspective or upright tool, leaving room around the building because the correction crops the frame
- Use a tilt-shift lens, which moves the image up without tilting the camera

I sometimes straighten them in Lightroom with the Transform tool, but only when the photograph calls for it. If the lean is the point, I leave it alone.

## Keeping the camera level: a worked example

With the camera level, a normal (rectilinear) lens covers as much above the centre of the frame as below it. How far up it reaches depends on the focal length. On a full-frame camera held upright, the long side of the sensor is 36 mm, so the top edge of the frame sits 18 mm above the centre.

Say the top of the building is 27 m above your camera.

1. With a 16 mm lens held upright, the frame reaches 18 ÷ 16 = 1.125 m up for every metre you stand back. 27 ÷ 1.125 = 24, so stand about 24 m away
2. With a 24 mm lens held upright, it reaches 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75 m up per metre. 27 ÷ 0.75 = 36, so stand about 36 m away
3. With the 16 mm lens held horizontally, the short side of the sensor is 24 mm, so the top edge sits 12 mm above centre. 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75, which also needs about 36 m

In each case the bottom half of the frame is mostly pavement. Crop it away afterwards. You give up pixels, but the verticals are true with no correction at all. If you cannot get that far back, either tilt and correct later or commit to looking up.

## Light

**Blue hour** is the best time for buildings with lit windows. For about twenty minutes after sunset the sky and the interior lights are close in brightness, so both hold detail.

[[guide:planner]]

The light changes fast, so meter again every few frames. Say the camera meters 2 seconds at f/8 and ISO 100. You close to f/11 for more depth of field. That is one stop less light, so the time doubles to 4 seconds.

If the windows still burn out, bracket. From a metered 1 second at f/8, two stops under is 1/4 s and two stops over is 4 seconds. Blend the frames later or pick the best one.

[[photo:The Caledonian Railway Bridge]]

**Side light** brings out texture in brick and stone. **Overcast** days suit detail and glass, with no hard reflections. Before you go, check which way the main facade faces. In the northern hemisphere, a west-facing wall gets the evening sun, and a north-facing one gets almost no direct sun in winter.

## Look up, look closer

The best architectural photographs are often not of the whole building. Stand in a courtyard or stairwell and look straight up. Fill the frame with a single repeating detail.

[[photo:Spiral]]

A single repeating detail, seen from directly below. Rings and beams converge on a disc of light in the centre.

[[photo:Courtyard skylight]]

Looking straight up from a courtyard. The glass roof sits near the middle, and the brick walls and their windows lean in towards it from every side.

## Symmetry and repetition

A straight-on picture only works if it is exact. Find the building's centre line, a door, a tower or a gap, and stand on it. Turn on the grid and move a step left or right until the edges of the facade sit the same distance from each side of the frame. Then check the top and bottom. A symmetrical picture that is a few centimetres off looks wrong in a way a loose composition never does.

[[photo:Sprinkenhof]]

Straight on and centred on the curved tower. Lit windows repeat across the dark brick, and the wet paving in front carries the light down towards the camera.

## The method in the field

1. Walk round the building before you set up. Note where the light falls and which side is cleanest
2. Decide: straight on, or looking up
3. For straight on, use the electronic level so the camera is level both side to side and front to back
4. Compose with room around the building if you might correct it later
5. Set f/8 to f/11 and focus on the facade
6. On a tripod, turn off image stabilisation, unless your lens is designed to detect a tripod
7. Check the edges for lamp posts, signs and half a person walking out of frame
8. Take a frame, check it, then adjust and go again

## Checking in camera

- **Grid lines.** Compare the verticals with the grid. If they are not parallel, you are tilted
- **Corners.** Zoom in. Wide lenses are often softest there, and bent lines show up first at the edges
- **Highlights.** Turn on the highlight warning. Bright sky and lit windows are the first things to clip
- **The whole frame, small.** At thumbnail size, the picture should read as either clearly straight or clearly deliberate

## Common mistakes

- **The half-way tilt.** Commit to level or to steeply up
- **No room to correct.** Perspective correction crops the edges, so leave space around the building
- **Burnt-out windows or sky.** Shoot at blue hour, or bracket
- **Curved straight lines.** Wide lenses often bow lines near the edges. Turn on the lens profile correction in Lightroom
- **Stretched corners.** Wide lenses stretch the edges of the frame. Keep important lines away from the corners
- **Clutter.** One step sideways can hide a sign or a bin behind a column

## Practical points

- Many buildings, shopping centres and stations do not allow tripods. Raise the ISO instead
- Private buildings and their courtyards may need permission to photograph
- Glass reflects you. Stand at a slight angle, or use the polariser

## Going further

- **Tilt-shift lenses,** which correct verticals at the moment you take the picture
- **Interiors,** where bracketing balances bright windows against a dark room
- **Long exposure,** to smooth the sky behind a building or clear moving people from a square
- **Abstract detail,** where a building becomes pure line and shape

> Either keep the lines straight or make it obvious you meant them to lean.
lessons.challenge: Choose one building. Photograph it straight on with the camera level, then from close by looking steeply up. Avoid anything in between. Check the straight-on frame against the grid before you leave.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What causes converging verticals?
* Tilting the camera upwards
- Using a long shutter speed
- Shooting at blue hour

Q: Which is one way to keep verticals straight without editing?
* Step back and use a longer lens, keeping the camera level
- Use a wider lens and tilt up further
- Use a higher ISO

Q: Why leave room around a building if you plan to correct the verticals?
* The correction crops the edges of the frame
- It makes the file smaller
- It keeps the sky blue

Q: At blue hour the camera meters 2 seconds at f/8. You close to f/11. What is the new time?
* 4 seconds
- 1 second
- 2 seconds

lessons.title: Street
lessons.summary: Candid moments of everyday life in public places. Be ready before the moment arrives, and treat the people in your pictures with respect.
lessons.body:
Street photography captures ordinary life as it happens: people, gestures, light and coincidence in public places. The best moments last a fraction of a second, so the whole craft is about being ready before they arrive.

[[guide:zone]]

## Zone focusing

Autofocus can be too slow, or lock on the wrong thing. Instead, set the focus manually to a distance and an aperture that give a wide band of sharpness, then forget about it. At 35 mm and f/8, focus at 3 m and everything from about 1.9 m to 7 m is sharp. Anyone who steps into that zone is in focus the moment you press the shutter.

A few more settings to try. These figures are for a full-frame camera; a smaller sensor gives more depth of field at the same framing and aperture.

- **28 mm at f/8, focused at 2.5 m:** sharp from about 1.4 m to 10 m
- **35 mm at f/11, focused at 3 m:** sharp from about 1.7 m to 15 m
- **28 mm at f/8, focused at about 3.3 m:** sharp from about 1.6 m to infinity

The last one is the hyperfocal distance. Focus there and everything from half that distance to infinity is acceptably sharp. It suits wide scenes. For people at conversational distance, a nearer zone keeps them crisper.

## Setting up for zone focus

- **Mode:** Shutter priority, or manual with auto ISO
- **Aperture:** f/8, or f/11 in bright light, for a deep zone of sharpness
- **Shutter speed:** 1/250 s to 1/500 s; 1/500 s or faster for cyclists and runners
- **ISO:** Auto, with a maximum you accept; expect around ISO 250 to 500 in open shade
- **Focal length:** 28 mm or 35 mm full frame
- **Focus:** Manual, zone focused at about 3 m, or 2.5 m at 28 mm
- **Exposure compensation:** Minus 1 to minus 2 stops when a shaft of light falls against deep shadow

1. Switch the lens or camera to manual focus
2. Set the aperture to f/8, or f/11 in bright light
3. Set the focus distance to about 3 m. Use the distance scale if your camera shows one, or focus on something about four paces away and leave it
4. Set the shutter speed to 1/250 s or faster, in shutter priority or manual, and let auto ISO cope with the light
5. Set a maximum ISO you are happy with, so the camera cannot quietly slow the shutter instead
6. Take a test frame of something 2 m away and something 6 m away, and zoom in to check both are sharp
7. Then stop thinking about settings and watch the street

## Freezing movement

A person walking covers roughly 1.4 m every second. At 1/250 s they move 1.4 ÷ 250 = 0.0056 m, under 6 mm, which looks sharp. At 1/30 s they move 1.4 ÷ 30, about 0.047 m, nearly 5 cm. That is enough to blur a hand or a foot. Cyclists and runners need 1/500 s or faster.

A worked example for the light. In bright sun, f/16 at ISO 100 gives about 1/100 s. At f/8, two stops brighter, that becomes about 1/400 s, so 1/250 s needs only around ISO 64. Step into open shade, often two to three stops darker, and auto ISO will rise to roughly ISO 250 to 500 to hold the same f/8 and 1/250 s.

## Small and quiet

A small camera with a fixed 28 mm or 35 mm lens draws far less attention than a big zoom. Set a fast enough shutter to freeze people walking, around 1/250 s or faster, and let auto ISO cope with the light.

This is where a small camera earns its place. Mine is a Leica D-Lux 8. It is truly pocket-sized and its monochrome mode is brilliant, which makes it ideal for street.

Black and white suits the street well. Sometimes I go out having decided to shoot only mono. Sometimes I decide in the edit, and sometimes on the spot, when the textures are there.

## Find the scene, then wait

Rather than chasing people, find a good background: strong light and shadow, a striking wall, a doorway, a reflection. Then wait for someone to walk into it. This is sometimes called fishing, and it produces far stronger pictures than snapping at random.

A worked scenario. Late in the day, a low sun throws a single shaft of light across a pavement between two buildings. Meter for the lit patch, not the shadow, or dial in one to two stops of negative exposure compensation, so the shadow drops to near black. Set the zone to the distance of the light. Stand still and wait. Many people may pass before one steps into it with the right stride, at the right point in the frame.

## What to look for

- Gesture and expression, the split second that tells a story
- Light: low sun, hard shadows, shafts of light between buildings
- Layers: something near, something in the middle, something far
- Juxtaposition: two things in the frame that comment on each other

[[photo:xiangqi]]

Gesture. A hand reaching for a piece, the other player waiting. The background is soft enough to leave the two men and the board as the whole story.

[[photo:hydrant]]

Juxtaposition. The hydrant and the seated man have the same pale top and dark body, and the same downward tilt. Neither would be a photograph on its own.

[[photo:chinatown]]

Layers. Someone close, a family in the middle, a crowd beyond, all on one pavement.

[[photo:Walk]]

Stillness against movement. A woman stands on the kerb with her head down over her phone, while the crossing signal above her shows a walking figure and other people walk past.

## Common mistakes

- **Too far away.** Everyone ends up small and unconnected. Work inside your zone, around 2 to 4 m
- **Autofocus hunting.** Switch to zone focus and the camera is always ready
- **Blurred people.** An automatic mode has chosen a slow shutter. Set 1/250 s and let the ISO rise
- **Busy backgrounds.** A step to one side or a lower angle can swap a cluttered shopfront for a plain wall
- **Awkward crops.** Watch the edges for feet cut at the ankle and heads cut by the frame
- **Raising the camera too late.** Have it up and framed before the person reaches the spot

## Checking your results

Check your first frame closely: zoom in on a face to confirm the zone is where you think it is and the shutter speed has frozen the walk. In hard sun, look at the histogram as well as the screen. After that, check during lulls, not after every frame. Looking down at the screen is the surest way to miss the next picture.

## Respect

In the UK it is generally legal to photograph people in public places, but legal is not the same as right. There is no general right not to be photographed in a public place. Harassment law still applies, and someone in a place where they can reasonably expect privacy is different, even if you can see them from the street. Some places that feel public, such as shopping centres and many railway stations, are private property, and the owner can ask you to stop.

Be open about what you are doing, smile, and if someone objects, delete the picture and move on. Take extra care with children and people in vulnerable situations. If you plan to use a picture commercially, you may need the person's written permission, usually called a model release. Advertising use normally needs one. Laws differ from country to country, and this is a general guide, not legal advice.

## Going further

- **Black and white,** which strips a scene back to light, shape and gesture
- **Layers,** working closer with a wider lens so the foreground, middle and background all carry something
- **Slow shutter and panning,** following a cyclist at around 1/15 s so they stay fairly sharp against a streaked background
- **A project,** such as one street photographed at different times of day across a year

> Be ready before the moment, not after it.
lessons.challenge: Find a good background with strong light. Set up zone focus at 3 m and f/8, check one test frame, then stay in one spot for twenty minutes and photograph whoever walks into the scene.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is zone focusing?
* Presetting focus and aperture so a band of distance is already sharp
- Letting autofocus track a moving person
- Focusing on the background only

Q: On full frame at 35 mm and f/8, focused at 3 m, roughly what is sharp?
* From about 1.9 m to 7 m
- Only subjects at exactly 3 m
- From about 0.5 m to infinity

Q: A person walks at about 1.4 m per second. Roughly how far do they move during 1/250 s?
* About 6 mm
- About 6 cm
- About 35 cm

Q: What is "fishing" in street photography?
* Finding a good scene and waiting for someone to walk into it
- Following people until they do something interesting
- Shooting from the hip without looking

lessons.title: Woodland
lessons.summary: A wood is the hardest landscape to photograph well. The trick is finding order in the chaos, and the right weather does half of it for you.
lessons.body:
Walk into a wood with a camera and everything looks beautiful. Look at the pictures later and most of them are a tangle of trunks and branches with nowhere for the eye to rest. Woodland photography is mostly about simplifying.

[[guide:mist]]

## What you need

- **A tripod.** Woods are dark, even at midday
- **A short telephoto,** somewhere around 70 to 200 mm, plus a wider lens for paths and mist
- **A polarising filter,** to cut the glare off wet leaves
- **A remote release,** or the 2-second self-timer
- **Waterproof boots.** The best mornings are usually the wettest underfoot

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority on a tripod with the 2-second timer; add about +1 stop in mist
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; use f/8 when leaves are moving, to gain shutter speed
- **Shutter speed:** Often 1/2 s to 1 s with a polariser; about 1/15 s if leaves move
- **ISO:** 100 for still air; raise to 400 to 800 only to freeze moving leaves
- **Focal length:** 70 mm to 200 mm full frame to pick out a few trunks; wider for paths and mist
- **Filter:** Polariser, turned slowly until the glare on wet leaves drops, then backed off a little

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Wait for the right conditions

**Mist and fog** are the woodland photographer's best friends. Each row of trees fades a little more than the one in front, which separates the layers and gives the picture depth. Still autumn and spring mornings after a clear, cold night are the most likely times.

To read the forecast for mist, look for three things: a clear sky overnight, little or no wind, and high humidity. The ground cools fast under a clear sky and chills the air above it. Be in place before sunrise, because mist often thins once the sun starts to warm the air.

[[guide:planner]]

**Overcast days** come next. Soft light means no harsh patches of sun and deep shadow, and colours look richer. Bright sunshine through a canopy is the hardest light of all: the camera cannot hold the bright spots and the shadows at once.

**After rain** the bark darkens, moss glows and colours saturate. A polarising filter cuts the glare off wet leaves and makes the difference obvious.

## Find a subject

A wood needs a focal point as much as any landscape. Look for one tree that stands apart: a different shape, a different colour, a trunk catching the light. A path or a burn can lead the eye through.

To see it, half-close your eyes. The detail drops away and only the main shapes are left: dark trunks, a pale gap, one bright tree. If nothing stands out when you squint, nothing will stand out in the photograph either. Edges of woods and clearings are good places to look, because a single tree there has room around it.

## Use a longer lens

A wide lens takes in everything, and in a wood everything is the problem. A short telephoto, somewhere around 70 to 200 mm, lets you pick out a small, tidy scene from the mess and compresses the trunks into a pattern.

A worked scenario. You stand at the edge of a beech wood on a misty morning. At 24 mm the frame holds the path, the sky, a fallen branch and forty trunks. At 135 mm, aimed into the mist, it holds five trunks in a row, each paler than the last. The second picture says more with less.

## Working out the exposure

Mist fools the meter. The camera tries to make the scene a mid grey, so bright mist comes out dull. Add about +1 stop of exposure compensation, then check the histogram: the graph should sit towards the right without touching the edge.

A polariser costs about one to two stops of light, so a reading of 1/4 s becomes somewhere between 1/2 s and 1 second.

Wind is the next problem. At 1 second, any breeze blurs the leaves. Here is a worked example. On an overcast morning the camera meters f/11, 1 second, ISO 100 with the polariser on, and the leaves are moving.

1. You want about 1/15 s, which is four stops faster: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8 → 1/15
2. Open the aperture one stop, from f/11 to f/8
3. Raise the ISO three stops, from 100 to 200, 400, then 800
4. One stop plus three stops is four, so f/8, 1/15 s, ISO 800 gives the same exposure

If the leaves are only stirring, wait for a lull between gusts instead and keep the lower ISO.

## The method in the field

1. Arrive early and walk for a few minutes without the camera out. Look before you shoot
2. Find one subject: a tree, a gap, a path
3. Start with the longer lens and widen only if the picture needs it
4. Set up the tripod and keep the camera level so trunks stay vertical
5. Check the top of the frame for bright patches of sky. Lower the camera or reframe until they are gone
6. Fit the polariser and turn it slowly, watching the glare on the leaves come and go
7. Set f/8 to f/11 and focus on the subject
8. Set the exposure, adding compensation in mist, and fire with the remote or the 2-second timer
9. Check the histogram and the leaves at full magnification, then go again

## Colour

Light that has come through a canopy can pick up a green tint, and mist can turn blue under automatic white balance. Shoot RAW so you can correct it later. In autumn, be careful not to push warm colours too far: orange beech leaves are already strong.

## Common mistakes

- **Too much in the frame.** Use a longer lens and build the picture around one tree
- **Bright sky at the top.** Small white patches pull the eye. Tilt down or move until they are gone
- **Leaning trunks.** Keep the camera level
- **Blurred leaves.** Raise the ISO, open the aperture, or wait for a lull
- **Grey mist.** Add exposure compensation
- **Dappled sun.** Wait for cloud, or come back on another day
- **Too much polariser.** At full strength it can strip all the sheen from leaves and flatten them. Turn it back a little

## Seasons

- **Spring:** fresh, pale green leaves, and bluebells, which peak in late April and May
- **Summer:** a full canopy and deep shade. Best on overcast days
- **Autumn:** colour usually peaks in late October
- **Winter:** bare trees show their structure, and frost or snow simplifies the floor

## Going further

- **Intentional camera movement,** moving the camera along the line of the trunks during the exposure
- **Long exposure** on a burn running through the wood
- **Black and white,** to show shape and structure without the distraction of colour
- **One wood through the year,** returning to the same tree each season

> Look for one tree, not the whole wood.
lessons.challenge: Go into a wood on an overcast day with a longer lens. Make five photographs, each built around a single tree. Squint at each scene before you shoot it.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Why does mist help woodland photographs?
* Each row of trees fades more, separating the layers
- It makes the colours brighter
- It allows faster shutter speeds

Q: What is the hardest light in a wood?
* Bright sun breaking through the canopy
- Soft overcast light
- Mist on a still morning

Q: Why use a longer lens in a wood?
* To pick out a small, tidy scene from the clutter
- To fit more of the wood in
- To make the trunks lean

Q: The meter reads 1 second at f/11, ISO 100, and the leaves are moving. Which settings give the same exposure at about 1/15 s?
* f/8 at ISO 800
- f/16 at ISO 200
- f/11 at ISO 200

lessons.title: Seascapes
lessons.summary: Waves, tides and wet rock. Read the sea before you shoot it, time the picture to the water, and keep yourself and your kit safe from it.
lessons.body:
The coast changes every few seconds and every few hours. Waves break and draw back, and the tide uncovers rock and pools, then floods them again. A seascape works when you read those changes and time the picture to them.

## Safety first

The sea is the one landscape subject that can come to you.

- **Check the tide table before you go.** Know the time of high and low water, and whether the tide is rising or falling while you are there
- **Never turn your back on the sea.** Waves arrive in sets, and a larger one can follow a quiet spell
- **Treat wet rock as ice.** Seaweed and the green film on rock near the waterline are slippery. Step on dry, rough rock where you can
- **Know your way off.** A rising tide can cut you off on a headland, a sandbar or a causeway. Lindisfarne's causeway floods twice a day, and people are still caught on it. Note your exit and leave while it is still dry
- **Stay back from cliff edges.** Edges can be undercut and grass can hide a drop. Never back up while looking through the camera
- In the UK, if someone is in trouble at the coast, call 999 and ask for the Coastguard

## Tides

On most British coasts there are two high tides and two low tides a day, a little over six hours apart. They come later each day, so yesterday's timing will not work today.

- **Low tide** exposes rock shelves, pools, ripples in the sand and long reaches of wet beach. It gives you foreground
- **High tide** brings the waves up against cliffs and rocks. It gives you energy and spray, but less room to stand
- **The hours in between** give water running around rocks, with somewhere safe to stand

The size of the tide changes through the month. **Spring tides**, around new and full moon, have the biggest range: the highest highs and the lowest lows. **Neap tides**, in between, have the smallest. A spring high tide reaches further up the beach than you expect.

[[photo:Reflections and Shadows]]

The wet sand mirrors the sunlit peaks under a grey and blue sky, so the mountains appear twice.

## Reading the waves

Watch for a few minutes before you take a frame.

1. Count the waves in a few sets. Note how far the biggest ones reach, and stand well back from that line
2. Find where the water does something interesting, such as running back off a rock or spreading over flat sand
3. Compose for that spot, then wait
4. Fire as a wave draws back, not as it arrives. The retreating water leaves lines and trails pointing into the frame
5. Shoot in bursts. No two waves are the same, and the best frame is often the third or fourth of a run

## Shutter speed for water

The shutter speed decides what the water looks like.

- **1/500 s or faster:** freezes spray and the curl of a breaking wave. Every drop is sharp
- **1/8 s to 1/2 s:** the backwash turns to fine white streaks while the wave keeps some shape
- **Longer:** the sea softens to mist. That belongs to the Long exposure lesson, which covers ND filters and timing in full

A worked example. On an overcast day the camera meters **f/11, 1/125 s, ISO 100**.

1. To freeze spray, you need 1/500 s, two stops faster: 1/125, 1/250, 1/500. Open two stops to f/5.6, or keep f/11 and raise the ISO two stops to 400
2. For backwash trails, fit a 6-stop ND filter at f/11. Six doublings of 1/125 s is 1/125 × 64, which is about 0.5 s

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Manual or shutter priority, because the shutter speed decides how the water looks
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; open to f/5.6 if needed to reach a freezing speed
- **Shutter speed:** 1/500 s to 1/1000 s to freeze spray; 1/8 s to 1/2 s for backwash streaks
- **ISO:** 100 for slow water; 400 or higher to reach 1/500 s or faster in dull light
- **Focal length:** 16 mm to 35 mm full frame for foreground rock; longer to pick out one wave
- **Filter:** 3-stop to 6-stop ND for backwash streaks; a polariser cuts glare but costs one to two stops

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Composition

A wide view of the sea is mostly flat water. Give it structure.

- **Foreground.** Rocks, pebbles, a pool or ribbed sand, close to the lens on a wide angle, give the eye a way in
- **Lines from the water.** Backwash running between rocks, the edge of a wave on the sand, or a channel draining at low tide all lead into the frame
- **A level horizon.** A tilted sea looks as if it is draining out of the picture. Use the level in the camera, and see the Where to put the horizon lesson for how high to place it
- **Scale.** A figure on the rocks or a building on the shore tells the viewer how big the cliffs and waves are

[[photo:Lofoten shore]]

Dark rock curves up from the foreground and leads the eye along the beach to the sunlit peak under heavy cloud.

[[photo:South Uist]]

A small stone building stands on the grass above the water, with hills behind. It gives the water and the hills a sense of scale.

## Light

The best coastal light is usually low.

- **Low sun** in the first and last hours lights the faces of cliffs and lays colour on the water
- **Side light** across rock brings out texture that vanishes at midday
- **Stormy days** give dark skies, rough water and short breaks of sun. Wait for the break, then work quickly
- **Backlit sea**, with the sun in front, turns spray and wave tops to glowing edges. See the Shooting into the sun lesson

The hard part is matching good light with a good tide. Check both before you go.

[[guide:planner]]

## Polariser

A polariser cuts the glare on wet rock, so its real colour shows, and it reduces the reflections on the surface of the water. Turn it slowly and watch the effect, because it changes with the angle to the sun. It also costs one to two stops of light. I use a Kase polariser.

Be careful on wet sand. Turned fully, a polariser can remove the very reflection you came for. See the Filters lesson for how it works.

## Kit care

Spray dries to a salty film that softens every frame and, left alone, damages kit.

- **Check the glass between frames.** Salt shows as soft, hazy patches. A lens hood keeps some of it off
- **Wipe gently.** Use a clean microfibre cloth. Do not rub dry salt or sand grains hard across glass
- **Change lenses away from the spray,** with your back to the wind
- **Rinse the tripod legs in fresh water** after standing in the sea. Salt left in the joints corrodes them
- **Keep sand out of the leg locks.** Open and clean any lock that feels gritty before it grinds

## Worked scenarios

- **Rock shelf at low tide.** An hour after low water on a rising tide, set the tripod low behind a pool. At f/11, ISO 100 on a dull day the meter reads 1/30 s. Fit a 3-stop filter: 1/30 × 8 = 8/30, about 1/4 s. Fire as each wave draws back over the shelf
- **Waves against a cliff at high tide.** From a safe height, use 1/1000 s at f/8, raising the ISO if needed, and shoot bursts as each set arrives
- **Wet sand at sunset.** Expose for the bright sky in the reflection, and fire as the water slides back

## Common mistakes

- **Soft pictures.** Salt on the glass. Check and wipe between frames
- **A sinking tripod.** Waves wash sand from under the feet. Push the legs well in and check the horizon after each wave
- **Getting caught by a wave.** You were watching the screen. Look up between every frame

## Checking in camera

1. Zoom in on the foreground rocks to check for salt haze or tripod movement
2. Read the histogram. White water clips easily, so keep the right edge clear except for small spray highlights
3. Look at the horizon line on the screen against the edge of the frame

## Going further

- **Long exposures** of the same rocks, to turn the sea to mist. See the Long exposure lesson
- **Reflections** in wet sand and pools. See the Reflections lesson
- **Telephoto seascapes,** picking out a single breaking wave or a sea stack from a distance. See the Telephoto landscapes lesson

> Watch the sea before you photograph it. It will tell you where to stand and when.
lessons.challenge: Check the tide table and pick a rocky shore on a falling tide. Watch three sets of waves before you set up. Then take the same composition at 1/500 s, 1/8 s and 1/2 s, firing each as a wave draws back, and compare how the water reads.
lessons.quiz:
Q: The camera meters f/11, 1/125 s, ISO 100. You want 1/500 s to freeze spray. Which change gets you there?
* Open the aperture two stops to f/5.6
- Open the aperture one stop to f/8
- Raise the ISO to 200

Q: When are tides at their biggest range?
* Spring tides, around new and full moon
- Neap tides, around new and full moon
- Spring tides, only in spring

Q: When is the best moment to fire for lines of water leading into the frame?
* As a wave draws back
- As a wave arrives
- In the flat calm between sets

Q: You fit a 6-stop ND filter to a metered 1/125 s. Roughly what is the new shutter speed?
* About 1/2 s
- About 1/20 s
- About 8 seconds

lessons.title: Macro
lessons.summary: Close enough that a drop of dew becomes a landscape. Depth of field shrinks to millimetres, so focus and stillness become everything.
lessons.body:
True macro means reproducing the subject at life size or larger on the sensor, a ratio of 1:1. A 10 mm beetle covers 10 mm of sensor. At that scale, the ordinary rules of focus and light stop applying in the way you are used to.

[[guide:focus]]

## What you need

- **A macro lens,** or a cheaper way to get close (see Equipment below)
- **A tripod** that goes low, or a focusing rail, which moves the camera forwards and back in fine steps
- **A remote release,** or the 2-second self-timer
- **A diffuser and a small reflector,** to soften and fill the light
- **Something to block the wind,** such as your body, a bag or a sheet of card

## The depth of field problem

At life size, depth of field is tiny. On a full-frame camera at f/8 only about a millimetre of the subject is sharp. At f/2.8 it is about a third of a millimetre, barely the thickness of a petal.

You can work it out. A common approximation for the total depth of field is 2 × f-number × 0.03 mm × (magnification + 1) ÷ magnification², where 0.03 mm is the usual full-frame standard for acceptable sharpness.

- **At 1:1 and f/8:** 2 × 8 × 0.03 × 2 ÷ 1 = 0.96 mm, about a millimetre
- **At 1:1 and f/2.8:** 2 × 2.8 × 0.03 × 2 ÷ 1 = 0.336 mm, about a third of a millimetre
- **At half life size (0.5×) and f/8:** 2 × 8 × 0.03 × 1.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2.88 mm, three times as much

Backing off a little is often the easiest way to get more of the subject sharp.

Closing the aperture helps, but only up to a point. Beyond about f/16 diffraction starts to soften the whole image. f/8 to f/11 is the usual compromise.

## Light loss up close

As a lens focuses closer, less light reaches the sensor. The effective aperture is roughly the f-number × (1 + magnification). At 1:1, f/8 behaves like f/8 × 2 = f/16. That is two stops less light. Through-the-lens metering allows for it automatically, but it is one more reason shutter speeds drop and diffraction arrives earlier than the f-number suggests.

## Focusing

- Set the focus manually and move the camera, not the focus ring
- Line the sensor up parallel with the most important plane of the subject, such as a wing or the face of a flower
- On an insect, the eyes must be sharp. Nothing else matters as much

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority on a tripod; manual when using flash
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; beyond f/16 diffraction softens everything, so stack instead
- **Shutter speed:** On a tripod, whatever the meter gives; handheld without flash, 1/250 s or faster
- **ISO:** ISO 100 to 400 on a tripod; 800 to 1600 handheld if the shutter is too slow
- **Focal length:** 90 mm to 105 mm macro lens (full frame) for a comfortable working distance
- **Focus:** Manual focus set to the magnification, then move the camera until the eyes are sharp
- **Drive:** 2-second timer or remote, with electronic first-curtain shutter if available

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## The method in the field

1. Find a subject sheltered from the wind
2. Set up low and make a rough composition
3. Turn the focus ring to the magnification you want, then leave it
4. Move the camera, or the rail, until the most important part is sharp
5. Line the sensor up with the subject's main plane
6. Set f/8 to f/11
7. On a tripod, turn off image stabilisation, unless your lens is designed to detect a tripod
8. Use the remote or the 2-second timer, and the electronic first-curtain or electronic shutter if your camera has one, to avoid vibration
9. Wait for a lull in the wind, then fire
10. Zoom in to check, then go again

## Focus stacking

Take a series of frames, each focused a little further into the subject, then blend them in software so the whole thing is sharp. It needs a still subject, a tripod and no wind. Many modern cameras can shoot the series for you.

Work out the number of frames before you start. Say the subject is 10 mm deep and you are at 1:1 and f/8, with about 1 mm in focus per frame. Step the focus about 0.5 mm each time so the sharp zones overlap. 10 ÷ 0.5 = 20 frames.

To blend them in Photoshop, load the frames as layers (from Lightroom: Edit In, Open as Layers in Photoshop). Select all the layers, choose Edit, Auto-Align Layers, then Edit, Auto-Blend Layers, and pick Stack Images.

## Light

Soft light suits most small subjects. An overcast sky is ideal. In sun, hold a diffuser between the sun and the subject, and use a small reflector to lift the shadows. A flash with a diffuser lets you work handheld, because its short burst freezes both your movement and the subject's.

The background matters as much as the subject. The further the background is behind the subject, the softer it goes. A small move to one side can put a dark, plain area behind the subject instead of a bright, busy one.

[[photo:Dahlia]]

A single dahlia against a garden that has dissolved into soft green and grey. The background is far behind the flower, so it carries no detail to compete with the petals.

## Equipment

A dedicated macro lens of 90 to 105 mm gives 1:1 and a comfortable working distance, so you do not scare insects or shade the subject. Close-up filters and extension tubes are cheaper ways to get close with lenses you already own.

- **Extension tubes** fit between the camera and the lens. With the lens focused at infinity, the magnification is the extension ÷ the focal length. A 25 mm tube on a 50 mm lens gives 25 ÷ 50 = 0.5×, half life size
- **Close-up filters** screw on the front and are rated in dioptres. With the lens at infinity, a +4 dioptre filter focuses at 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 m

## When to go

Early morning is best. The air is still, dew is on everything, and insects are cold and slow until the sun warms them up.

## Checking in camera

- Zoom in to full magnification on the most important part, such as the eyes
- Check the background for bright spots that pull the eye
- Look at the histogram. White petals clip easily
- For a stack, check that the first frame is sharp at the front of the subject and the last at the back

## Common mistakes

- **Focusing with the ring at 1:1.** It changes the magnification and the framing. Move the camera instead
- **f/22 for more depth.** Diffraction softens everything. Stay at f/8 to f/11 and stack
- **Wind.** Shield the subject, or wait
- **Your own shadow.** Check where the light is coming from before you lean in
- **Ghosts in a stack.** If the subject moves during the series, the blend shows halos. Shoot fewer frames, faster, or wait for stiller air
- **Disturbing the subject.** Do not move insects or damage plants for a picture

## Going further

- **Focus stacking on a rail,** for larger and deeper subjects
- **Flash macro,** for insects that will not keep still
- **Abstract macro,** using water drops, frost and textures that stop looking like anything recognisable
- **Beyond 1:1,** with specialist lenses that go to several times life size

> At this scale, a breath of wind is an earthquake.
