lessons.quiz:
Q: What does a 1:1 reproduction ratio mean?
* The subject appears life size on the sensor
- The subject fills the whole frame
- The lens is 100 mm long

Q: Why not just use f/22 for more depth of field?
* Diffraction softens the whole image
- f/22 lets in too much light
- Macro lenses do not go that far

Q: On an insect, what must be sharp?
* The eyes
- The legs
- The background

Q: A subject is 10 mm deep and you move the focus 0.5 mm between frames. How many frames do you need?
* 20
- 5
- 50

lessons.title: Abstract
lessons.summary: Take away the context and a photograph stops being of something. It becomes shape, line, colour and texture. Composition matters more, not less.
lessons.body:
An abstract photograph does not ask the viewer to recognise what it shows. It works on shape, line, colour, tone and texture alone. The subject can be anything: peeling paint, sand ripples, a reflection, the corner of a building.

[[guide:crop]]

## Get closer

The easiest way into abstraction is to remove context. Move in or zoom in until the frame holds only part of the subject. A whole boat is a boat. A curve of its hull against a stripe of water is a composition.

[[photo:angel]]

The Angel of the North, cropped until it is mostly line and tone. Without the whole figure, the ribs and the diagonal of the wing become the subject.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority
- **Aperture:** Widest available, such as f/2.8, for fields of soft colour; f/8 for flat textures shot square on
- **Shutter speed:** 1/500 s to 1/1000 s to freeze reflections into hard ribbons; around 1/15 s to smooth them
- **ISO:** 100 to 400; raise it only if the handheld shutter speed drops too low
- **Focal length:** 70 mm to 200 mm full frame, for picking small compositions out of a larger scene
- **Picture style:** Monochrome preview while shooting RAW, so the file keeps its colour

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Look for the elements

- **Line:** cracks, edges, cables, the boundary between two colours
- **Shape:** repeated forms, a single strong silhouette
- **Colour:** two colours side by side, or one colour in many shades
- **Texture:** rust, bark, stone, frost, best shown by light raking across from the side
- **Tone:** blocks of light and dark, especially in black and white

## Where to look

- **Industrial areas and harbours:** rust, peeling paint, coiled rope, stacked containers
- **Modern buildings:** glass, repeated windows, the line where two facades meet
- **The shore:** sand ripples, layers in rock, foam patterns left by a wave
- **Woods and gardens:** bark, frost on leaves, the veins of a single leaf
- **Indoors:** light through a blind, the curve of a glass, water in a sink

The same place gives different pictures as the light moves. A wall that looks flat at noon can show every crack when the sun is low and to one side.

## How to see it

Abstraction starts before the camera comes out. A few habits help.

- **Name the element, not the object.** Not "a wall" but "a pale diagonal crack across rust". If you can name it that way, you can frame it
- **Squint.** Detail drops away and the shapes and tones are left
- **Use a longer lens to scan.** Zooming in on a building, a hillside or a harbour shows small compositions you cannot pick out by eye
- **Preview in black and white.** Set a monochrome picture style. If you shoot RAW, the file keeps its colour, but the screen shows only tone and shape
- **Turn it round.** If it still works on its side or upside down, it does not depend on the subject

## The rules still apply

Without a recognisable subject, balance, contrast and placement carry the whole image. Thirds, leading lines and negative space all still work. A weak abstract is usually just a weak composition with nothing to hide behind.

[[photo:Triangle]]

Buildings seen from below frame a triangle of pale sky. The windows give texture, but the picture is the shape of the gap.

## Worked scenarios

**A peeling wall.** Wait until the light rakes across it from the side, so every flake throws a shadow. Stand square to the wall so the whole surface is at the same distance and stays sharp at f/8. Find one boundary, such as old paint meeting new, and place it on a third. Move in until nothing tells you it is a wall.

**Reflections in a harbour.** Use a longer lens on the water below brightly painted boats. Fast shutter speeds freeze the reflections into hard-edged ribbons of colour. Slower ones, around 1/15 s, smooth them into soft bands. Take both and compare.

**Looking up between buildings.** Stand where two or three buildings meet and point the camera straight up. The sky becomes a shape cut out by the walls. Turn the camera until that shape sits cleanly in the frame.

**A field of soft colour.** Open the lens to its widest aperture, focus on something close, and let everything behind it melt into colour. Move until one sharp edge sits against the blur. For the same subject size, a longer lens gives a softer background than a wide one at the same aperture.

**Sand ripples.** Go out when the sun is low, so each ripple has a lit side and a shadow side. Shoot from above, looking down, so there is no horizon to give scale.

## Ways to make one

- Shoot reflections in water, glass or polished metal
- Use a very shallow depth of field so most of the frame is soft colour
- Move the camera during the exposure (see the lesson on ICM)
- Turn the camera so the viewer cannot tell which way is up

[[photo:Cathedral in motion]]

Vertical streaks run through the trees and the spires. The detail has gone, but the shapes and the warm light on the stone survive.

## Checking in camera

- **Look at it small.** If it works at the size of the screen thumbnail, it will work large
- **Check the edges.** One recognisable object at the edge, a door handle or a sign, pulls the picture back to being of something
- **Check the tones.** The histogram shows whether you have real blocks of light and dark or just a mid grey mass
- **Rotate it later.** Try all four orientations in the edit. One is often clearly stronger

## Common mistakes

- **Half abstract.** The subject is still recognisable, so it reads as a poor record of a thing. Go closer, or step back and make it a proper record
- **No structure.** Everything has equal weight and the eye has nowhere to go. Find one dominant line, shape or tone
- **Relying on an effect.** Blur or shallow focus alone is not a picture. There still has to be a shape underneath
- **Too many elements.** Two or three things working together are stronger than six competing

## Titles

A title can open an abstract up or close it down. "Untitled" leaves it entirely to the viewer. Naming what it is can spoil the puzzle. Choose deliberately.

## Going further

- **A series,** on one theme, colour or material, so the pictures explain each other
- **Pairs,** setting two abstracts side by side that echo in shape or colour
- **Black and white,** where tone and texture carry everything
- **ICM and macro,** two other routes into abstraction, each with its own lesson

> Stop asking what it is. Ask whether it works.
lessons.challenge: Spend an hour photographing one ordinary object, such as a bike, a wall or a boat, without ever showing the whole thing. At home, rotate each frame through all four orientations and keep the strongest.
lessons.quiz:
Q: What is the easiest way into abstraction?
* Remove context by moving or zooming in
- Use a wider lens
- Add more elements to the frame

Q: Which light best shows texture?
* Light raking across from the side
- Flat light from behind the camera
- Light from directly overhead at noon

Q: Do composition rules apply to abstract photographs?
* Yes, more than ever
- No, anything goes
- Only the rule of thirds

Q: Why set a monochrome picture style while looking for abstracts?
* The screen shows only tone and shape, while a RAW file keeps its colour
- It makes the lens sharper
- It permanently removes colour from RAW files

lessons.title: City breaks
lessons.summary: Two or three days, a lot of famous places and no time to wait for the light. Travel light, plan around the sun, and look beyond the postcard.
lessons.body:
A city break gives you two or three days, a long list of famous places and very little time to wait for the light. My wife and I go on city breaks. Good pictures from a weekend like that come down to three things: a light bag, a short plan built around the light, and a lot of walking.

## Light kit

You will be on your feet from before sunrise until after dark. Everything you carry, you carry all day.

- **One body and one general zoom.** Something covering roughly 24 to 70 mm on full frame handles streets, interiors and most landmarks. Add a wide lens only if your list is full of interiors
- **A small tripod.** In cities I use a Peak Design carbon-fibre tripod, because it is lighter and quicker to set up
- **A pocket camera.** Mine is a Leica D-Lux 8. It is truly pocket-sized, its monochrome mode is brilliant, and it is great for street, so it comes out when a big camera would draw attention
- **Spare batteries and cards,** and comfortable shoes

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority by day; manual on the tripod at blue hour and indoors
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11 for landmarks and tripod shots; f/4 or wider for handheld interiors
- **Shutter speed:** 1/30 s or faster handheld indoors; several seconds on the tripod, such as 10 s
- **ISO:** Lowest native ISO, usually 100, on the tripod; 400 to 1600 handheld indoors
- **Focal length:** 24 to 70 mm full frame for most scenes; around 16 mm for interiors
- **Stabilisation:** On when handheld, off when the camera is on the tripod

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Planning a shot list

Without a list, a weekend becomes the same postcard views everyone else takes. Use four headings:

- **Landmarks:** the two or three places the city is known for
- **Details:** doors, tiles, signs, ironwork, street names, textures
- **People:** markets, cafes, crossings, buskers, the life of the place
- **Night:** a viewpoint, a lit street, a bridge or a waterfront

Then put each landmark on a map and note which way it faces. A facade facing east is lit at sunrise; one facing west catches the evening. Group nearby places together, so each morning and evening has one area, not five.

## Early starts

Around sunrise, cities are empty. The light is low and soft, and nobody is standing in front of the landmark.

Sunrise moves a long way through the year. In the UK it comes before 5 am in midsummer and after 8 am in December, so a winter city break makes early starts far easier. Look up the times before you go, and aim to be in place for the blue hour before sunrise, not the sunrise itself.

[[guide:planner]]

## Midday: interiors, shade and details

When the sun is high and hard, go inside. Stations, churches, museums and old stairwells have their own light. One of my brothers is an architect, which is probably why I notice the design of a building, and interiors are where that design is easiest to see.

Outside, work in the shade. Narrow streets, courtyards and the shady side of a square give soft, even light for details: a painted door, a tiled step, a sign, a pattern of windows.

[[photo:Green Staircase]]

Green glazed steps, tiled walls and polished wooden rails, with two flights splitting left and right. Shot at 16 mm, f/11 and 10 seconds at ISO 50, on a tripod, from dead centre.

For more on lines, verticals and standing in the middle, see the Architecture lesson.

## Blue hour and night

The evening blue hour is the second fixed point of the day. Be at your night location before sunset, set up, and shoot as the sky darkens and the lights come on. The useful window is short, so do not plan two night locations far apart. The Night and blue hour in cities lesson covers exposure, white balance and timing in detail.

[[photo:Speicherstadt balconies]]

After dark in Hamburg's Speicherstadt. A column of lit, curved balconies climbs the red brick, floor after floor. Straight on and dead centre.

## Famous landmarks, seen fresh

Everyone has the postcard. Three ways to make your own picture:

- **Change the angle.** Go lower, higher, round the side or further back with a long lens. Use a gap between buildings as a frame
- **Include the context.** Show what stands next to it, the street in front, the weather over it. A landmark among its neighbours says more about the city than one cut out on its own
- **Add a human element.** A passer-by, a cyclist, a statue or a crowd gives scale and a story

[[photo:Fab4 and Liver Birds]]

The Beatles stride along Liverpool's Pier Head, with a Liver Bird watching from the top of the Royal Liver Building. The tower is the landmark, but the four bronze figures in front make it a picture of the city rather than of a building.

## Tripods and courtesy

- **Check before you go.** Many cathedrals, museums, galleries, stations and some viewpoints ban tripods or need a permit. The venue's website usually says so
- **Keep walkways clear.** Set up against a wall or railing, keep the legs tucked in, and stay off steps, doorways and narrow pavements
- **Fold it when asked.** If staff say no, the answer is no
- **Have a plan without it.** Brace against a pillar, rest the camera on a wall, and raise the ISO

## Photographing people

The Street lesson covers zone focusing and respect in detail. On a city break, add a few points. Some countries give people stronger rights over their own image than the UK does, so check the rules where you are going. Do not photograph inside places of worship during services. If you want a portrait of a stallholder or a busker, ask, and show them the picture.

## Weather

- **Overcast** gives soft, even light. It suits details, interiors, street and black and white. Leave flat white sky out of the frame, or let it become a plain backdrop
- **Rain** gives reflections in puddles and wet pavements, umbrellas, and colour from lit signs after dark
- **Bright sun** gives hard shadows. Use them for graphic street pictures, and save the interiors for later

If the forecast shows one wet day and one dry one, put the landmarks on the dry day and the interiors and reflections on the wet one.

## A simple day plan

1. Blue hour and sunrise: your main landmark, with the streets empty
2. Early morning: walk the old streets while the low sun lights the facades
3. Mid-morning: markets and people, as the city wakes up
4. Midday: interiors, shade and details. Rest, eat and charge batteries
5. Late afternoon: street, as the light lowers and the shadows lengthen
6. Sunset and blue hour: your night location, on the tripod
7. After dark: lit streets, handheld, with the pocket camera

## Worked scenarios

**A cathedral that bans tripods.** The camera meters the nave at f/8, 1/4 s, ISO 400. You can hold 1/30 s steadily. From 1/4 s to 1/30 s is three stops (1/8, 1/15, 1/30). Open the aperture two stops to f/4, and you need one more stop from the ISO: 400 doubles to 800. Settings: f/4, 1/30 s, ISO 800.

**A landmark crowded at midday.** Take a detail with a longer lens, such as a carving or a window, and put the wide view on the list for tomorrow's sunrise.

## Common mistakes

- **Too many places.** You spend the weekend travelling between them. Pick fewer and stay longer
- **The postcard at midday.** The worst light and the biggest crowds. Move it to the morning
- **Only landmarks.** The details and the people are what make a set feel like a place
- **A tripod in the way.** Keep it tight to a wall, and fold it when people need to pass

## Checking your results

Check each evening, not just at home. Zoom in on handheld interior shots to make sure they are sharp, and look at the histogram on night frames, because the screen looks brighter in the dark than the picture is. Tick off the shot list, move anything you missed to tomorrow, and back up the cards before you sleep.

## Going further

- **A set of twelve.** Edit the weekend down to twelve photographs that tell the story of the city: landmarks, details, people and night
- **The same city in another season,** with different light, different sunrise times and a different crowd
- **Planning,** using the Planning a photography trip lesson to read the weather and the sun before you book

> Get up early, carry less, and look up.
lessons.challenge: On your next city break, write a shot list with two landmarks, five details, three people pictures and one night view. Photograph one landmark at sunrise and again at midday from the same spot, then compare the light and the crowds.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Which four headings make a balanced city shot list?
* Landmarks, details, people and night
- Sunrise, sunset, rain and sun
- Wide, standard, telephoto and macro

Q: A nave meters at f/8, 1/4 s, ISO 400 and tripods are banned. You open to f/4 and want 1/30 s. What ISO do you need?
* ISO 800
- ISO 3200
- ISO 200

Q: What is the best use of hard midday sun on a city break?
* Interiors, and details in the shade
- Wide views of the main landmark
- Long exposures of the skyline

Q: Where should a tripod go in a busy public place?
* Against a wall or railing, legs tucked in, clear of steps and doorways
- In the middle of the pavement, where the view is best
- On the steps, where it is out of the crowd's line of sight

lessons.title: Found details
lessons.summary: Street art, signs, worn surfaces and the small things everyone walks past. Slow down, get close, and let a detail carry the whole picture.
lessons.body:
Every town is full of small things nobody looks at: a painted door, a hand-lettered sign, a ledge of rusting spikes. Found detail photography is about noticing them, then isolating them so other people notice too. The work is in the looking.

## Learning to notice

Most people walk a street at eye level and at speed. Change either.

- **Slow down.** Walk at half your usual pace and stop often
- **Look down.** Drain covers, kerbstones, road markings, cobbles
- **Look up.** Ironwork, old shop names above modern fronts, faded painted adverts, spikes on ledges
- **Take the side street.** Back lanes and service doors carry more paint, wear and repair than the main street
- **Check doorways and ledges.** Doors collect layers of paint, stickers and scratched names

Walk the same short route more than once. The third pass finds what the first missed.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, so depth of field stays under control as you move between details
- **Aperture:** About f/4 to f/5.6 for details with depth; f/8 to f/11 for flat signs and murals shot square-on
- **Shutter speed:** 1/125 s to 1/500 s handheld; use the faster end at longer focal lengths
- **ISO:** 100 to 800; shaded lanes and overcast streets often need the upper end
- **Focal length:** 50 mm to 100 mm full frame; at 50 mm, stand 1.4 m from a 1 m sign
- **Focus:** Single point on the detail; for a wall shot at an angle, a third of the way in

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## Isolating the detail

A detail only works if the viewer sees it as clearly as you did, so remove everything else.

1. **Move closer.** Most first attempts are taken from where you first noticed the thing. Take three more steps
2. **Use a longer focal length.** It picks one detail out of a busy wall, or reaches a sign across a road
3. **Use a shallow depth of field** when the detail has depth, such as spikes or a door handle, so what is in front and behind goes soft
4. **Fill the frame.** If an edge adds nothing, crop in with your feet or the zoom

A worked example for reach. A full-frame sensor is 36 mm wide. To fill the width of the frame with a sign 1 m wide, stand at 1 m × focal length ÷ 36. At 50 mm that is 1 × 50 ÷ 36, about 1.4 m away. At 100 mm it is 1 × 100 ÷ 36, about 2.8 m. Double the focal length and you can stand twice as far back.

[[photo:Spikey]]

Metal spikes set into a ledge in Liverpool, there to stop pigeons landing. The nearest and farthest spikes fall soft, so the eye settles on the row in between.

## Light

- **Overcast light** is even and shadowless. It suits murals, signs and painted surfaces, because colour and lettering are recorded without hard shadows cutting across them
- **Side light,** low sun raking across a surface, throws every crack, chip and brushstroke into relief. It suits rough stone, peeling paint, rust and carved lettering
- **Direct frontal sun** is usually the weakest. It flattens texture and adds glare on gloss paint

Note which way a surface faces and come back when the light skims it.

## Shooting flat artwork square-on

A flat painting, sign or poster should usually be photographed square-on. If the camera is tilted or off to one side, the rectangle turns into a tapering shape. This is called keystoning, and it makes flat art look as if it is falling away.

1. Stand opposite the centre of the work, with the lens level with that centre
2. Keep the back of the camera parallel to the surface, neither tilted up nor turned sideways
3. Turn on the grid and line its verticals up with the edges of the work
4. Use a moderate focal length rather than your widest, so straight edges near the frame stay straight
5. Check the two side edges are parallel before you press the shutter

If the art is high up, step back and zoom in rather than tilting the camera. Some lean can be fixed in editing. I sometimes straighten converging verticals with Lightroom's Transform tool, only when the photo calls for it. Correcting crops away part of the frame, so leave room at the edges.

## When an angle is better

Square-on suits a single piece. A long wall of names, a row of shutters or a repeating pattern can work better shot along its length, because the angle makes it recede and run on. Focus a third of the way in, and let the far end soften if that helps the sense of distance.

[[photo:Wall of Fame]]

The Wall of Fame on Mathew Street, Liverpool. Shot along the wall at an angle, the rows of names run on out of the frame, with visitors' own names scratched in between.

## Context or isolation

Isolating a detail does not mean removing every clue to where it is. A painted face cropped tight is about the painting. The same face with a strip of scratched stone and a few cobbles is about a painting on a street, worn by the people who pass it. That margin of surrounding wear often tells the story.

Keep surroundings that show age, use or place. Cut clutter. When in doubt, take both.

[[photo:Rotten]]

A painted portrait on a pair of doors in Liverpool, framed with the stone surround and the cobbles, so the running paint and the names scratched into the stone either side stay in the picture. The artist is unknown.

## Black and white for texture

Remove the colour and texture, shape and tone carry the picture. Rust, worn stone and flaking paint often get stronger in mono. Bright street art may not, because the colour may be the point. Sometimes I decide on the spot, when the textures are there. The Black and white lesson covers converting and judging tones.

## Humour and juxtaposition

Found details are often funny: a sign that contradicts what sits beside it, a "keep clear" notice with a bin parked in front of it. Look for two things that comment on each other, and frame tightly enough that the joke reads at once. For juxtapositions involving people, see the Street lesson.

## Respect

- **Credit street artists by name when you know it.** Many sign their work. When you do not know, say "artist unknown". Do not guess
- **Never claim the artwork as your own design.** Your photograph is your work. The painting in it is not. Copyright in a mural normally stays with the artist, so ask before using a photograph of one commercially. This is a general guide, not legal advice
- **Do not trespass.** If reaching it means crossing a fence or entering a derelict building, leave it

## Titles and series

A title can add what the picture cannot show: a place, a name, a twist. Keep it short and avoid repeating what is plainly visible. When the subject is someone else's artwork, keep your title and the credit separate.

A set of details becomes a project. Pick one subject, such as painted doors, pigeon spikes or old shop lettering, and photograph it the same way each time: same distance, same angle, same treatment. Nine or twelve consistent images hold together better than thirty mixed ones.

## Worked scenarios

**A mural across a busy road, in bright sun.** Come back on a dull day if you can. If not, stand directly opposite its centre, zoom in to fill the frame, keep the camera level and wait for a gap in the traffic.

**A tangle of rusted railings.** Too much is going on. Get close to one finial, open the aperture to about f/4 and let the rest blur into a pattern behind it.

## Common mistakes

- **Keystoned artwork.** The camera was tilted. Level it, step back and zoom
- **Flat texture.** The light is behind you. Come back when it rakes across the surface
- **Glare on gloss paint or glass.** Move a step to one side, or use a polariser. See the Filters lesson
- **All context cropped away.** Leave a little surrounding wear

## Checking your results

Zoom in to check the texture or lettering is sharp. For flat work, compare the side edges with the frame edges. Check the histogram so the brightest paint is not clipped.

## Going further

- **Abstract,** when the detail stops being of something and becomes shape and colour. See the Abstract lesson
- **Macro,** for details smaller than a coin. See the Macro lesson
- **Revisiting** the same wall over months as it is painted over, weathered and painted again

> The picture was always there. You just had to stop walking.

lessons.title: Behind the shot: Deadvlei
lessons.summary: Flooded roads, a barefoot wade and a quiet spell before the crowds. One photograph and how it was made.
lessons.body:
[[shot:first-light]]

## Why I was there

We were in Namibia on a photography holiday with the brilliant James Kerwin. Most of the trip was urbex: abandoned villages slowly being reclaimed by the sand. Deadvlei was the big landscape stop.

## Getting there

Saying it was easy would be a lie. Heavy rain had flooded the roads, and parts of them were close to impassable. Somehow the four-by-fours pushed through rivers of muddy water, and we got there just as the sun was about to come up over the dunes.

We parked, took off our shoes and socks, and waded across more flooded ground, the wet sand shifting under our feet, to reach the trees. Then we set up and started shooting.

## The moment

We had a good stretch of time before the sun cleared the dunes. It was the best part of the morning: the light was still workable, the trees threw long shadows across the pan, and the crowds hadn't arrived yet.

Once the sun was fully up, the light turned very bright and the best of it was gone.

## How I shot it

The pan itself was dry: just crusty, sun-baked ground, despite all the water we had waded through to get there.

This was taken in that early window. The first sun is catching the tree, while the dune behind it is still in shadow.

I shot it on the tripod at 400 mm. The honest reason for the long lens was practical. Standing well back meant I didn't have to walk into the scene and end up in someone else's photograph. With a group of photographers all working the same trees, that matters.

It also changes the picture. From that far back, the dune stops looking like a dune and becomes a plain dark backdrop that fills the frame behind the tree. The Telephoto landscapes lesson explains why.

The settings were f/10 at 1/100 s. With the tree and the dune both so far from the camera, f/10 was enough to keep everything sharp.

## Starting settings

- **Mode:** Aperture priority, or manual on a tripod in the early window
- **Aperture:** f/8 to f/11; f/10 is enough when the tree and the dune are both far away
- **Shutter speed:** 1/60 s to 1/250 s on a tripod in early light; 1/100 s worked here
- **ISO:** 100 to 400; start at the lowest and raise it only if wind moves the tree
- **Focal length:** 200 mm to 400 mm full frame, to stand back and turn the dune into a backdrop
- **Focus:** On the tree with magnified live view, then switch to manual
- **Exposure:** Expose for the sunlit tree and let the shaded dune fall dark

These are starting points. Take a frame, check the histogram, and adjust one thing at a time.

## In the edit

I can't remember exactly what I did to this one. Whatever it was, it will have been light. That's how I edit everything: Lightroom and a few small adjustments, nothing that changes what was there.
lessons.challenge: Next time you are somewhere busy, resist walking in closer. Step back, use a longer lens, and see what it does to the picture.
